video game strike") 2024 * [WGAW staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Writers_Guild_Staff_Union_Strike "2026 Writers Guild Staff Union Strike") 2026 |

From May 2 to September 27, 2023, the [Writers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America") (WGA)—representing 11,500 [screenwriters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriters "Screenwriters")[[2]](#cite_note-3)—went on [strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_action "Strike action") over a labor dispute with the [Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Motion_Picture_and_Television_Producers "Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers") (AMPTP).[[3]](#cite_note-Vox_2023-05-02-4)[[4]](#cite_note-wgacontract2023/on-strike-5) Lasting 148 days, the strike is tied with the [1960 strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike "1960 Writers Guild of America strike") as the second-longest labor stoppage actioned by the WGA, only behind the [1988 strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike "1988 Writers Guild of America strike") (153 days).[[5]](#cite_note-deadline/1235201504-6)[[6]](#cite_note-7) Alongside the [2023 SAG-AFTRA strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SAG-AFTRA_strike "2023 SAG-AFTRA strike"), which lasted between July and November, it was part of a series of [broader Hollywood labor disputes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Hollywood_labor_disputes "2023 Hollywood labor disputes"). Both strikes contributed to the biggest interruption to the American film and television industries since the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_television_in_the_United_States "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on television in the United States").

The strike caused significant economic impact: some studios halted ongoing or future productions or reduced some staff,[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-9)[[9]](#cite_note-10) while certain production agreements were jeopardized as some studios were able to use [force majeure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force_majeure "Force majeure") clauses to terminate those agreements.[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12) Strike action also affected other areas of the entertainment ecosystem,[[12]](#cite_note-13) including the VFX industry[[13]](#cite_note-14) and prop making studios.[[14]](#cite_note-15)

After a tentative agreement, union leadership voted to end the strike starting from September 27, 2023.[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[1]](#cite_note-end-1) On October 9, the WGA membership officially ratified the contract with 99% of WGA members voting in favor of it. The WGA secured increases to minimum wage, final compensation, pension and health fund rates, improvements to terms related to length of employment and size of writing teams, and increases to [residual payments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residual_(entertainment_industry) "Residual (entertainment industry)") for domestic and foreign [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") works. The union also secured regulation of [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence "Generative artificial intelligence") (AI), prohibiting exploitation of writers' material to train AI models, produce [digital recreations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_media "Synthetic media"), and efforts to use AI to reduce writers or their pay.[[16]](#cite_note-17)

## Issues in the strike

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Issues in the strike")]

[![A picketer is carrying a sign deriding film studios' proposals to replace writers with generative AI.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/AI_Protest_Sign_2023_WGA_Strike.jpg/250px-AI_Protest_Sign_2023_WGA_Strike.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AI_Protest_Sign_2023_WGA_Strike.jpg)

A picketer protesting against replacing writers with [generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence "Generative artificial intelligence")

One of the main points of disagreement between the writers and the producers was the [residuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residual_(entertainment_industry) "Residual (entertainment industry)") from [streaming media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media");[[17]](#cite_note-hollywoodreporter/1235404087-18) the WGA claimed that the AMPTP's share of such residuals had cut much of the writers' average incomes compared to a decade prior.[[18]](#cite_note-19)[[19]](#cite_note-20) Writers also wanted strict and harsh limits on [generative artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence "Generative artificial intelligence"), such as [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT"). They were willing to concede that writers themselves may have uses for such technology, but they demanded that the Agreement state that genAI would not be used to replace writers.[[20]](#cite_note-21)[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-auto1-23)

The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") and its aftermath saw major reductions in the workforce and [cancellations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancellation_(broadcasting) "Cancellation (broadcasting)") of multiple film and television projects to save money on basic residuals and music licensing costs, though Apple and Amazon remained outliers. The ensuing fall of "[Peak TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Television_(2000s–present) "Golden Age of Television (2000s–present)")" worsened conditions for all filmmaking workers, but due to their roles in development and pre-production, the first two steps in the filmmaking process, writers were hit fastest.[[23]](#cite_note-24)

On May 2, 2020, the latest Minimum Basic Agreement (MBA) became the collective bargaining agreement that covered most of the work done by WGA writers.[[24]](#cite_note-wga/contracts/mba-25)[[25]](#cite_note-sagaftra/wgaamptp/strike-26) The Minimum Basic Agreement was an agreement that established a minimum wage for television and film writers. In television, the Minimum Basic Agreement only applied to those who wrote for [broadcast television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_broadcasting "Television broadcasting") shows and not for [streaming television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_television "Streaming television"). This was very clear when comparing [late-night talk shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late-night_talk_show "Late-night talk show") that were produced for broadcast television, such as *[The Late Show with Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Late_Show_with_Stephen_Colbert "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert")* by [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), versus *[The Problem with Jon Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Problem_with_Jon_Stewart "The Problem with Jon Stewart")*, produced for streaming by [Apple TV+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_TV+ "Apple TV+"). The writers who worked for *The Problem* were not covered by the MBA and therefore had to negotiate individually with the streaming company for their pay, and as a result, they were paid less than writers who wrote for *The Late Show* while doing the same amount of work. This pattern held true with other shows in the two categories.[[3]](#cite_note-Vox_2023-05-02-4) The MBA expired on May 1, 2023.[[5]](#cite_note-deadline/1235201504-6)[[26]](#cite_note-wga/contracts/mba20-27)

The WGA estimated that its proposals would yield writers about US$429 million a year, whereas the AMPTP's offer would yield $86 million.[[3]](#cite_note-Vox_2023-05-02-4)[[27]](#cite_note-latimes/2023-05-02/newsletter-wga-strike-amptp-28)

One disputed issue is the Guild wanting requirements for "mandatory staffing" and "duration of employment" terms to be added to their contract, which would require all shows to be staffed with a minimum number of writers for a minimum amount of time, "whether needed or not" per the AMPTP.[[28]](#cite_note-LAist_2023-05-01-29)[[29]](#cite_note-WSJ_2023-05-03-30)

Another important proposal that the WGA is advocating for is to ensure each member of a writing team receives their own pension and their own health care funds. The AMPTP rejected this proposal and did not offer a counterproposal. At the same time, there was a tentative agreement between the WGA and AMPTP to have 0.5% of negotiated minimums for all WGA minimums shifted into pensions and health funds.[[22]](#cite_note-auto1-23)[[30]](#cite_note-2023-05-01_Variety-31)

## Timeline of negotiations and strike activity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Timeline of negotiations and strike activity")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Writers_Guild_of_America_strikers_outside_Warner_Brothers_Studios_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Writers_Guild_of_America_strikers_outside_Warner_Brothers_Studios_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Writers_Guild_of_America_strikers_outside_Warner_Brothers_Studios_(cropped).jpg)

A strike captain leads [WGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America") strikers outside [Warner Bros. Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Studios_Burbank "Warner Bros. Studios Burbank").

### April 2023

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: April 2023")]

On April 18, 2023, 97.85% of members of the [Writers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America") (WGA) voted to [go on strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_action "Strike action") if they failed to reach a satisfactory agreement with the [Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Motion_Picture_and_Television_Producers "Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers") (AMPTP), which represents [the major film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_film_studios "Major film studios") and [television studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Three_(American_television) "Big Three (American television)") in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States"), by May 1.[[31]](#cite_note-32) The AMPTP engaged in lengthy negotiations with the WGA on behalf of [Amazon Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Studios "Amazon Studios") (as well as [MGM Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Holdings "MGM Holdings")), [Apple Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Studios "Apple Studios"), [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Studios "Lionsgate Studios"), [NBCUniversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBCUniversal "NBCUniversal"), [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), [Paramount Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global"), [Sony Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Pictures "Sony Pictures"), [the Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company"), and [Warner Bros. Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. Discovery") (WBD),[[32]](#cite_note-33) but failed to reach a deal before the mandated deadline.

### May 2023

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: May 2023")]

As a result, the leadership of the [Writers Guild of America, West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America,_West "Writers Guild of America, West") (WGAW) and [Writers Guild of America, East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America,_East "Writers Guild of America, East") (WGAE) unanimously approved a strike on the eve of May 2, the first of its kind since the [2007–2008 strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007–08_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike "2007–08 Writers Guild of America strike") fifteen years prior.[[17]](#cite_note-hollywoodreporter/1235404087-18)

*[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* reported that the WGA had set some prospective rules for writers during the strike. The Writers Guild stated that "writers cannot do any writing, revising, pitching, or discussing future projects with companies that are members of the AMPTP."[[33]](#cite_note-auto-34)

The Writers Guild also stated that [fiction podcasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction_podcast "Fiction podcast") that are produced by companies against which the Guild and its members are striking must stop production. The Guild said that they hoped that writers of animated series not covered by the Writers Guild but by [the Animation Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Animation_Guild,_IATSE_Local_839 "The Animation Guild, IATSE Local 839") would seek advice from the Writers Guild on whether or not their work as a writer was counter to the activities of the strike and, if so, to cease such work for the duration of the strike. The Guild noted that while they cannot punish non-Guild writers who write for companies against which the union is striking, they promise to bar such writers from future Guild membership.[[33]](#cite_note-auto-34)

The WGA instructed members to begin [picketing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picketing "Picketing") on May 2, 2023, at 1:00 p.m. [PDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Daylight_Time "Pacific Daylight Time").[[17]](#cite_note-hollywoodreporter/1235404087-18) Some places that the WGA has picketed include [AMC Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMC_Networks "AMC Networks"), [Amazon/Culver Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Studios "Amazon Studios"), [MGM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer"), [CBS Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radford_Studio_Center "Radford Studio Center"), [CBS Television City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_City "Television City"), [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Studios_(division) "Walt Disney Studios (division)"), [20th Century Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Studios "20th Century Studios"), [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Films "Lionsgate Films"), [Starz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starz_Inc. "Starz Inc."), [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), [Paramount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures"), [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Entertainment_Studios "MTV Entertainment Studios"), [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Pictures "Sony Pictures"), [Universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures"), [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") (including its [Burbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Studios_Burbank "Warner Bros. Studios Burbank") division), [30 Rock/NBCUniversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30_Rockefeller_Plaza "30 Rockefeller Plaza"), [Broadway Stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Stages "Broadway Stages"), [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO"), [Silvercup Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvercup_Studios "Silvercup Studios"), [Steiner Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_Studios "Steiner Studios"), [Warner Bros. Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. Discovery"), and Warner Bros. Discovery Upfront.[[34]](#cite_note-35)

During the strike, the WGA instructed writers facing financial hardship due to the strike to apply to the [Entertainment Community Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Community_Fund "Entertainment Community Fund"). The Entertainment Community Fund helps people in the entertainment industry with financial trouble find affordable housing and maintain health care and senior care coverage. On May 10, 2023, it was reported that writers had pledged $1.7 million to the Entertainment Community Fund. Among the prominent donors were showrunners and producers [J. J. Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Abrams "J. J. Abrams"), [Greg Berlanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Berlanti "Greg Berlanti"), [Adam McKay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_McKay "Adam McKay"), [Ryan Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Murphy_(producer) "Ryan Murphy (producer)"), [Shonda Rhimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shonda_Rhimes "Shonda Rhimes"), [Michael Schur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schur "Michael Schur"), and [John Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wells_(filmmaker) "John Wells (filmmaker)").[[35]](#cite_note-36)[[36]](#cite_note-37)

### June 2023

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: June 2023")]

On June 7 and 8, 2023, picketing in the Northeast (namely in New York) was paused due to poor air quality from the [2023 Canadian wildfires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Canadian_wildfires "2023 Canadian wildfires"). Strike activity resumed on the 9th when air quality improved.[[37]](#cite_note-38)

On June 9, 2023, [Lionsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionsgate_Studios "Lionsgate Studios") suspended *[BMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMF_(TV_series) "BMF (TV series)")* [line producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_producer "Line producer") Ian Woolf following an altercation with striking writers who were picketing outside of *BMF*'s production headquarters. According to first-hand accounts from writers Gabriel Alejandro Garza and Tom Smuts, Woolf attempted to [intimidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intimidation "Intimidation") Garza and Brian Egeston, who were picketing on the sidewalk next to the studio's entrance, by [accelerating his car towards them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle-ramming_attack "Vehicle-ramming attack") and stopping just short of hitting them. After first claiming that he did not see them, Woolf later admitted to trying to scare them. According to Smuts, Woolf later unsuccessfully tried to convince [Teamsters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teamsters "Teamsters") Local 728 to [cross picket lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strikebreaker "Strikebreaker"), but they refused. Lionsgate released a statement saying, "We take acts of intimidation and threats of violence seriously and investigate them thoroughly... As we continue to investigate, we have sent home the individual involved." The WGA also released a statement, which read, "Workers should not be threatened with physical harm when exercising their right to publicly protest and picket against unfair wages and working conditions."[[38]](#cite_note-39)[[39]](#cite_note-40)

### July 2023

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: July 2023")]

On July 12, 2023, *[Deadline Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadline_Hollywood "Deadline Hollywood")* reported that the AMPTP and the major Hollywood studios did not plan to return to negotiations with the WGA until late October 2023 at the earliest. The studio executives who anonymously spoke with *Deadline* stated that by October, many writers would be financially strained to the point where they would lose their housing, which they believed would allow them to be in a better position to dictate the terms of any new deal. Representatives for the AMPTP distanced themselves from the anonymous sources, claiming they remained committed to signing a deal as soon as possible.[[40]](#cite_note-41)

### August 2023

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: August 2023")]

On August 1, 2023, the WGA announced that it would meet with the AMPTP on the following Friday to discuss negotiations regarding the strike. The location of the meeting was not disclosed. A spokesman for the AMPTP, speaking in relation to the strikes of the WGA and SAG-AFTRA, said, "we remain committed to finding a path to mutually beneficial deals with both unions."[[41]](#cite_note-42)[[42]](#cite_note-2023-08-01_Variety-43) Both parties met on August 4, 2023, but no agreement was reached.[[43]](#cite_note-44)

On August 10, 2023, the AMPTP and the WGA agreed to resume contract negotiations, with the first meeting set for August 11.[[44]](#cite_note-45) After that meeting, the Writers Guild sent a note to its 11,500 members saying the AMPTP had indicated a willingness to make concessions in some areas, including finding ways to safeguard writers from artificial intelligence technology. The note added, however, that the AMPTP had said studios "were not willing to engage" on other Writers Guild proposals, including success-based residual payments from streaming services. The note said guild leaders would not return to negotiations until studios were willing to engage on all proposals.[[45]](#cite_note-46) Later on the same day the WGA sent a message to members saying that they had received a counterproposal and were evaluating it.[[46]](#cite_note-47)

On August 21, 2023, picketing was canceled in Los Angeles due to [Hurricane Hilary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hilary "Hurricane Hilary").[[47]](#cite_note-48) The union, meanwhile, remained relatively silent beyond the message of August 18, 2023: "Everybody is trying to step up and make a resolution," one executive told *THR*. "There's more positive momentum this week than last."[[48]](#cite_note-49) On August 22, 2023, AMPTP presented a proposal suggesting rules for AI content,[[49]](#cite_note-theregister/2023/08/24/studios-50) but talks between the studios and the writers remained at a stalemate until late September.[[50]](#cite_note-51) On August 30,[[51]](#cite_note-madeadline-52) [California State Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Treasurer "California State Treasurer") [Fiona Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiona_Ma "Fiona Ma") sent letters[[52]](#cite_note-maletter-53) to [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), The Walt Disney Company, [Comcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comcast "Comcast"), [Warner Bros. Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. Discovery"), [Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), [Paramount Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global") and [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)"), telling them to return to negotiations and settle the strikes.[[53]](#cite_note-ma-54) She states that the impact of the strikes "paralyzes Hollywood and reverberates across the state, affecting countless businesses, thousands of pension fund beneficiaries, and millions of Californians."[[53]](#cite_note-ma-54)

### September 2023

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: September 2023")]

On September 6, [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") suspended deals with [Mindy Kaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindy_Kaling "Mindy Kaling"), J. J. Abrams, Greg Berlanti, and [Bill Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Lawrence_(TV_producer) "Bill Lawrence (TV producer)"). It had announced the day before that the strikes would impact its 2023 earnings by $500 million.[[54]](#cite_note-kaling-55)

On September 8, the WGA released a statement claiming that there are member companies that have shown a "desire and willingness to negotiate an agreement that adequately addresses writers' issues... [and who] have said they are willing to negotiate on proposals that the AMPTP has presented to the public as deal breakers,"[[55]](#cite_note-0708hr-56) and that they have asked them to leave the AMPTP in order to negotiate independently with the WGA.[[55]](#cite_note-0708hr-56)[[56]](#cite_note-0708v-57)[[57]](#cite_note-0708dh-58) A few hours later, the AMPTP released a statement refuting that claim, saying, "The AMPTP member companies are aligned and are negotiating together to reach a resolution. Any suggestion to the contrary is false."[[58]](#cite_note-59)[[59]](#cite_note-deadline2-60)

On September 11, 2023, *[The Drew Barrymore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Drew_Barrymore_Show "The Drew Barrymore Show")* resumed episodes without writers and was picketed by guild members. Two audience members were turned away for wearing WGA pins.[[60]](#cite_note-61) Barrymore would be removed as host of the upcoming 74th [National Book Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award "National Book Award") the following day.[[61]](#cite_note-62)[[62]](#cite_note-63)[[63]](#cite_note-64) On September 17, Barrymore changed her decision and announced that the show would remain on hiatus while the strike was ongoing.[[64]](#cite_note-change-65)

On September 12, in an interview with *[TheWrap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TheWrap "TheWrap")*, a studio executive said that "the showrunners are quite pissed [...] they are mad at the guilds and feel that they are not responding to the studios' offer. Now even the higher-paid members of the guild are expressing concern over the inability to end the strike."[[65]](#cite_note-rescheduled-66) In addition, while there were plans for a meeting between the WGA and top [showrunners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showrunner "Showrunner") on September 15,[[66]](#cite_note-rescheduled2-67) the meeting was cancelled on that day due to plans for an upcoming meeting between the WGA and AMPTP the following week.[[67]](#cite_note-cancelled0915-68)

On September 13, American comedian and political commentator [Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher "Bill Maher") announced on Twitter that he will resume production of his show *[Real Time with Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_with_Bill_Maher "Real Time with Bill Maher")*.[[68]](#cite_note-realtime-69) However, on September 18, Maher changed his mind, stating: "My decision to return to work was made when it seemed nothing was happening and there was no end in sight to this strike. Now that both sides have agreed to go back to the negotiating table I'm going to delay the return of *Real Time*, for now, and hope they can finally get this done."[[69]](#cite_note-realtime2-70) Earlier in September, he suggested that the [Governor of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_California "Governor of California") [Gavin Newsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom") should help end the strike.[[70]](#cite_note-maher-71)

On September 14, the AMPTP said that the WGA met with them the previous day and agreed to restart negotiations the following week. A few minutes after the news, the WGA confirmed this.[[67]](#cite_note-cancelled0915-68)[[71]](#cite_note-72) Four days later, it was announced that the union and studios would resume negotiations on September 20[[72]](#cite_note-73) with studio CEOs [David Zaslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Zaslav "David Zaslav") ([Warner Bros. Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Discovery "Warner Bros. args.summary:
The 2023 Writers Guild of America (WGA) strike was a major labor dispute between the WGA (representing 11,500 screenwriters) and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP). It lasted from May 2 to September 27, 2023 (147 days), tying with the 1960 strike as the second-longest WGA strike behind 1988. The strike was part of broader 2023 Hollywood labor disputes alongside the SAG-AFTRA strike.

**Key Issues:**
- Poor streaming residuals cutting writers' average incomes compared to a decade prior
- Need for minimum staffing requirements and duration of employment terms
- Limits on generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) to prevent replacement of writers
- Ensuring each writing team member receives individual pension and healthcare funds

**Timeline Highlights:**
- April 18, 2023: 97.85% of WGA members voted to authorize a strike
- May 2, 2023: Strike began with picketing at major studios including Disney, Netflix, Warner Bros., Paramount, Sony, Universal, and others
- June 7-8: Picketing paused in NYC due to Canadian wildfire smoke
- August 22: AMPTP presented AI-related proposals, but talks remained at a stalemate
- September 20-23: Intensive negotiations with studio CEOs (David Zaslav, Bob Bakish, Bob Iger, Donna Langley, Ted Sarandos)
- September 24: Tentative agreement reached
- September 27: Strike officially ended at 12:01 a.m. PDT
- October 9: Contract ratified with 99% member approval

**Outcome:** The WGA secured increases to minimum wage, final compensation, pension and health fund rates, improvements to employment terms, increases to residual payments for streaming works, and regulation of AI prohibiting exploitation of writers' material to train AI models or reduce writers' pay.

The strike caused significant economic impact, halting productions, leading to force majeure contract terminations, and affecting the broader entertainment ecosystem including VFX and prop-making industries.

### The Impact of AI-Based Artistic Productions on Aesthetic Perception, Artistic Appreciation, and Creativity: A Meta-Analysis Study

*Mevlüt Ünal*

  

#### Abstract

  

This meta-analytic investigation synthesized empirical findings from 37 peer-reviewed experimental and quasi-experimental studies (N = 1,920) to evaluate the psychological impact of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated art on aesthetic perception, artistic appreciation, and creativity. A random-effects model yielded a significant, moderate overall negative effect size of Hedges' g = -0.37 (95% CI [-0.43, -0.31], p < .001), demonstrating that explicit awareness of AI involvement reduces positive aesthetic and creative evaluations relative to human-made art. High baseline heterogeneity (I² = 87.2%) prompted categorical moderator analyses across six variables.

Statistically significant moderating effects (p < .05) were identified for outcome type, AI type, cultural context (operationalized via Triandis’s four-way typology), and publication year; conversely, art form and sample type were non-significant. Notably, the anti-AI devaluation penalty was most pronounced for explicit creativity outcomes (g = -0.44) and within culturally vertical-individualist societies (g = -0.41). Funnel-plot inspections and Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill analysis indicated minimal asymmetry, establishing that these findings are robust against publication bias. Ultimately, this synthesis provides critical, quantified evidence of contemporary psychological barriers toward machine-driven artistry, offering profound implications for the evolving domains of human-AI co-creativity, digital aesthetics, and cross-cultural technology reception

args.summary: This is an academic journal article (IJONMES, Vol 10, No 1, 2026) by Mevlüt Ünal presenting a meta-analysis of 37 peer-reviewed experimental and quasi-experimental studies (N=1,920) examining the psychological impact of AI-generated art on aesthetic perception, artistic appreciation, and creativity. Using a random-effects model, the study found a significant moderate negative overall effect size (Hedges' g = -0.37, 95% CI [-0.43, -0.31], p < .001), indicating that explicit awareness of AI involvement reduces positive aesthetic and creative evaluations compared to human-made art. High baseline heterogeneity (I² = 87.2%) was observed. Statistically significant moderating effects (p < .05) were found for outcome type, AI type, cultural context (using Triandis's four-way typology), and publication year, while art form and sample type were non-significant. The anti-AI devaluation penalty was most pronounced for explicit creativity outcomes (g = -0.44) and within culturally vertical-individualist societies (g = -0.41). Funnel-plot inspections and Duval and Tweedie's trim-and-fill analysis indicated minimal asymmetry, confirming robustness against publication bias. The article is published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

## Highlights

*   •Cross-cultural study on perceptions of AI art in the U.S., Japan, and China. 
*   •China values AI art quality; U.S. and Japan prioritize ethical concerns. 
*   •Participants in Japan show neutral attitudes, reflecting limited AI experience. 
*   •U.S. participants emphasize human creativity's role in AI-assisted art. 
*   •Ethical concerns differ by country: privacy in China, misinformation in the U.S. 

## Abstract

This study investigates the perceptions and attitudes toward generative AI art across three major global economies: the United States, Japan, and China. As leaders in AI development, these countries exhibit distinct viewpoints regarding the integration of AI into the creative process. The investigation was conducted using an online questionnaire, which gathered responses from participants in the three countries. The survey consisted of questions that assessed participants’ experiences with AI tools, their views on AI-generated art in various forms, and their ethical concerns regarding its use. The results indicate that participants in China are generally more optimistic about the value of AI-generated art, prioritizing the quality of the final product over ethical concerns. In contrast, participants in the U.S. and Japan emphasize the importance of human creativity and express skepticism about AI art, primarily due to ethical concerns such as misinformation and intellectual property issues. While Chinese participants focus on data privacy and intellectual property protection, U.S. participants are more concerned with misinformation and fake content. Japan, despite having the least experience with AI tools, presents attitudes that often fall between the positions of the U.S. and China. This study provides valuable insights into cross-cultural differences in attitudes toward AI art, offering guidance for educators, policymakers, and AI developers on integrating AI into the art and design sectors in a sustainable, ethical, and culturally adaptive manner.

args.summary: This is a scientific article published in Sustainable Futures (Volume 10, December 2025) by Suomiya Bao from the University of Tsukuba, titled "Cross-cultural attitudes toward generative AI in Art: Implications for sustainable creativity in the U.S., Japan, and China." The study investigates perceptions of generative AI art across three major economies using an online questionnaire. Key findings include: (1) Chinese participants are generally more optimistic about AI-generated art, prioritizing the quality of the final product over ethical concerns; (2) U.S. and Japanese participants emphasize the importance of human creativity and express skepticism about AI art, primarily due to ethical concerns such as misinformation and intellectual property issues; (3) Chinese participants focus on data privacy and intellectual property protection, while U.S. participants are more concerned with misinformation and fake content; (4) Japan, despite having the least experience with AI tools, presents attitudes that often fall between the U.S. and China. The article notes that Japan has the least AI tool experience among the three countries. The study provides guidance for educators, policymakers, and AI developers on integrating AI into art and design sectors in a sustainable, ethical, and culturally adaptive manner. The article has been cited by 4 other publications and has 59 Mendeley readers.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838)Abstract

Recent advancement in Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rendered image-synthesis models capable of producing complex artworks that appear nearly indistinguishable from human-made works. Here we present a quantitative assessment of human perception and preference for art generated by OpenAI’s DALL·E 2, a leading AI tool for art creation. Participants were presented with pairs of artworks, one human-made and one AI-generated, in either a preference-choice task or an origin-discrimination task. Results revealed a significant preference for AI-generated artworks. At the same time, a separate group of participants were above-chance at detecting which artwork within the pair was generated by AI, indicating a perceptible distinction between human and artificial creative works. These results raise questions about how a shift in art preference to favour synthetic creations might impact the way we think about art and its value to human society, prompting reflections on authorship, authenticity, and human creativity in the era of generative AI.

**Keywords:**visual perception, generative AI, DALL·E, artworks, appreciation, discrimination

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838)Introduction

1
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become ubiquitous in our everyday lives. With each iteration in technological capabilities, the gap between AI and human ability seems to narrow. One such advancement has been the recent wave of image-synthesis models; AI image-generation tools that have evolved to a level of sophistication such that it is nearly impossible to distinguish between photographs of real human faces and those generated by a computer ([Moshel et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref16); [Nightingale and Farid, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref17)). The fact that AI is able to fool the human visual system’s perception of faces—one of our most deeply-rooted and evolutionarily relevant brain functions—is certainly cause for concern ([Westerlund, 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref29)), but how does it fare against what has arguably been the cultural benchmark of human creativity throughout history: Art?

Addressing this question has increasing importance for understanding the changing landscape of the art world and the role of technology in shaping artistic production and consumption. Separately from concerns that centre on questions of intellectual property and privacy violations ([Smits and Borghuis, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref27); [Zhou and Nabus, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref30)), AI-generated art also raises fundamental questions about how we might (re)define creativity ([Epstein et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref8); [Oksanen et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref18)), an ability considered until now to be essentially human-specific. This issue has captured interdisciplinary interest, with researchers across computer science, philosophy, and psychological and social sciences joining forces to investigate how we process and interact with the AI-generated works that we are increasingly exposed to in advertising, social media, and scams ([Baidoo-Anu and Ansah, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref2); [Epstein et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref8); [Millet et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref15); [Oksanen et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref18); [Ooi et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref20)).

Previous research has shown a consistent trend of negative bias towards AI-generated art ([Agudo et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref1); [Chamberlain et al., 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref5); [Chiarella et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref6); [Gangadharbatla, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref9); [Horton et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref13); [Millet et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref15); [Ragot et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref25)), however, this research has primarily examined the impact of knowing whether the art was created by AI or humans (rather than assessing artworks’ intrinsic aesthetic qualities). Whether or not humans exhibit a reliable preference for the _intrinsic aesthetic qualities_ of (unlabelled) human- or AI-generated art has received comparatively less attention. Therefore, there is lack of understanding in current literature of how people respond to AI art separately from biases related to authorship attribution, which will be increasingly important as AI-generated art continues to proliferate, and contextual information such as authorship attribution becomes more scarce.

Here, we aimed to address this critical gap in the literature by examining observer preferences for human-made _vs._ AI-generated art in the absence of any knowledge of the artworks’ origins. The novelty of this study also resides in providing an objective and quantitative assessment of the human perception of artificial art made using OpenAI’s DALL·E 2, one of the most advanced AI tools for art generation.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fn0001) With high-level performance for representational image generation, DALL·E 2 represents a step change in the field, as technology and synthetic representational artworks publicly accessible before its release were often much more rudimentary in complexity of composition and general verisimilitude ([Pan et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref21)). Here we focus on how observers perceive and appreciate the aesthetic qualities of DALL·E 2 artworks by comparing human observers’ appreciation of unlabelled AI-generated and human-made art and testing observers’ ability to distinguish between the two.

To assess human observers’ appreciation and discrimination of non-abstract artworks generated by both humans and AI, we paired 50 lesser-known real artworks by famous representational artists (absent in the WikiArt’s “famous work” section) with 50 artificial artworks generated in a similar style using OpenAI’s DALL·E 2 with comparable visual features (e.g., colour, style, composition), as depicted in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig1). Online observers viewed these image pairs in either a preference judgement task (Experiment 1, _“Which artwork do you like the most?”_, 127 participants) or a real-artificial discrimination task (Experiment 2, “_Which artwork was generated by a computer?”_, 137 participants) (see [Figure 2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig2)). To minimise bias and conceal the true purpose of each experiment (i.e., comparing human- vs. AI-generated), in both cases the 50 matched image pairs appeared randomly intermingled with random pairs (e.g., Human-made vs. Human-made) drawn from the full image set. We also assessed online observers’ art experience to test its potential influence on the appreciation and discrimination of these images.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838)Methods

2
### Participants

2.1
Online participants from Western Sydney University were recruited via the university (SONA) participant management system in exchange for course credits. We recruited 127 participants in Experiment 1, including 31 males, 95 females, and 1 non-binary with mean age of 22.27 (SD = 5.89), and 137 participants in Experiment 2, including 26 males, 109 females, and 2 non-binary with a mean age of 21.76 (SD = 6.99). Our participants reported on average a medium level of expertise in art, with subjective ratings of interest in art of 63.32 (SD = 29.68) and 62.22 (SD = 28.12), knowledge of art history of 30.81 (SD = 25.41) and 28.41 (SD = 26.46), artistic personality of 53.32 (SD = 28.35) and 52.49 (SD = 29.00) on a scale of 0 to 100, in Experiment 1 and 2, respectively.

The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of Western Sydney University. All participants provided written informed consent prior to the study. The experiment was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant guidelines and regulations for research involving human research participants.

### Stimuli

2.2
Stimuli in Experiments 1 and 2 were 50 images of real artworks and 50 images of AI-generated artworks representative of various artistic styles (Baroque, Romanticism, Impressionism and Post-impressionism). Each image was presented at 200 × 200 pixels, which, assuming a standard laptop screen, corresponds to approximately 6 × 6 degrees visual angle (note this varies depending on the participant’s own device). Real and synthetic artworks were matched across artistic styles to form 50 pairs of images shown in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig1). The real images were 50 lesser-known artworks by famous representational artists retrieved from Wikimedia Commons[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fn0002) and WikiArt.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fn0003) The selection process involved manually skimming through the publicly accessible catalogues of artists whose works have proliferated to the point that they are significantly represented in the training data of DALL-E 2. Since there is no direct metric to measure the degree of popularity for many a given work, selection was made based on the following criteria: Absence in the “famous work” section on WikiArt and whether the work could be reasonably assumed to be representative of the associated artist’s style (e.g., While Vincent van Gogh’s catalogue features many charcoal drawings, these were excluded as they do not fit with the general perception of his art style).

The AI-generated stimuli were created with DALL·E 2, an image diffusion model that generates high-quality, complex images based on textual prompts input by the user.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fn0004) Briefly described, this process relies on a text encoding model (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training; CLIP) to link textual input to visual output by use of a two-stage model involving a “prior” image caption embedder and an “encoder,” which work in tandem to extract information relevant to the desired visual output ([Ramesh et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref26)). After sufficient training, the CLIP model is frozen and the now-embedded semantic information it produced is used to train a diffusion ‘decoder’ that allows for the process to be inverted. DALL·E 2 employs a diffusion model named Guided Language to Image Diffusion for Generation and Editing, which after training, allows for text-conditional image generation. This is achieved by training a Markov chain to make certain inferences using a set of sample images, which are iteratively provided with more Gaussian noise until it is able to reverse the generation process ([Ho et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref12)). This model is then trained using a generative adversarial network (GAN), where two networks, a generator and a discriminator, are locked in a zero-sum game and continually pushed to greater levels of image generation refinement ([Poltronieri and Hänska, 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref23)). The result is a highly accessible and versatile AI image-generation tool that can convert textual prompts into detailed realistic images.

DALL·E 2 was used with 36 unique prompts that included both an artist’s name and the type of artwork (e.g., “Paul Cezanne style still life painting,” see [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig1)). DALL-E generates several images in response to each prompt. Several prompts were used multiple times (e.g., Claude Monet style garden painting). To minimise bias in the selection process, the generated images were manually compared to famous artists’ works found on Wikimedia Commons[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fn0005) and WikiArt,[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fn0006) focusing on comparable visual features (e.g., colour, style, composition) before inclusion. As with the real images, the primary selection criterion was whether a given outputted image could reasonably be assumed to be representative of the respective artist’s style. Manual selection was employed to remove clear outliers, and the selected images were then cropped to remove the DALL·E logo in the bottom-right corner.

To account for selection bias, image statistics were analysed using a GIST image descriptor in MATLAB, focusing on overlapping low-level visual similarities within each category (i.e., AI- or human-made stimuli). This could influence overall appraisal, e.g., should the selected AI stimuli possess a particular visual feature that the human stimuli do not have, this may result in one category being judged as more or less visually appealing as a whole to a given participant. The GIST descriptor greatly reduces image size and quality to rudimental features to compare input data for overlapping features ([Oliva and Torralba, 2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref19)). The results of this statistical image analysis were then mapped onto a matrix, which showed only a minor overlap between categories and was thus deemed too small to induce potential biases. We also calculated aposteriori luminance, root mean square contrast and entropy to test their potential contribution to our results (individual image values and category distributions are presented in [Supplementary material](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#SM1)).

The experiment ran online in participants’ web browsers ([Grootswagers, 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref11)), was coded using the javascript framework jsPsych, version 7.3 ([De Leeuw, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref7)), and ran on Pavlovia ([Peirce et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref22)).

### Procedure

2.3
Experiments 1 and 2 had the same experimental procedure and design, differing only in terms of participant instruction. At the start of the experiment, participants reported their demographic information, along with their art expertise, operationalised through three questions: (1) “_Rate your interest in art_,” (2), “_Rate your knowledge of art history_,” and (3) “_How artistic are you?_” Participants indicated their response using a slider coded to a value between 0 and 100. Next, in the main part of the experiment, the 50 pairs of artworks shown in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig1) were presented once in a random order with the human-made and AI-generated stimuli being randomly presented either on the left or right side. Participants in Experiment 1 were not aware of the true aim of the study. They were not informed of the origin of the artworks and were simply instructed to select which one of the two images they preferred (see [Figure 2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig2)). Participants in Experiment 2 were told that one in each pair was AI-generated and instructed to click on it (see [Figure 2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig2)). Fifty additional trials with unique 50 pairs randomly drawn from the 100 (human and AI) artworks were included in each experiment (but not analysed) to ensure that participants remained naïve to the experimental manipulation. The 100 trials in total were performed by participants at a self-selected pace. Each pair of images remained onscreen until a selection was made. The total duration of the experiment was about 5 min. Participants could only participate in either Experiment 1 or Experiment 2 to ensure participants in Experiment 1 were not aware of the presence of AI-generated stimuli.

### Data and statistical analysis

2.4
AI preference scores from Experiment 1 and AI detection accuracy scores from Experiment 2 of each participant were averaged across the 50 pairs of stimuli and then submitted to one-sample _t_-tests to examine deviations from the 50% chance level. The scores for each pair of images were also averaged across all participants within each experiment separately to test the image-wise correlation between the two experiments using Pearson correlations. A principal component analysis was conducted on the three expertise scores and data on the first dimension (71 and 76% variance explained in Experiment 1 and 2, respectively) were used to test the effect of expertise on AI preference and AI detection accuracy in Experiment 1 and 2 using Pearson correlations.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838)Results

3
Experiment 1 revealed a significant preference for AI-generated artworks. Without being provided with any information about the origin/authorship of the artworks, participants in the preference task indicated they preferred the AI-generated artworks significantly more often than the human-made artworks (AI-preference scores significantly above 50% chance-level) [_t_(126) = 5.39, _p_< 0.001, _d_ = 0.48; [Figure 2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig2)].

Interestingly, when a separate group of participants in Experiment 2 were asked to detect which one of the two artworks was made by a computer, they could do so significantly better than chance. A one-sample t-test indicated AI detection accuracy was significantly above 50% [_t_(136) = 3.62, _p_< 0.001, _d_ = 0.31] although a smaller effect size was observed compared to Experiment 1 ([Figure 2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig2)).

Image-wise correlational analysis revealed a positive relationship between AI preference and AI detection accuracy scores associated with each pair [_t_(48) = 3.23, _p_ = 0.002, _r_ = 0.42]. As shown in [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#fig3), the AI-generated artworks that Experiment 1 participants tended to prefer were also those that Experiment 2 participants were better able to detect, suggesting there may be features in the artworks driving both preference for and detection of AI-generated art. Importantly, this correlation remains almost identical when controlling for potential differences in mean luminance, root mean square contrast and entropy between human-made and AI-generated stimuli [_t_(48) = 3.15, _p_ = 0.003, _r_ = 0.42] suggesting that there are other more complex visual features influencing participants’ preference and discrimination.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838)Discussion

4
There is a burgeoning sentiment that AI-image generation technology has reached a point of refinement that challenges our traditional understanding of the human perception and appreciation of art ([Epstein et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref8); [Oksanen et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref18)). Our results evidence this claim, revealing that in the absence of attribution labels, human observers systematically prefer AI-generated artworks over stylistically similar artworks painted by real people. Should this effect prove universal, it could constitute a paradigm shift in art appreciation, favouring synthetic works over those created by human artists, which has the potential to transform the art world, while also raising new questions about authorship, authenticity, and the role of human creativity in the age of generative AI.

Our findings stand in contrast to prior research on subjective evaluations of computer-generated artwork, which have largely reported a negative bias towards AI art ([Agudo et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref1); [Caporusso et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref4); [Chiarella et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref6); [Gangadharbatla, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref9); [Kirk et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref14)). This work has primarily examined the role of authorship attribution in AI art perception, rather than the aesthetic value of the artworks themselves. Thus, the observed negative bias in these studies appears to relate to our explicit prejudice against artificially-generated content (i.e., if an artwork is labelled as computer-generated, we tend not to like it). In contrast, here we obtained observer preference decisions in the absence of any authorship label—a neutral presentation format that encouraged observers to judge the inherent aesthetic qualities of the artworks—and assessed authorship discrimination in a separate experiment. This approach allowed us to obtain a quantitative assessment of the degree to which observers prefer the inherent artistic qualities of real artworks made by humans vs. those created by new AI image-generation models, free from external biases.

Although observers in the first experiment consistently preferred artworks generated by DALL·E 2 over those made by human artists, it was not the case that these AI artworks were indistinguishable from human creations. In Experiment 2, a separate group of observers were asked to explicitly judge which of the two artworks in each pair was generated by a computer. We found they could reliably do so above chance-level. Moreover, there was a positive correlation between the image-pairs’ AI-preference and AI-detection scores, suggesting that the same visual features that made the AI-generated artworks more detectable to participants in Experiment 2 also made those artworks more appealing to participants in Experiment 1 ([Van Geert and Wagemans, 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref28)). This intriguing pattern underscores the role that explicit bias against artificial creations has likely played in prior investigations ([Agudo et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref1); [Caporusso et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref4); [Chiarella et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref6); [Gangadharbatla, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref9); [Kirk et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref14)) of the aesthetic appeal of AI-generated artworks: When participants do not know the artworks are computer-generated, they freely prefer them. Interestingly, we found no evidence that these effects were moderated by observers’ art expertise, suggesting that the features in question are broadly accessible. However, our results suggest that they are not related to luminance, contrast and entropy, and that other visual features might have a more important role; a possibility which future research will no doubt explore in detail. This is an important research avenue together with examining the influence of contextual and authorship information on these effects to better understand the human perception of AI-generated artworks.

More generally, these results suggest that the technology behind DALL·E 2, in striving for stronger verisimilitude in computer-generated art, has evolved to do so by extrapolating (or exploiting) existing known biases in human cognition. On this thinking, DALL·E’s capacity to produce works that observers tend to prefer over human artworks could possibly be explained by the fact that its training dataset comprises images of artworks that are broadly popular and likely considered to be aesthetically pleasing. This is in line with recent research on “deepfakes,” wherein AI-generated faces not only fool observers with their hyper-realistic nature, but are also associated with enhanced perceptions of trustworthiness ([Boháček and Farid, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref3); [Groh et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref10); [Nightingale and Farid, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref17)). These findings raise critical concerns about the exact nature of the cognitive processes that could be targeted and manipulated using generative AI, and therefore, about its large-scale deployment without detailed investigation.

In a world increasingly shaped by the algorithms around us, the current findings suggest that as AI continues to evolve towards human capabilities, it may be poised to redefine our understanding of creative expression altogether. If AI-generated content can reach or even surpass aesthetic equivalence with human creation, the question of whether something can truly be considered “art” if it has no human architect becomes more complicated. Although AI image diffusion models currently still depend on some level of human intervention to produce artwork (from the initial production of training data to programming to user input), it seems increasingly likely that this necessity will decrease in future as the technologies progress. Our results are an initial step towards untangling the complex interaction between generative AI and human aesthetic preference; clearly, systematic examinations of AI-generated artworks’ features are needed to fully understand the mechanisms and implications of AI preferences. A clear future avenue for this field will be to combine parametric feature variations in AI-artwork with systematic manipulations of artwork-attribution (AI or human), to determine how low and mid-level visual featural differences interact with the documented negative bias associated with AI attribution ([Chamberlain et al., 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref5); [Chiarella et al., 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref6); [Horton et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref13); [Millet et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref15); [Ragot et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref25)). Indeed, this bias may well be shifting with the rapid adoption of AI technology in the wider population ([Epstein et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref8); [Oksanen et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref18); [Prasad Agrawal, 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750838#ref24)).

In addition, it will be important to consider additional presentation parameters that may contribute to or modulate observer preferences: For example, here we presented artworks at a relatively small size, cropped from their original dimensions to conform to a 1:1 ratio. Since these aspects necessarily change the composition (and therefore appreciation) of the artwork, it will be necessary to explore whether our results hold under different presentation formats, as well as across real-world and digital presentation formats. Digital presentation might have favoured AI-made works. Some critical features in human-made works such as texture might have been lost with their digital representation. Furthermore, while specific efforts have been made to account for selection bias using image statistics, our design required some degree of curation to omit clear outliers produced by DALL-E 2 that did not match the criteria laid out in advance. Critically, this means that our results do not automatically apply to the state of AI-image generation as a whole, but rather illustrate the height of its capabilities. In juxtaposing samples of the acme of traditional art with that which AI is capable of producing, we get a better view of the perception of AI as it continues to progress. Future studies should expand on this further by including a broader selection of images and removing the potential for selection bias through human intervention entirely. Importantly, excluding famous human-made artworks might have favoured AI artworks. Including famous human-made artworks assuming they could have been tested on completely naïve participants with no previous exposure could have increased preference for human-made works. There might be features in these artworks resulting in higher preference independently of how famous they are.

Moreover, future research could investigate the effects of expertise further as this was only succinctly assessed in this online experiment across three generic questions. Variations in the type of expertise and the number of years could be more deeply examined. Demographics such as age and cultural background could also be explored. They might influence how participants perceive and appreciate these artworks and the features they might focus on. It can also be noted that the AI-preference we report here is, by design, derived from a constrained set of artistic styles. As such, future work expanding this line of investigation could look to systematic comparisons of different styles. These are necessary steps for future research to reach a broader understanding of the perception of digital artworks in the general population. This has implications for the art market, museums, curators, and future artists, with new insights into the type of artworks, in the digital space in particular, people might prefer. It might also be important to extend this research in future studies to other creative domains. The production of movies and music, for instance, are all changing quickly with generative AI. Understanding similarities and differences across domains, could help identify universal mechanisms in this new generation of AI models biassing human perception and preference.

To conclude, our findings suggest that we might be observing with recent advances in AI technology a shift in art preference to favour synthetic creations, raising critical questions about the way we think about art and its value to our society. As the field of generative-AI continues to accelerate—spurring equal parts concern and excitement—there can be no doubt as to the urgency in this challenge. DALL·E 2 will soon be superseded by the next generation of algorithms with as-yet unknown capabilities. Understanding how the human experience intersects with this technology will be critical to ensuring its positive impact on our society.

args.summary:
This study published in Frontiers in Psychology (2025) by van Hees, Grootswagers, Quek, and Varlet quantitatively assessed human perception and preference for AI-generated art versus human-made art. Using OpenAI's DALL·E 2, researchers created 50 AI-generated artworks matched in style (Baroque, Romanticism, Impressionism, Post-impressionism) with 50 lesser-known works by famous representational artists. 

In Experiment 1 (127 participants), viewers were asked which artwork they preferred without knowing the origin. Results showed a significant preference for AI-generated artworks (t(126)=5.39, p<0.001, d=0.48). In Experiment 2 (137 participants), a separate group was asked to identify which artwork was computer-generated; they performed significantly above chance (t(136)=3.62, p<0.001, d=0.31), though with a smaller effect size.

A positive correlation was found between AI-preference and AI-detection scores (r=0.42, p=0.002), suggesting the same visual features driving preference also made AI artworks detectable. Art expertise did not significantly moderate these effects. The findings contrast with prior research showing negative bias toward AI art, which the authors attribute to those studies' use of authorship labels. When participants are unaware of AI origin, they freely prefer AI-generated works. The study raises questions about authorship, authenticity, and human creativity in the era of generative AI.

# The intersection of artificial intelligence and digital media art: exploring new frontiers of creativity

## Abstract

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the creative process in digital media art, yet existing generative models often struggle to balance realism, interactivity, and creative diversity. This study proposes a hybrid framework that integrates generative adversarial networks (GANs), reinforcement learning (RL), and particle swarm optimization (PSO) to generate dynamic and interactive artworks that evolve in real time based on audience engagement. The core innovation lies in combining GANs’ image realism with RL’s adaptive responsiveness, while PSO optimizes hyperparameters for faster convergence and higher generative quality. Style transfer is applied prior to principal component analysis (PCA) to enhance stylistic diversity before dimensionality reduction. The model training using the WikiArt dataset of over 80,000 paintings, the proposed system demonstrates superior performance compared to established benchmarks, including StyleGAN2, VQGAN + CLIP, and diffusion models. To evaluate perceptual quality and user engagement, a structured user study incorporating semi-structured interviews and a questionnaire-based survey was conducted with 200 participants, capturing quantitative and qualitative assessments of realism, creativity, interactivity, and overall user satisfaction toward the AI-generated artworks. Quantitative evaluation using Fréchet inception distance (FID), inception score (IS), and CLIP-score, along with user studies, shows significantly improved realism (M = 4.6, SD = 0.8), creativity (M = 4.5, SD = 0.7), and interactivity (M = 4.4, SD = 0.6) on a 5-point Likert scale. This work contributes a reproducible framework for computational creativity that bridges artificial intelligence and digital media art, advancing human–AI co-creation and interactive aesthetic design.
