## Introduction

The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the artistic industry, particularly the digital media art sector, whereby technological advancement is moving toward aesthetic experimentation (Shen & Yu, [2021](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR31 "Shen Y, Yu F (2021) The influence of artificial intelligence on art design in the digital age. Sci Program 2021:4838957")). The tools that are being developed through artificial intelligence are changing traditional art practices, suggesting new forms of creating, processing, and experiencing digital artifacts (Ursu et al., [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR32 "Shugrina M (2023) Designing intelligent tools for creative people. IEEE Comput Graph Appl 43(3):102–110")). This transformation has given the artists, designers, and technologists the opportunity to experiment with the adaptive, interactive, and algorithmically mediated modes of artistic production. The old concept of authorship, originality, and aesthetic value is being redefined once more with the emergence of digital systems as productive agents in creative processes (Aris et al., [2023](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR6 "Aris S, Aeini B, Nosrati S (2023) A digital aesthetics? Artificial intelligence and the future of art. J Cyberspace Stud 7(2):219–236"); Ranciere, [2019](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR28 "Rancière J (2019) The future of the image. Verso Books")). Consequently, AI is no longer viewed as a purely technical device but a ground-shifting one that alters the nature of art nowadays.

Digital media art relies on AI that is dictated by various computational techniques, which include machine learning models, neural networks, and deep generative architecture (Anantrasirichai et al., [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR5 "Anantrasirichai N, Bull D (2022) Artificial intelligence in the creative industries: a review. Artif Intell Rev 55(1):589–656")). One of them is generative adversarial networks (GANs), which demonstrated enormous possibilities in the process of generating photos and novel stylistic compositions that are aesthetical (Alqahtani et al., [2021](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR3 "Alqahtani H, Kavakli-Thorne M, Kumar G (2021) Applications of generative adversarial networks (GANs): an updated review. Arch Comput Methods Eng 28:525–552")). On a larger scale, the advantages of computational creativity are generalized to deep generative modeling algorithms, such as the variational autoencoders and autoregressive models, since they can be used to generate complex visual structures (Bond-Taylor et al., [2021](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR8 "Bond-Taylor S, Leach A, Long Y, Willcocks CG (2021) Deep generative modelling: a comparative review of VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, energy-based and autoregressive models. IEEE Trans Pattern Anal Mach Intell 44(11):7327–7347"); Regenwetter et al., [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR28 "Rancière J (2019) The future of the image. Verso Books")). These developments have enabled automatic generation of artworks and also have enabled experimentation on the stylistic and conceptual frontiers (Adeleye, [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR1 "Adeleye I (2024) The AI effect: rethinking design workflows for enhanced productivity and creativity, 2(1), 1–19")) (Ahlanger et al., [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR2 "Ahanger TA, Aljumah A, Atiquzzaman M (2022) State-of-the-art survey of artificial intelligent techniques for IoT security. Comput Netw 206: 108771. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.comnet.2022.108771
                  
                ")).

Access to bulk art data has also helped to drive more advancement in AI-based creativity. The datasets, including the WikiArt, allow machine learning models to evaluate the stylistic trend of the different periods in art and of specific artists (Choudhury, [2020](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR13 "Choudhury MD (2020) Automated identification of painters over WikiArt image data using machine learning algorithms (Doctoral dissertation, National College of Ireland)")) (Bhardwaj et al., [2023](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR7 "Bhardwaj R, Kadam T, Waghule S, Shendurkar S, Sarag B (2023) Creative AI using DeepDream. In: International conference on image processing and capsule networks. Springer Nature, pp 281–296")). Although this type of database can increase the ability of models to acquire complex visual representations, there is still a concern about stylistic homogenization and the loss of artistic uniqueness. Creativity is generally perceived to be a dynamic process of exploration, variation, and adaptation as opposed to pure imitation (Lubart, [2001](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR23 "Lubart TI (2001) Models of the creative process: past, present and future. Creat Res J 13(3–4):295–308")) (Desikan et al., [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR15 "Desikan BS, Shimao H, Miton H (2022) WikiArtVectors: style and color representations of artworks for cultural analysis via information theoretic measures. Entropy 24(9):1175")). Thus, AI as a system in the field of digital media art needs to move beyond high-fidelity reproduction and work to support adaptive and exploratory creative processes.

Although progress has been significant in generative modeling, there are still a number of limitations. Most traditional generative systems are more focused on visual realism than on dynamism in response to user input or the environment (Bond-Taylor et al., [2021](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR8 "Bond-Taylor S, Leach A, Long Y, Willcocks CG (2021) Deep generative modelling: a comparative review of VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, energy-based and autoregressive models. IEEE Trans Pattern Anal Mach Intell 44(11):7327–7347")) (Guljajeva et al., [2023](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR16 "Guljajeva V, Canet Sola M, Clarke IJ (2023) Artistic strategies to guide neural networks. Preprint at arXiv 
                  https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2307.07521
                  
                ")). This limits effective human-AI co-creation, with creative work developing in real-time interaction. The interactive and co-creative paradigms become more accepted as the crucial elements of the modern creative ecosystems (MacGregor et al., [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR24 "MacGregor S, Cooper A, Searle M, Kukkonen T (2022) Co-production and arts-informed inquiry as creative power for knowledge mobilisation. Evid Policy 18(2):206–235"); Rojek-Adamek, [2021](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR29 "Regenwetter L, Nobari AH, Ahmed F (2022) Deep generative models in engineering design: a review. J Mech Des 144(7):071704")). The concept of adaptive learning, such as optimization-based methods used in dynamic contexts (Wang et al., [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR35 "Viazovetskyi Y, Ivashkin V, Kashin E (2020) StyleGAN2 distillation for feed-forward image manipulation. In: European conference on computer vision. Springer, pp 170–186")), can be proposed as a possible direction for providing responsive and evolving artistic systems. Nevertheless, when adaptive mechanisms are combined with deep generative models, the issues of training stability, reward creation, and computational efficiency arise (Anantrasirichai et al., [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR5 "Anantrasirichai N, Bull D (2022) Artificial intelligence in the creative industries: a review. Artif Intell Rev 55(1):589–656")) (Manovich, [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR25 "Manovich L (2024) Separate and reassemble: generative AI through the lens of art and media histories. MATRIZes 18(2):7–18")) (Zebari et al., [2020](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR42 "Zebari R, Abdulazeez A, Zeebaree D, Zebari D, Saeed J (2020) A comprehensive review of dimensionality reduction techniques for feature selection and feature extraction. J Appl Sci Technol Trends 1(1):56–70")).

As a reaction to these issues, the proposed study suggests a self-adaptive and aesthetically knowledgeable generative system that combines profound generative modeling with adaptive learning reasoning. This goal is to increase real-time interactivity, ensure stylistic consistency, and enhance computational stability in digital media art systems. The proposed solution will focus on creative and technical limitations to advance the creation of adaptive, intelligent, and aesthetically responsive AI architectures in the digital artistic practice of the next generation.

The major aim of the paper is to present a new and flexible design of interactive digital media art capable of overcoming the problem of generative accuracy, real-time reactivity, and dimensionality in the creative AI systems. The major contributions are highlighted below:

* This study proposes a novel hybrid framework that integrates GANs and RL for interactive digital media art: This framework combines the capability of GANs to generate realistic and good-looking images and RL in offering real-time feedback to adjust the digital artworks in response to the user’s actions and the surroundings.
* The GANs’ generative accuracy and responsiveness using PSO for model optimization: In this study, PSO is applied to tune the parameters of both GAN and RL models to improve the quality of the generated outputs and to offer faster response to changes that may be requested by the audience of the interactive media applications.
* Employing PCA and neural feature selection for dimensionality reduction and content refinement: PCA is useful in reducing the number of calculations in the model by selecting the best features from the large art datasets, and the neural network feature selection enhances the input data to enhance the aesthetic compatibility and the relevance of generative outputs.
* Validating the framework’s effectiveness with superior performance in realism, creativity, and audience engagement compared to baseline models: The proposed framework has been proven to offer higher realism, more artistic creativity, and more attractive interactive experiences than the generative models in the generation of digital media art.

The paper is structured as follows: Section “Literature review” reviews the literature, Section “Materials and methods” presents the research questions, Section “Results” outlines the methodology, Section “Discussion” reports the results, and the final section concludes with implications and future research directions.

## Literature review

AI has become a popular topic in the digital media art context, and many studies have been dedicated to the use of AI in creative processes. AI has thus improved artistic skills and appearance in digital media art through emerging methods like AI-generated content, deblurring, and noise reduction for HCI interfaces (Chen, [2022](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR12 "Chen C (2022) Study on the innovative development of digital media art in the context of artificial intelligence. Comput Intell Neurosci 2022: Article 1004204")) (Siri et al., [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR33 "Siri A, Olcese G, Diana S (2024) Artificial intelligence and creativity: anthropological, sociological and pedagogical reflections. Geopolit Soc Secur Freedom J 7(1):1–19")) (Wagan & Sidra, [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR36 "Wagan SM, Sidra S (2024) Revolutionizing the digital creative industries: the role of artificial intelligence in integration, development, and innovation. SEISENSE J Manag 7(1):135–152")). Such developments have been assessed using practical applications, including the creation of AI instruments for content creation and optimization, leading to user satisfaction ratings of 3.316 to 3.684 as observed by (Wang and Zhang, [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR43 "Wang J, Zhang J (2024) Research on the theory and innovation strategy of digital media art development basedon artificial intelligence technology. Appl math nonlinear sci 9(1):972–973")). However, the integration of AI in art generation brings several philosophical and legal issues related to the authorship for copyright, and originality of work, since the generative AI models in question have limitations to the level of original intent of the human artist (Ho & Shim, [2024](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR17 "Ho AG, Shim K (2024) Investigating emotional responses to generative art. Arch Des Res 37(3):65–79")).

Besides content generation, AI has also been applied in the area of new media art, especially in VR and AR (Ye et al., [2023](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR40 "Ye C, Ganbat T, Xu L (2023) Application of artificial intelligence generated technology in new media art. Highlights Sci Eng Technol 68:313–319")). These applications enable artists to extend the conventional art experiences and provide unique interactive features. In addition, AI recommendation systems have become popular in content creation and delivery, and research indicates that 62% of users depend on AI recommendations to improve creative practices (Li, [2019](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR22 "Li Y (2019) Impact of artificial intelligence on creative digital content production. J Digit Art Eng Multimed 6(2):121")). Still, there are some questions related to the further consequences of AI for the art industry, such as the risk of AI dominating over artists, and the problems of ownership and transparency (Elfa et al., [2023](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR4 "Ali Elfa MA, Dawood MET (2023) Using artificial intelligence for enhancing human creativity. J Art Des Music 2(2):3"); Nasser El Erafy, [2023](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#ref-CR26 "Nasser El Erafy A (2023) Applications of artificial intelligence in the field of media. Int J Artif Intell Emerg Technol 6(2):19–41")).

AI and digital media art offer new creative opportunities, but several research questions are unanswered. One major issue is the conflict between creative human input and AI outcomes since many of the present studies focus on enhancing technical performance instead of facilitating an organic interaction between artists and AI. Some of the main issues raised include questions of who does an artwork, how original an artwork is, and where intuition in art lies, particularly when using artificial intelligence. Furthermore, there is an absence of consideration of the ethical and cultural ramifications linked to AI using art, such as property rights in created content, imbalanced datasets, and subsequently racially stereotypical generation and depiction. Current rules governing AI art are not coherent, and issues of credit and ownership remain unanswered. More research is still required to ascertain the extent to which AI impacts audience perception and audience emotions towards the art piece. Further, the connection of AI with these novel technologies, including augmented reality and virtual reality applications and blockchain-based platforms, is a future opportunity that can revolutionize the new digital art environment. Closing these gaps will contribute to a more accountable and integrated society’s responsible approach to AI innovation in the arts, broadening artistic space. ### Data sources

The WikiArt Dataset is the primary source of the primary data, which was used to train generative models and includes more than 80,000 paintings of various genres, such as abstraction, portraits, landscapes, and surrealism. In this dataset, much variation is maintained, and that is why this is the best dataset to use to develop AI systems to create artworks that can replicate most of the traditional art forms. To enhance the variety and richness of the training data, other synthetic datasets were also generated by using style transfer and image augmentation. Style transfer allows for features such as the roughness, lines, and color distribution of one piece of art to be copied to another piece of art. This method enables one to include more artistic features in the training data, while image augmentation includes such changes as rotations and changes in color, which also increases the variety of the data. These combined datasets enable the AI model to generate artwork in conventional styles and also establish that it can generate new forms.

### Data preprocessing

Preprocessing of data was done to normalize inputs and increase the generalization of the model. All WikiArt dataset images were downsampled to 256 × 256 pixels to have the same spatial dimensions and decrease bias caused by scale. The pixel values were brought into the range [0,1] by division by 255, which enhanced numerical stability, and it helped to avoid gradient explosion during training. The augmentation methods of random rotation, horizontal/vertical flipping, cropping, and color jittering were used to reduce overfitting and enhance data diversity. To increase the range of style, a number of images were subjected to neural style transfer to add the variability of brushstroke textures, chromatic distributions, and composition features. A pre-trained VGG16 network was then used to extract the features, and the high-dimensional feature vectors were reduced to a *d*-dimensional feature using the principal component analysis (PCA) dimension reduction technique that still retained most styles variance. Besides, the RGB images were converted to other color spaces (Lab and HSV) in order to better represent perceptual colors. Tonal distribution was improved by contrast enhancement through histogram equalization and automated loss of outliers through the use of noisy or low-quality samples. Lastly, K-means clustering was utilized to cluster images according to stylistic similarity so that it can represent the styles in an organized manner and have better control when handling downstream generation tasks.

Table [2](/articles/s41599-026-07132-z#Tab2) describes the preprocessing methods employed in order to optimize the training dataset to generate artwork. Photos were scaled down to 256 × 256 and brought to [0,1] to make the computation stable. Generalization was enhanced by data augmentation (rotation, flipping, cropping, change in brightness/contrast). Style transfer added to the stylistic diversity, and PCA minimized the features’ dimensionality with a little loss of information. Histogram equalization was used to improve contrast, and K-means clustering to group images based on their similarities in terms of style in order to generate them structurally. A combination of these steps guaranteed a computationally and diversity-rich dataset.

### Principal component analysis (PCA)

PCA was applied to reduce the dimensionality of feature vectors. Let \(X\in {{\mathbb{R}}}^{n\times d}\) be the matrix of feature vectors, where *n* is the number of samples and *d* is the dimensionality. The covariance matrix *C* is:

$$\,C=\frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits\_{i=1}^{n}\left({X}\_{i}-\mu \right){\left({X}\_{i}-\mu \right)}^{T}$$

(2)

Where *μ* is the mean vector. PCA computes eigenvectors of *C* to project data onto principal components.

### Clustering with K-means

To segment images by style, K-means clustering minimizes the objective:

$$\,J=\mathop{\sum }\limits\_{i=1}^{k}\mathop{\sum }\limits\_{j\epsilon {S}\_{i}}{{\rm{||}}{x}\_{j}-{\mu }\_{i}{\rm{||}}}^{2}$$

(3)

where \({\mu }\_{i}\) is the centroid of the cluster \({S}\_{i}\), and \({x}\_{j}\) is a data point.

### Model architecture

At the core of this system lies the GAN, which consists of two components: the Generator and the Discriminator are two types of models. The Generator’s role is to generate images from noise vectors randomly generated and convert them into the latent space of the artwork and features. With the help of deep convolutional layers, it produces photorealistic images that may resemble actual artworks. The Discriminator, a convolutional neural network, assesses these generated images, differentiating between real artwork and fake images created by the Generator. The Generator and Discriminator participate in an adversarial process, meaning that the main goal of the Generator is to generate such images that would be classified correctly by the Discriminator as fake, while the Discriminator’s goal is to classify images generated by the Generator and the actual images as fake. This is controlled by the minimax game determined by the objective function:

$$\,{{\mathscr{L}}}\_{\mathrm{GAN}}={{\mathbb{E}}}\_{x \sim {p}\_{\mathrm{data}}}\left(x\right)\left[\log D\left(x\right)\right]+{{\mathbb{E}}}\_{z \sim {p}\_{z}}\left(z\right)\left[\log \left(1-D\left(G\left(z\right)\right)\right)\right]$$

(4)

Where \({p}\_{\mathrm{data}}\left(x\right)\) data (*x*) is the real data distribution, \({p}\_{z}\left(z\right)\) is the noise distribution, and *G*(*z*) and *D*(*x*) represent the Generator’s output and the Discriminator’s evaluation, respectively. The Generator minimizes the loss function:

$${{\mathscr{L}}}\_{G}=-{{\mathbb{E}}}\_{z \sim {p}\_{z\left(z\right)}}\left[\log \left(D\left(G\left(Z\right)\right)\right)\right]\,$$

(5)

While the Discriminator maximizes:

$$\,{{\mathscr{L}}}\_{D}={{\mathbb{E}}}\_{x \sim {p}\_{\mathrm{data}}\left(x\right)}\left[\log \left(D\left(x\right)\right)\right]+{{\mathbb{E}}}\_{z \sim {p}\_{z}\left(z\right)}\left[\log \left(1-D\left(G\left(z\right)\right)\right)\right]$$

(6)

This adversarial training improves the Generator’s ability to produce high-resolution artwork that closely mirrors the diversity and stylistic richness of the training dataset.

### RL integration

The integration of RL in the system introduces the element of interactivity, where the piece of artwork created can change in real-time based on the interactions with the user, e.g., clicks or zooms. The RL agent dynamically changes the different visual elements of the work, like the color scheme, composition, and texture, as the user interacts with it. The reward function is meant to provide feedback to the RL agent in these interactions. The rewarding mechanism \({R}\_{t}\) is given as

$$\,{R}\_{t}=f\left({s}\_{t,}{a}\_{t}\right)$$

(7)

Where \({s}\_{t}\) is the state of the artwork at time \(t,{a}\_{t}\) Is the action taken by the RL agent, and \({R}\_{t}\) Represents the feedback received. The RL agent aims to maximize the cumulative reward over time, computed as:

$${\mathscr{R}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits\_{t=0}^{T}{\gamma }^{t}{R}\_{t}$$

(8)

Where *γ* is the discount factor, and *T* is the time horizon. The agent updates its policy. \({\pi }\_{\theta }\left({a|s}\right)\) Using Policy Gradient methods, the gradient is computed as:

$$\,{\nabla }\_{\theta }J\left(\theta \right)={\mathbb{E}}\left[{\nabla }\_{\theta }\log {\pi }\_{\theta }\left({a}\_{t}|{s}\_{t}\right){R}\_{t}\right]$$

(9)

In this way, the RL agent can constantly modify the artwork based on what the user likes and what the user does, ensuring that the art is dynamically modified as time goes on. To ensure the two parts of the GAN and RL perform to their highest level of performance, the system employs the PSO. PSO is motivated by the collective behavior of birds or fish, which means that each particle is a possible solution in the hyperparameter space.

Each particle *i* adjusts its velocity. \({\upsilon }\_{i}\left(t\right)\) and position \({x}\_{i}\left(t\right)\). At time *t* based on its personal best experience and the experiences of its neighbors. The velocity update is given by:

$$\,{\upsilon }\_{i}\left(t+1\right)={\omega \upsilon }\_{i}\left(t\right)+{c}\_{1}{r}\_{1}\left({p}\_{\mathrm{best},i}-{x}\_{i}\left(t\right)\right)+{c}\_{2}{r}\_{2}\left({g}\_{\mathrm{best}}-{g}\_{\mathrm{best}}-{x}\_{i}\left(t\right)\right)$$

(10)

Where *w* is the inertia weight \({c}\_{1}\) and \({c}\_{2}\) are acceleration coefficients, and \({r}\_{1}\) and \({r}\_{2}\) are random numbers. This ensures efficient exploration of the hyperparameter space, optimizing key parameters such as the learning rate, latent space size, and network architecture. PSO allows the system to converge more quickly, improving the efficiency and performance of the GAN and RL models.

### PSO-based hyperparameter optimization

Considering the sensitivity of GANs to the parameters of hyperparameters, particle swarm optimization (PSO) was also used to tune the unimportant parameters of training. The optimization was based on learning rate, momentum, latent noise variance, and the ratio between the update of the generator and the discriminator, with the aim of the optimization to improve adversarial stability and reduce mode collapse. In this model, every particle is a candidate set of hyperparameters in a multidimensional search space, whose value is updated in accordance with personal best fitness and global best fitness. The fitness function combines minimized Frechet inception distance (FID), maximized inception score (IS), and minimized generator loss variance together to assess image quality, diversity, and convergence stability. Through a tradeoff between exploration and exploitation, PSO converges well to optimal configurations to maximize fidelity and diversity in generated artworks.

Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is used to tune key hyperparameters \((\eta ,\,\lambda ,\,\alpha )\) for GAN and RL components. The velocity update rule for each particle \(i\) is:

$${v}\_{i}^{t+1}={{wv}}\_{i}^{t}+{c}\_{1}{r}\_{1}\left({p}\_{i}-{x}\_{i}^{t}\right)+{c}\_{2}{r}\_{2}(g-{x}\_{i}^{t})$$

(11)

where \(w\) is the inertia weight, \({c}\_{1}\) and \({c}\_{2}\) are acceleration coefficients, and \({r}\_{1}\), \({r}\_{2}\) are random factors. This process accelerates convergence and improves generative stability.

### Implementation details for reproducibility

The hybrid GAN-RL-PSO architecture was adopted with clearly defined settings of the architectural and optimization settings to guarantee reproducibility. The Generator is encircled by 4 transposed convolutional layers (kernels = 4, strides = 2, padding = 1) with a batch normalization and ReLU activation, followed by a final tanh layer generating 256 × 256 × 3 RGB images at a 100-dimensional latent code sampled by a standard normal distribution. The Discriminator has four convolutional layers with the same kernel parameters, LeakyReLU activation (*a* = 0.2), and the last sigmoid layer. Both networks were trained using the Adam optimizer (learning rate = 2 × 10−⁴, *β*₁ = 0.5, *β*₂ = 0.999) with binary cross-entropy loss.

Adaptive interaction in the reinforcement learning (RL) module is presented by an environment that is modeled (S, A, R). The state \({S}\_{t}\) combines latent representations of generated images as well as real-time user interaction measures (e.g., cursor motion, zoom/pan action, and attention time). The action space is continuously varied with the latent inputs to the generator to change the color palette, scale of texture and compositional structure. The reward aspect is formulated as

$${r}\_{t}=\alpha {E}\_{t}+\beta {Q}\_{t}+\gamma {C}\_{t}$$

(12)

where \({E}\_{t}\) represents normalized engagement, \({Q}\_{t}\) user satisfaction, and \({C}\_{t}\) a latent-space creativity coefficient; coefficients were set to *α* = 0.4, *β* = 0.4, *γ* = 0.2. Policy optimization employed a Policy Gradient method (learning rate = 1 × 10⁻⁴, batch size = 32, discount factor = 0.95) with updates every ten interaction cycles.

Particle Swarm optimization (PSO) was applied for joint hyperparameter refinement across GAN and RL modules. Thirty particles evolved over fifty iterations (inertia weight *w* = 0.7; acceleration coefficients *c*₁ = 1.4, *c*₂ = 1.6). The search space included GAN learning rates [1e−⁵, 1e−³] and RL reward weights (*α*, *β*, *γ*) within [0.1, 0.5], with a fitness function minimizing FID while maximizing user engagement.

Experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM), Intel Core i9-13900K CPU, and 64 GB RAM using PyTorch 2.1 and TensorFlow 2.15. GAN pretraining required approximately 7 h, followed by 1.5 h of RL fine-tuning, enabling reliable replication of the proposed framework.

### Algorithm 1

**GAN training procedure (DCGAN configuration)**

* Input: Real image batch \({x}\_{\mathrm{real}} \sim {D}\_{\mathrm{train}}\); latent vectors \(z \sim N(0.I)\)
* Output: Trained Generator (G) and Discriminator (D)
* Initialize the Generator (G) and Discriminator (D) with random weights. Set the optimizer as Adam (learning rate = 2 × 10−⁴, *β*₁ = 0.5, *β*₂ = 0.999).
* For each training epoch:
* For each minibatch of real images \({x}\_{\mathrm{real}}\) from the training set:

  + Train the Discriminator:
* Sample random noise \(z\) from the latent space.
* Generate fake images \({x}\_{\mathrm{fake}}=G(z)\).
* Compute the discriminator loss
* \({L}\_{D}=-[\log D\left({x}\_{\mathrm{real}}\right)+\log (1-D({x}\_{{fake}}))]\).
* Update D to minimize \({L}\_{D}\).

  + Train the Generator:
* Sample new noise \(z\) from \(p(z)\).
* Generate fake images \({x}\_{\mathrm{fake}}=G(z)\).
* Compute the generator loss \({L}\_{G}=-\log (D({x}\_{\mathrm{fake}}))\).
* Update G to minimize \({L}\_{G}\).
* Repeat until convergence or until the Fréchet inception distance (FID) stabilizes.
* Return the trained Generator (G) and Discriminator (D).

### Algorithm 2

Reinforcement Learning (RL) Interaction Loop

* Input: Artwork state \({s}\_{t}\); user engagement metrics \({e}\_{t}\) (clicks, zooms, dwell time)
* Output: Updated artwork parameters *a t* a t and evolved image \(G(z,\,{a}\_{t})\)
* Initialize policy parameters \(\theta\) for the RL agent.
* For each interaction cycle \(t=1\) to \(T\):
* Observe current state \({s}\_{t}\) (visual features + engagement data).
* Select action \({a}\_{t} \sim {\pi }\_{\theta }({a}\_{t}/{s}\_{t})\): modify style, color, or texture.
* Generate new artwork \(G(z,{a}\_{t})\) and display it to the user.
* Collect feedback metrics \({e}\_{t}\) (interaction time, satisfaction score, engagement level).
* Compute reward:
* \({r}\_{t}=\,\alpha \cdot \mathrm{Engagement}+\,\beta \cdot \mathrm{Satisfaction}+\gamma \cdot \mathrm{Creativity}\,\mathrm{index}\)
* Update policy parameters:
* \(\theta \leftarrow \theta \eta {r}\_{t}{\nabla }\_{\theta }\log {\pi }\_{\theta }({a}\_{t}/{s}\_{t})\)
* Continue until the cumulative reward converges.
* Return optimized policy \({\pi }\_{\theta }^{\* }\).

### Algorithm 3

Particle swarm optimization (PSO) configuration and tuning

* Input:
* Swarm of particles \(P=\{{p}\_{1},\ldots ,{p}\_{N}\}\); parameter bounds for learning rates and reward weights \((\alpha ,\,\beta ,\,\gamma )\)
* Output:
* Optimized parameter configuration \({\theta }^{\* }\)
* Initialize *N* = 30 particles with random positions within parameter bounds.
* Assign initial velocities \({v}\_{i}=0\); set inertia weight \(w=0.7\); learning coefficients \({c}\_{1}={c}\_{2}=1.5\).
* Evaluate fitness for each particle:
* \({f}\_{i}={w}\_{1}\left(1/\mathrm{FID}({G}\_{i})\right)+{w}\_{2}({\mathrm{Engagement}}\_{i})\)
* For each iteration (max = 50):
* Update velocity:
* \({v}\_{i}={{wv}}\_{i}+{c}\_{1}{r}\_{1}\left({p}\_{i}^{\mathrm{best}}-{p}\_{i}\right)+{c}\_{2}{r}\_{2}({g}^{\mathrm{best}}-{p}\_{i})\)
* Update position:
* \({p}\_{i}={p}\_{i}+{v}\_{i}\)
* Re-evaluate fitness; update \({p}\_{i}^{\mathrm{best}}\) and \({g}^{\mathrm{best}}\).
* Stop when global best fitness stabilizes or reaches threshold *ε* = 1e−³.
* Return the best configuration \({\theta }^{\* }={g}^{\mathrm{best}}\).

### Training process

The hybrid architecture is trained in 2 successive steps: GAN pretraining and fine-tuning it with RL. During the pretraining phase, GAN is trained using the WikiArt dataset or adversarial minimax loss whereby Generator is trained to generate fake images using latent noise vectors and a few samples are real and the others fake due to the Generator. To generate visually consistent and naturalistic output, the Generator is trained with a modified training that provides the Generator with the pattern of style, texture, and structure of the composition in a gradual learning process. After convergence, a reinforcement learning (RL) agent is introduced to enable the adaptive refinement, which is possible based on real-time user interaction aspects such as clicks, zoom behavior, and duration of attention. Based on the policy gradient framework, the agent is formulated to maximize an expression of rewarding value by the use of engagement measures, satisfaction measures, and creativity measures by adjusting visual properties in a continuous action space, e.g., the distribution of color, the texture of objects, and the focus of the composition. Two step training enables this to be possible so that there is high visual fidelity that is learned through adversarial training and high visual fidelity is achieved through user-driven optimization resulting in a realistic and adaptively-creative generative system.

### Evaluation metrics

The proposed system was tested through both quantitative and qualitative measures in reference to artistic quality, interactivity, and computer efficiency. The concept (realism) was measured with the help of a user-rated questionnaire (scale: 1–100) and it was an indicator of perceived visual authenticity of the works in comparison to traditional artworks. Creativity was also measured through ratings by the participants regarding novelty, originality, and esthetic value, which shows the capability of the system to produce something non-repeated, of stylistically different outputs. Interactivity and engagement were measured by behavioral analytics, including frequency of clicks, zoom/pan operations, and time of interaction and related to responsiveness and the capacity to respond to the relevant variables and conditions of the RL module. The viability of the operation with respect to interactive deployment was quantified by the evaluation of the training time, convergence iterations and real-time generation latency to achieve the viability. Finally, the user satisfaction was gathered with the help of the post-experiment questionnaires to receive the overall experience and perceived usability. There are the perceptual measures of visual fidelity, behavioral measures of adaptive creativity, and practical efficiency, all combined into one measure of visual fidelity.

This academic article published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (Volume 13, 2026) presents a hybrid framework combining Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to generate dynamic, interactive digital artworks that evolve in real-time based on audience engagement.

**Key Components:**
- **GANs** generate realistic images
- **RL** enables adaptive responsiveness to user interactions (clicks, zooms, dwell time)
- **PSO** optimizes hyperparameters for faster convergence and higher generative quality
- **PCA** with style transfer reduces dimensionality while preserving stylistic diversity

**Training Data:** WikiArt dataset of over 80,000 paintings, augmented with synthetic datasets via style transfer and image augmentation.

**Methodology:** Images resized to 256×256, normalized to [0,1], with augmentation (rotation, flipping, cropping, color jittering). Features extracted via pre-trained VGG16, reduced via PCA. K-means clustering used for stylistic grouping.

**Results:** The proposed GAN-RL-PSO system achieved superior performance compared to StyleGAN2, VQGAN+CLIP, and diffusion models:
- FID: 14.8 (lowest)
- Inception Score: 4.52 (highest)
- CLIP-score: 0.81 (highest)
- User study (200 participants) on 5-point Likert scale: Realism (M=4.6, SD=0.8), Creativity (M=4.5, SD=0.7), Interactivity (M=4.4, SD=0.6)

**System Performance (0-100 scale):** Realism 85, Creativity 90, Interactivity 78, Efficiency 70, User Satisfaction 88.

**Implementation:** NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM), Intel Core i9-13900K, 64GB RAM, PyTorch 2.1, TensorFlow 2.15. GAN pretraining ~7 hours, RL fine-tuning ~1.5 hours.

The paper contributes a reproducible framework for computational creativity, advancing human-AI co-creation and interactive aesthetic design in digital media art.

## Guide to the EU AI Act - Summary

The EU AI Act, adopted in March 2024, is the world's first comprehensive AI regulation, categorizing AI applications by risk level and setting requirements for transparency, oversight, and accountability. Implementation is staggered: prohibited AI practices and AI literacy requirements took effect on February 2, 2025, with most remaining provisions applying from August 2, 2026. Under the Digital Omnibus on AI (fully adopted and in force as of July 2026), Annex III high-risk obligations have been extended to December 2, 2027, with a further extension to August 2, 2028 for systems governed by existing EU sectoral safety legislation.

**Key Milestones:**
- **February 2, 2025:** Prohibited AI practices, AI literacy obligations, and Article 50 transparency requirements for user-facing AI systems came into force.
- **August 2, 2026:** Article 50 transparency obligations apply (machine-readable labeling deadline extended to December 2, 2026 for content already on the market).
- **December 2, 2027:** High-risk (Annex III) obligations apply under the Digital Omnibus extension.

**Prohibited AI Practices:** Manipulative techniques, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring, predictive crime risk assessments, untargeted facial recognition scraping, emotion inference in workplaces/schools, biometric categorization based on sensitive characteristics, and real-time remote biometric identification in public for law enforcement (with limited exceptions).

**Penalties:** Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for transparency violations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect information. SMEs and startups are subject to the lower figure.

**Risk Categories:**
- **Unacceptable risk** – banned entirely
- **High risk** – permitted subject to assessments, documentation, human oversight (includes healthcare, employment, law enforcement, critical infrastructure, education, border management)
- **General Purpose AI (GPAI)** – transparency requirements, training data summaries, copyright compliance; systemic-risk GPAIs face additional obligations including evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting, and cybersecurity
- **Minimal/no risk** – no restrictions

**AI Literacy:** Providers and deployers must ensure staff develop sufficient AI knowledge and skills, regardless of risk level.

**Governance:** An AI Office within the European Commission will coordinate enforcement. In March 2026, the European Parliament approved the EU's signature of the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, the first legally binding international AI treaty.

**Consent & Data Privacy:** Companies collecting or processing personal data for AI training must obtain valid consent, maintain transparency, and update consent when purposes change. Article 50 requires disclosure when interacting with AI systems (chatbots, virtual assistants), labeling of AI-generated content, and notification of emotion recognition/biometric systems.

**Exemptions for Law Enforcement:** Real-time biometric identification in public requires prior judicial authorization, is limited to specific serious crimes and emergencies (terrorism, missing persons, trafficking), and is restricted by time and location.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The **Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act)** is a European Union regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) concerning artificial intelligence, establishing a common regulatory and legal framework for AI within the EU. It entered into force on 1 August 2024, with provisions phased in over 6 to 36 months. The Act was proposed by the European Commission on 21 April 2021, passed by the European Parliament on 13 March 2024 (523-46-49), and unanimously approved by the EU Council on 21 May 2024.

**Key Provisions:**
- **Risk-based classification** of non-exempt AI applications into four levels: unacceptable risk (banned), high-risk (subject to security, transparency, and quality obligations), limited risk (transparency obligations), and minimal risk (unregulated). A separate category for general-purpose AI (e.g., ChatGPT) was added in 2023.
- **Exemptions** for AI used for military, national security, or pure scientific research purposes.
- **Governance bodies** established: AI Office (European Commission), European Artificial Intelligence Board, Advisory Forum, and Scientific Panel of Independent Experts.
- **Penalties** for non-compliance: up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for banned practices; up to €15 million or 3% for other violations.
- **Regulatory sandboxes** for controlled testing environments.
- The Act applies extraterritorially to providers outside the EU with users within the EU.

**Reactions:**

--- SOURCE 9: EU AI Act - Updates, Compliance, Training ---
URL: https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# EU AI Act Summary

## Overview
The EU AI Act is a comprehensive regulatory framework establishing harmonised rules for the development, placement on the market, and use of AI systems in the European Union. It follows a proportionate, risk-based approach categorizing AI systems into four levels: unacceptable risk (prohibited), high risk, transparency risk, and minimal/no risk.

## Key Timeline (as of August 2026)
- **21 April 2021**: European Commission proposal published
- **9 December 2023**: Council and Parliament reach provisional agreement
- **13 March 2024**: European Parliament approves the AI Act (523 votes in favor)
- **12 July 2024**: Published in the Official Journal; enters into force August 1, 2024
- **2 February 2025**: Chapters I & II (general provisions and prohibited practices) apply
- **4 February 2025**: Commission publishes Guidelines on prohibited AI practices
- **6 February 2025**: Commission publishes Guidelines on AI system definition
- **19 July 2025**: Commission approves Guidelines on GPAI model obligations
- **2 August 2025**: GPAI model obligations enter into application
- **17 March 2026**: EDPS publishes Compass for its role as market surveillance authority
- **7 May 2026**: Council and Parliament reach provisional agreement on Omnibus VII simplification measures
- **16 June 2026**: European Parliament approves simplification measures
- **20 July 2026**: Guidelines on Article 50 transparency obligations published
- **2 August 2026**: AI Act generally applies (current date)
- **2 December 2026**: Watermarking obligations and nudifier app ban apply
- **2 August 2027**: Article 6(1) on high-risk classification rules applies

## Eight Prohibited AI Practices
1. Harmful AI-based manipulation and deception (subliminal techniques)
2. Harmful exploitation of vulnerabilities (age, disability, socio-economic)
3. Social scoring systems
4. Individual criminal offense risk assessment/prediction
5. Untargeted scraping of internet/CCTV for facial recognition databases
6. Emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions
7. Biometric categorization to deduce protected characteristics
8. Real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement (with narrow exceptions)

## Risk Categories
- **Unacceptable risk**: Prohibited under Article 5
- **High risk**: Subject to requirements and conformity assessment (includes critical infrastructure, education, employment, healthcare, banking, law enforcement, migration, justice)
- **Transparency risk**: Subject to Article 50 transparency obligations
- **Minimal to no risk**: Not regulated; voluntary codes of conduct

## Key Developments in 2026
- **Omnibus VII simplification**: Postpones high-risk AI obligations (stand-alone: 2 Dec 2027; embedded safety components: 2 Aug 2028); delays watermarking to 2 Dec 2026; extends SME exemptions to small mid-caps (SMCs); bans nudifier apps
- **Article 50 Guidelines**: Extend transparency obligations to third-country providers/deployers whose output is used in the EU
- **EDPS Compass**: EDPS designated as market surveillance authority for EU institutions

## Overlap with Other Regulations
- **NIS 2 Directive**: Intersection on cyber resilience, risk management, incident reporting for AI systems in critical infrastructure
- **DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act)**: Dual compliance for AI in financial services (credit scoring, fraud detection, trading, AML)

## Definition of AI System
A machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from input how to generate outputs (predictions, content, recommendations, decisions) that can influence physical or virtual environments.

## Legal Interpretation Notes
- The Guidelines for Article 50 increase regulatory divergence between the US and EU
- Commercial divergence: Multinational AI providers may need different operational models for Europe vs. other jurisdictions
- Political divergence: Europe emphasizes societal protection; US policy emphasizes innovation and competitiveness
- The simplification measures reflect three realities: unrealistic timelines, competitiveness concerns, and need for standards availability
</summary>

The AI Act sets harmonised rules for the development, placement on the market and use of AI systems in the European Union, following a proportionate risk-based approach., The placing on the market, putting into service or use of certain AI systems intended to distort human behaviour, whereby physical or psychological harms are likely to occur, is forbidden., The Commission repeats that providers established in third countries remain subject to Article 50 whenever the output is used in the European Union., The AI Act remains the destination, but the original journey plan was unrealistic., Dual Compliance Burden is the regulatory challenge where companies and organizations must comply with two or more overlapping legal frameworks governing similar aspects of their operations.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a client alert from Lowenstein Sandler LLP, published October 31, 2024, authored by Mary J. Hildebrand, providing a comprehensive overview of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024. The Act, effective August 2, 2024, is the world's first comprehensive legal framework for regulating AI, with most provisions phased in over two years.

**Key points covered:**

1. **Extraterritorial Scope**: The Act applies to AI Systems placed on the EU market or used in the EU by companies worldwide, and has influenced U.S. AI policy (including President Biden's Executive Order) and state AI laws.

2. **Risk-Based Approach**: Four risk categories exist:
   - **Unacceptable Risk**: Banned as of February 2, 2025 (e.g., manipulative techniques, facial recognition scraping, social scoring)
   - **High Risk**: Subject to strict mandatory requirements (e.g., biometrics, critical infrastructure, employment, education, law enforcement)
   - **Limited Risk**: Transparency requirements for chatbots and deep fakes
   - **Minimal Risk**: No mandatory requirements (e.g., spam filters)

3. **Regulated Entities**: Providers (developers) face the most stringent obligations; Deployers/Users, Importers, and Distributors have more limited requirements but may become directly responsible if they rebrand or substantially modify AI Systems.

4. **General-Purpose AI Models (GPAI)**: Later additions covering generative AI, with additional obligations for high-impact models with systemic risk.

5. **Penalties**: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for banned AI Systems. Startups/SMEs subject to lower of same percentages.

6. **Next Steps**: Organizations should inventory AI Systems, audit risk levels, establish data governance, and train stakeholders. Compliance roadmaps should remain flexible as laws evolve.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report (May 2024) by the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence (GPAI) provides a comprehensive overview of algorithmic transparency instruments in the public sector, with a focus on repositories/registers of public algorithms. 

**Key Concepts:** Algorithmic transparency is a multifaceted concept encompassing capacity, principle, standard, right, obligation, and instrument. It derives from democratic rights to information and enables oversight, accountability, and protection of fundamental rights (due process, access to services). Transparency is not absolute and may be limited by privacy, intellectual property, and national security concerns.

**Classification of Instruments:** The report proposes a new taxonomy:
1. **Supply-driven (proactive) instruments:** Repositories of public algorithms, user-driven proactive publications, and automated responses triggered by user interactions.
2. **Demand-driven (reactive) instruments:** Responses to information requests and judge-ordered disclosures.

**Mapping of Repositories:** The report mapped 79 repositories of public algorithms worldwide. Of these, 87% are active, 9% under construction, and 4% deactivated. By publisher: 62% national public bodies, 21% subnational public bodies, 8% civil society/private organizations, 6% universities, and 3% supranational bodies. The US leads with 37 active repositories, followed by the Netherlands (14), France (4), and Colombia (3). Notable repositories include the UK's Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (37 variables per system), AI-WATCH (46 variables), and Colombia's systems registry (40 variables).

The report is the first phase of a larger project that will include three in-depth case studies with stakeholder interviews.
</summary>

Feature papers are submitted upon individual invitation or recommendation by the scientific editors and must receive positive feedback from the reviewers.

Editor’s Choice articles are based on recommendations by the scientific editors of MDPI journals from around the world. Editors select a small number of articles recently published in the journal that they believe will be particularly interesting to readers, or important in the respective research area. The aim is to provide a snapshot of some of the most exciting work published in the various research areas of the journal.

 Lisa Khairil is a Biomedical Science student with a strong academic focus on laboratory and clinical research. She is currently pursuing her studies in Malaysia, where she has developed practical and theoretical expertise in areas such as microbiology, haematology, molecular diagnostics, and laboratory techniques. Her academic training includes hands-on experience in centrifugation, chromatography, microscopy, and clinical specimen handling, alongside research exposure in experimental design and data analysis. In addition to her academic work, Lisa is actively involved in student-led scientific initiatives, contributing to collaborative projects and academic events through club organisations such as the Biovarsity Club at Management & Science University, Shah Alam. Her research interests include neuroscience, diagnostic innovation, and the application of artificial intelligence in laboratory medicine. She aims to pursue a career in biomedical research and clinical diagnostics, with a long-term goal of contributing to advancements in disease detection and personalised medicine. They are committed to continuous learning and aspire to publish high-quality research in peer-reviewed scientific journals.

                        <strong>Figure 2</strong><br/>
                                                    <p>Regulatory pathways and the clinical validation gap in AI diagnostics. The schematic illustrates U.S. Food and Drug Administration pathways for AI diagnostic device authorisation. In contrast, de novo and premarket approval pathways involve higher evidentiary requirements. These findings suggest that strong computational performance does not necessarily ensure reliable clinical generalisability.</p>

## Abstract

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the life sciences has accelerated significantly between 2022 and 2026, accompanied by global investment exceeding USD 100 billion and widespread expectations of a transformative impact in drug discovery. Despite these advances, the extent to which AI has improved clinical outcomes remains unclear. This study presents a structured narrative review evaluating the economic, technical, clinical, and regulatory dimensions of AI adoption in drug discovery. Current evidence indicates that clinical attrition rates remain high, with approximately 90% of drug candidates entering clinical development failing to achieve regulatory approval. Although AI systems such as AlphaFold have achieved high structural prediction accuracy, with predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) scores exceeding 90 for well-structured proteins and root mean square deviation (RMSD) values comparable to experimental methods, limitations persist in modelling protein dynamics, post-translational modifications, and protein–ligand interactions. Clinical case studies demonstrate that while AI can accelerate early-stage discovery timelines, these advantages do not consistently translate into improved late-stage success rates. Furthermore, reproducibility challenges, limited data transparency, and regulatory gaps continue to constrain reliable implementation. These findings suggest that AI in drug discovery is currently in a transitional phase characterised by high investment but limited validated clinical impact. Future progress will depend on strengthening validation frameworks, improving data sharing practices, and aligning regulatory standards with real-world clinical performance.

[AlphaFold](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=AlphaFold); [drug discovery](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=drug+discovery); [artificial intelligence](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=artificial+intelligence); [protein structure prediction](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=protein+structure+prediction); [reproducibility crisis](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=reproducibility+crisis); [clinical translation](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=clinical+translation); [AI bubble](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=AI+bubble)

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Evolution of Artificial Intelligence in Life Sciences

Artificial intelligence (AI) has undergone rapid development within the life sciences, progressing from traditional machine learning approaches to more advanced deep learning architectures, large-scale foundation models, and generative systems capable of designing novel biological entities. This technological evolution has been accompanied by substantial financial investment and growing expectations that AI will significantly accelerate drug discovery processes. However, the translation of computational advances into clinically effective therapies remains uncertain, as clinical attrition rates in pharmaceutical development remain high, with approximately 90% of drug candidates failing to achieve regulatory approval [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B1-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)].

The evolution of AI in the life sciences can be broadly classified into four stages: (i) conventional machine learning (ML), involving statistical prediction models; (ii) deep learning (DL), employing multilayer neural networks for high-dimensional biological data; (iii) foundation models trained on large-scale multimodal datasets; and (iv) generative biology systems capable of designing novel proteins, molecular structures, and biological interactions. Machine learning methods initially enabled pattern recognition in biological datasets, while deep learning facilitated the analysis of complex, high-dimensional data such as genomic sequences and medical images. More recently, foundation models trained on large biological datasets have enabled generalisable representations, while generative models have expanded the scope of AI applications to include de novo molecular design and protein engineering [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B2-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B3-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)].

### 1.2. Study Hypothesis and Objectives

This review hypothesises that despite substantial advances in computational capability and investment, current AI-driven drug discovery platforms remain constrained by biological complexity, limited reproducibility, and insufficient clinical validation.

## 2. Methodology

### 2.1. Literature Search Strategy

A structured narrative review methodology was employed to evaluate the clinical, technical, economic, and regulatory dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) in drug discovery and life sciences between 2017 and 2026. Literature searches were conducted using the PubMed (National Center for Biotechnology Information, Bethesda, MD, USA), Scopus (Elsevier B.V., Amsterdam, The Netherlands), Web of Science (Clarivate Analytics, Philadelphia, PA, USA), and Google Scholar (Google LLC, Mountain View, CA, USA) databases. Additional regulatory and industry reports were retrieved from official sources including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and major pharmaceutical or biotechnology company reports.

The search strategy combined keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms including: “artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “deep learning”, “drug discovery”, “AlphaFold”, “AI in healthcare”, “clinical validation”, “reproducibility crisis”, “AI regulation”, “FDA AI guidance”, “digital health”, “generative biology”, “protein structure prediction”. Boolean operators (“AND”, “OR”) were used to refine database searches.

### 2.2. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Studies were included if they: were published between January 2017 and February 2026; were written in English; included peer-reviewed original research articles, systematic reviews, clinical trial reports, regulatory guidance documents, or high-impact industry analyses; and addressed AI applications in drug discovery, diagnostics, structural biology, clinical trials, or biomedical regulation. Studies were excluded if they: lacked methodological transparency; were non-scientific opinion pieces without supporting evidence; focused exclusively on non-biomedical AI applications; or contained duplicated or superseded findings.

### 2.3. Study Selection and Screening

Titles and abstracts identified through database searching were initially screened for relevance. Full-text articles were subsequently reviewed to determine eligibility based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Priority was given to studies with quantitative validation, regulatory relevance, multicentre datasets, or clinically translated outcomes. In addition to peer-reviewed literature, selected regulatory guidance documents, public clinical trial databases (ClinicalTrials.gov), and financial analyses relevant to AI-biotechnology investment trends were incorporated to provide a contextual evaluation of translational and economic challenges.

### 2.4. Data Extraction and Narrative Synthesis

Relevant information relating to AI-assisted drug discovery timelines, clinical trial outcomes, regulatory developments, reproducibility concerns, validation frameworks, and economic investment trends was extracted and synthesised narratively. Emphasis was placed on identifying discrepancies between computational performance claims and clinically validated outcomes.

## 3. The Economic Dimensions of the AI Bubble

### 3.1. Investment Surge (2022–2026)

Between 2022 and 2026, the life sciences investment landscape changed substantially due to the increasing adoption of AI technologies. In 2024, global investment in healthcare reached a peak, with total funding exceeding USD 100 billion, representing an 80% increase from the previous year [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B4-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. In the first quarter of 2025, spending on healthcare AI had nearly tripled compared to 2024 levels, reaching about USD 1.4 billion [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B5-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. In the first half of 2025, 62% of all digital health investments went to AI-focused startups, representing a substantial increase in venture capital allocation toward AI-focused healthcare platforms [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B6-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. Several AI-focused biotechnology firms experienced rapid valuation growth during this period, reflecting strong investor expectations regarding the potential of AI-assisted therapeutic discovery and precision medicine platforms. As part of the broader investment surge in 2026, NVIDIA and Eli Lilly announced a landmark $1 billion AI co-innovation lab aimed at transforming pharmaceutical research and development [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B7-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. These investment patterns suggest that commercial enthusiasm for AI healthcare platforms expanded substantially faster than the accumulation of clinically validated therapeutic outcomes. Although global AI healthcare investment exceeded USD 100 billion, this still represents a relatively small proportion of the estimated USD 300–350 billion annual global pharmaceutical R&D expenditure.

### 3.2. The AI Hype Cycle in Drug Discovery

The adoption of AI in drug discovery follows a trajectory consistent with the Gartner Hype Cycle ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#fig_body_display_pharmaceuticals-19-00916-f001)), characterised by an initial phase of rapid technological breakthroughs and inflated expectations, followed by a period of disillusionment driven by practical limitations in clinical translation. Early successes, particularly in protein structure prediction and molecular modelling, contributed to heightened optimism regarding the potential of AI to revolutionise pharmaceutical research. However, subsequent challenges in validation, reproducibility, and regulatory approval have tempered these expectations, highlighting a gap between theoretical capability and real-world implementation [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B3-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)].

![Image 19: Pharmaceuticals 19 00916 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/pharmaceuticals/pharmaceuticals-19-00916/article_deploy/html/images/pharmaceuticals-19-00916-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#fig_body_display_pharmaceuticals-19-00916-f001)

**Figure 1.** Adapted Gartner-style technology adoption curve illustrating major phases of AI expansion in life sciences between 2022 and 2026. The figure integrates representative indicators including investment growth, FDA-authorised AI-enabled medical devices, clinical attrition rates, regulatory adaptation, and translational validation challenges. 

The progression through the Gartner Hype Cycle was associated with measurable indicators including venture capital inflows exceeding USD 100 billion, increasing FDA submissions for AI-enabled medical products, rapid growth in AI-biotech partnerships, and subsequent market corrections among publicly traded AI-drug discovery firms.

Examples of measurable indicators associated with these phases include venture capital investment exceeding USD 100 billion globally, more than 950 FDA-authorised AI-enabled medical devices by 2025, increasing AI-biotechnology merger activity, and persistent clinical attrition rates comparable to traditional pharmaceutical development.

### 3.3. Mega-Rounds and Market Concentration

Large funding rounds exceeding USD 100 million increasingly dominated the investment landscape during this period [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B8-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. Large-scale funding rounds accounted for approximately 46% of total investment in digital health companies during the first quarter of 2025, indicating a strong concentration of capital among a limited number of firms. Representative examples include Xaira Therapeutics, which raised over USD 1 billion in launch funding [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B9-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)], and Lila Sciences, which secured approximately USD 550 million to support AI-guided biological engineering platforms [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B10-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. Major technology companies, including Microsoft, Google, and NVIDIA, have established strategic partnerships with biotechnology firms to capitalise on this trend [[11](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B11-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. As of 2023, most of the investment is still in the United States, which received USD 67 billion in AI healthcare funding, much more than China’s USD 7.8 billion [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B12-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. There is a heavy concentration of money in a few companies and a single country. This concentration of capital may increase sector-wide vulnerability if highly valued AI-biotechnology platforms fail to achieve clinically validated translational outcomes. Overall, setbacks among a small number of dominant firms may disproportionately influence investor confidence across the broader AI-biotechnology sector.

The concentration of AI healthcare investment among a limited number of firms suggests increasing market centralisation. This trend may be quantified using the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI), commonly applied in economic competition analysis, where a small number of large funding rounds disproportionately dominated total sector investment.

Representative funding figures summarised in [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#table_body_display_pharmaceuticals-19-00916-t001) were obtained from publicly reported investment disclosures and industry analyses [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B8-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[9](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B9-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B10-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B11-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B12-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)].

![Image 20](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#table_body_display_pharmaceuticals-19-00916-t001)

### 3.4. Valuation Concerns and Market Corrections

Without clear evidence of a measurable return on investment, increasing signs emerged that some companies may have been overvalued as the current AI-driven valuation cycle reached its peak. The rapid growth of AI-biotech platforms between 2020 and 2026 was accompanied by unprecedented investor enthusiasm, followed by periods of valuation correction [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B13-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[14](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B14-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. As once-prominent AI firms struggled to meet important clinical milestones, the market started to see many company mergers and restructuring efforts by the end of 2024. After their early clinical results failed to meet the high expectations set when they raised funding, companies like BenevolentAI, Exscientia and Recursion experienced internal changes and saw their market values decline [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B15-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. BenevolentAI experienced substantial valuation contraction following pipeline setbacks, while several AI-biotech firms reported substantial valuation declines during 2024 market corrections. A clear example of this trend was Recursion acquiring Exscientia in 2024. Companies with strong biological research and those that were primarily driven by speculative investment enthusiasm began to be distinguished by the market after these changes. These developments suggest a shift toward investment strategies that prioritise demonstrated clinical outcomes over algorithmic novelty.

### 3.5. Return on Investment Reality

The discrepancy between substantial investment and the limited number of clinically successful AI-assisted therapeutics represents a major challenge for the current technology valuation cycle. Demonstrating a clear return on investment remains challenging despite more than a decade of substantial investment and expectations that AI would accelerate drug development. Many AI-discovered candidates fail before reaching clinical testing, and only a limited number of AI-assisted therapeutics have progressed to regulatory approval. Although AI has accelerated candidate identification and early-stage discovery workflows, it has not yet reversed the persistent increases in pharmaceutical development costs and timelines despite substantial technological advances [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B16-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. Notably, clear evidence of improved commercial return on investment remains limited. Compared with traditional pharmaceutical development, current AI-assisted approaches have accelerated early-stage discovery but have not yet demonstrated substantially improved late-stage clinical success rates.

Recent analyses suggest that AI-assisted drug discovery platforms may reduce early-stage target identification and hit discovery timelines by approximately 30–70% compared with conventional workflows. However, despite accelerated computational screening and lead optimisation, overall clinical success rates remain broadly comparable to traditional pharmaceutical development, with estimated approval probabilities remaining within the industry baseline range of approximately 8–12%. Furthermore, available evidence indicates that reductions in late-stage development costs and regulatory timelines remain limited, as Phase II and Phase III attrition continue to be primarily driven by biological complexity, safety concerns, and insufficient clinical efficacy rather than computational inefficiency alone.

From an investment perspective, return on investment (ROI) in pharmaceutical R&D is commonly assessed using development timelines, clinical success probabilities, and overall development costs. Although AI-assisted platforms have demonstrated measurable reductions in target identification and lead optimisation timelines, evidence for proportional improvements in clinical approval rates or late-stage development efficiency remains limited. Therefore, the economic value of AI currently appears to derive primarily from early-stage productivity gains rather than from substantial reductions in overall development risk or clinical attrition.

To date, only a limited number of AI-assisted therapeutics have reached commercialisation. Therefore, direct ROI calculations based on product revenue remain premature. Thus, development timelines, attrition rates, and clinical progression metrics are currently used as surrogate indicators of economic performance.

Estimates presented in [Table 2](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#table_body_display_pharmaceuticals-19-00916-t002) are derived from published analyses of AI-assisted drug discovery timelines, pharmaceutical development benchmarks, clinical success rate studies, and industry assessments of pharmaceutical R&D productivity and return on investment [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B16-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[17](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B17-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[18](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B18-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[19](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B19-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[20](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B20-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B21-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B22-pharmaceuticals-19-00916),[23](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916#B23-pharmaceuticals-19-00916)]. # Beyond Legacy Tools: Defining Modern AI Drug Discovery for 2025 and Beyond

---

by [Andrii Buvailo, PhD](https://www.linkedin.com/in/andriibuvailo/), [Oleg Kucheriavyi, PhD](https://www.linkedin.com/in/oleg-kucheriavyi/)  |  *updated on*

### In this report:

* Intro: The New Framework
* [“AI Drug Discovery” is About Holism](#section1)
* ["AI Drug Discovery" is About Building Software](#section2)
* [Access to Data is King](#section3)
* [Validation is Critical for AI Drug Discovery Platforms](#section4)
* [Grand Vision of AI Drug Discovery for 2025 and Beyond](#section5)

  

### Disclaimer

This report aims to provide an educational, balanced, and pragmatic perspective on AI-driven drug discovery (AIDD). No part of this report should be construed as promotional content or marketing communication.

Some companies featured are past or current clients, and certain organizations provided factual input during the research process. All analysis and conclusions were developed independently to ensure objectivity.

This report does not constitute investment advice or an endorsement. While we strive for accuracy and neutrality, we accept no liability for decisions made based on this content. Readers are encouraged to conduct their own due diligence.

In 2025, it seems there is still a lack of a robust definition of an emerging category of artificial intelligence-driven drug discovery companies (hereinafter, AIDD).

The purpose of this report is to suggest a qualitative framework for classification of AIDD companies, combining the four key attributes that define the leading players in this area:

* Focus on holism vs reductionism in biology
* Creating robust AI platforms (software)
* Priority of data acquisition
* Technology validation (via demonstrable ability to discover novel targets, discovery and develop clinical-grade drug candidates rapidly, a track record of platform partnerships, scientific publications, patents, and so on)

We will delve deeper into framework discussion below, but in a nutshell, it boils down to this:

 ![AI drug discovery (AIDD) framework](/static/img/ai_report/ai_pipelines_2024_framework.c5f2561ca38e.webp) 

Diagram 1

 

Indeed, abstracting from specific characteristics of a tech stack and platform design, there are three key value points of an AI platform on business outcome:

1. Is a computational platform scalable and robust enough to impact the R&D workflow, people collaboration patterns, and daily decision making of a wide range of specialists of a given organization to make a productivity difference?
2. Is it able to represent biology in silico down to sufficient depth, but also sufficient breadth to be able to grasp relevant and useful dependencies, patterns, network biology effects, to be able to impact scientific decision-making beyond mainstream research workflows?
3. Is the AI platform capable of addressing the above two questions in a repeatable, stable, standardized way across all levels of R&D workflows in the organization? Would a third-party collaborator be able to get sustainable value out of using the AI software if they had access?

In our opinion, AIDD is about being able to answer “yes” to all three questions. This is what makes the AIDD platform a tangible business asset.

## “AI Drug Discovery” is About Holism

As we explore the newly suggested framework, one key distinction emerges: the difference in what we attempt to model and represent computationally in today’s AI-driven landscape versus what was typically addressed using earlier generations of computational tools.

A helpful starting point is to consider the conceptual gap between traditional software—developed decades ago and still widely used in drug discovery for specific tasks—and modern AI-enabled platforms that are increasingly positioned as end-to-end solutions. While both types of tools play valuable roles, their underlying philosophies differ significantly.

In simple terms, “traditional” or “legacy” cheminformatics and bioinformatics rely on human-driven approaches: cheminformatics uses predefined chemical descriptors (like molecular weight or logP), statistical methods and some machine learning approaches for tasks like QSAR modeling and docking, while bioinformatics applies statistical methods, including dimensionality reduction techniques, to analyze complex biological datasets (e.g., genomics, proteomics) and uncover potential drug targets. These methods are hypothesis-driven, modular, and work with smaller, well-structured datasets.

> Conceptually, legacy computational systems and simpler machine learning methods are useful in the paradigm of “biological reductionism.” And they do a great job there, even today.

Classical reductionist approach example is structure-based drug discovery, where it is believed modulating a specific protein is an answer to a drug discovery problem (it sometimes is). The computational part, therefore, is mostly focused on narrow-scope tasks like fitting a ligand into a protein pocket (docking), or, computationally identifying a new type of chemistry for a given target (ligand-based virtual screening).

In stark contrast, cutting edge AI-driven drug discovery companies attempt to shift to a systems biology level, a **hypothesis-agnostic** approach, using deep learning-based systems to integrate largely multimodal data (phenotype, omics, patient data, chemical structures, texts, images, etc.) to construct complex and comprehensive biology representations (e.g. “knowledge graphs”).
