[![Jcp 05 00077 g004](/jcp/jcp-05-00077/article_deploy/html/images/jcp-05-00077-g004.png "Jcp 05 00077 g004")](/jcp/jcp-05-00077/article_deploy/html/images/jcp-05-00077-g004.png)

Qualitative comments (see [Section 4.6](#sec4dot6-jcp-05-00077)) also highlighted the role of false positives (reported by ~27% of users) in eroding trust in AI, even when they believed it was technically effective. This discrepancy shows the importance of explainability for ongoing use of a solution.

### 4.2. Reliability and Validity of Constructs

The reliability and validity assessment of the measurement model is presented in [Table 2](#table_body_display_jcp-05-00077-t002), which reports factor loadings, Cronbach’s alpha, composite reliability, and average variance extracted (AVE), confirming that the constructs meet accepted psychometric standards.

**Table 2.**
Measurement reliability and validity.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.3. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM)

The outcomes of the structural equation modelling are summarized in [Table 3](#table_body_display_jcp-05-00077-t003), where the standardized path coefficients and their significance levels provide empirical evidence for the hypothesized relationships.

**Table 3.**
Structural path results.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.4. Subgroup Analysis

Findings show urban users and younger participants report higher trust and adoption. Low literacy associates with higher perceived risk, and fraud victims report lower transparency satisfaction, consistent with false-positive frustration.

### 4.5. Integration with Theoretical Frameworks

The results adhere to three different theoretical frameworks.

* Privacy Calculus: Users recognize the benefits of AI fraud detection (91.2% saw it as more effective than conventional detection) but saw privacy risks (95.4% ranked as high risk); hence, there was less willingness among users to use AI fraud detection. As is the issue in the privacy and trust literature, the benefits do not outweigh the perceived losses (see Table 5).
* TAM/UTAUT: Perceived usefulness emerged as the strongest driver of trust, which ultimately predicts intention to adopt, while perceived ease of use in this case was not significant when trust and risk were accounted for. Although ease of use is a factor in adoption, it appears that trust is salient in security-sensitive contexts, and perceived usefulness will trump ease of use.
* XAI (Explainable AI): Transparency and explainability were significant predictors of trust in AI fraud detection. This suggests that if AI’s behaviours include transparency in communicating decisions, user confidence can be maximized, and, as a result, the negative effects of errors and false positives would be minimized.

Overall, the integration shows that adoption is not only a matter of technical effectiveness but also of managing privacy risks and improving transparency to strengthen trust.

### 4.6. Qualitative Themes

Quantitative analysis of open-ended responses to the survey (Q13–Q20) were conducted inductively using Braun and Clarke’s thematic coding framework. Coding and stemming were performed in NVivo. Three main themes emerged: Explainable AI decisions, privacy and data controls, and socio-regulatory context. The themes added context for the quantitative results which assisted in making the association between risk and trust perceptions in adopting AI.

Theme 1—Explainable AI Decisions

Participants frequently referenced the lack of explainability of AI-based fraud detection as a common concern. Many expressed their frustration in knowing nothing about why certain transactions were considered risky or when an account had been temporarily blocked. One participant explained their confusion:

> “I want to know why my transfer was flagged—was it the amount, location or something else?”

This describes a clear difference we see in the quantitative results where a total of 91.2% of participants believed AI was performing adequately (see [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_jcp-05-00077-f004)), while only 29.8% said they felt very satisfied with AI transparency (see [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_jcp-05-00077-f004)). Some participants described that Explainable AI (XAI) would again build their confidence by providing more quality/specificity in the alert and also some real-time communications.

Theme 2—Privacy and Data Ownership

Concerns about silent data collection were prevalent. Users seemed uncomfortable with the ability of the application to collect things like location, contact lists, and any related metadata without a clear path to consent. One user simply wrote:

> “Apps collect location and contacts without clearly telling me, who sees this and for how long?”

This further reinforces the quantitative results of users having privacy concerns with 94.4% (see [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_jcp-05-00077-f003)). Overall, these responses reflect the Privacy Calculus trade-off: users see the potential value of AI in being able to extract fraud, but they perceive high privacy risks, limiting adoption. Calls for standardized consent, clear policies, and data minimization were common.

Theme 3—Socio-regulatory Context

Trust in AI was heavily influenced by socio-regulatory context, meaning the social trust framework of society (legitimacy of regulators) and the cultural context. Respondents from countries with stronger enforcement of data protection laws reported greater trust (mean trust level 7), while other respondents were more suspicious of institutions because there was no enforcement. One respondent explained:

> “When rules are enforced, it is easier to trust AI, particularly if banks have to report incidents transparently”

This theme highlights why subgroup differences were present ([Table 3](#table_body_display_jcp-05-00077-t003)), with urban and digitally literate individuals reporting significantly greater trust compared to rural, low literacy groups. More importantly, for the purposes of this STF, regulatory trust and institutional transparency were key drivers of intention to adoption.

To explore heterogeneity across user groups, subgroup analyses were conducted, and the results are presented in [Table 4](#table_body_display_jcp-05-00077-t004), demonstrating significant differences in trust and adoption across demographic categories.

**Table 4.**
Subgroup differences in trust and adoption.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

**Integration of Themes**

These themes triangulated the quantitative findings:

* Explainability accounts for the dissatisfaction toward transparency after speaking highly of how effective the AI is.
* The concerns of privacy explain the 66.9% of participants who felt discomfort sharing their personal data.
* The regulatory context connects subgroups and variations in trust and adoption. In the final analysis, the qualitative evidence demonstrated that embracing AI-secured MFSs in emerging markets requires not only a technical but also a social and institutional understanding.

### 4.7. Comparative Analysis with Prior Studies

A comparative overview with prior studies is provided in [Table 5](#table_body_display_jcp-05-00077-t005), highlighting areas of convergence and divergence between the present findings and those reported in earlier research.

**Table 5.**
Comparison with prior findings.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

## 5. Discussion

### 5.1. Theoretical Integration

This study contributes to theoretical debates on technology adoption in mobile financial services (MFSs) by integrating three dominant models—Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Privacy Calculus, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). The results confirm that trust serves as the central mediator between perceived usefulness and adoption intention. In line with TAM [[16](#B16-jcp-05-00077)], users who perceived AI systems as effective in detecting fraud were significantly more likely to trust and subsequently adopt such solutions. However, ease of use—traditionally a strong determinant in TAM—was not significant once trust and privacy risks were considered. This suggests that in security-critical contexts such as financial services, trust outweighs usability, a finding consistent with recent extensions of TAM in high-risk domains.

The results also strongly support the Privacy Calculus framework [[17](#B17-jcp-05-00077)]; despite recognizing the superior effectiveness of AI compared to rule-based systems (91.2% agreement), users’ high levels of privacy concern (95.4%) significantly reduced their willingness to adopt (see [Table 5](#table_body_display_jcp-05-00077-t005)). This highlights the cost–benefit trade-off central to Privacy Calculus: perceived gains in fraud protection are offset by fears of data misuse, opaque data-sharing practices, and weak regulatory enforcement.

Finally, UTAUT [[7](#B7-jcp-05-00077)] is particularly useful for exploring contextual drivers. The subgroup analysis shows that urban users and digitally literate users had higher trust and adoption levels, whereas lower-literate users and users that had been defrauded had higher risk levels and lower satisfaction in transparency. Our findings add to UTAUT’s related existing literature as well, because although our analysis highlights the importance of facilitating conditions and social influence as constructs in UTAUT, we also show that culture-related expectations of fairness and institutional credibility are related to perceived ease of states and adoption.

### 5.2. Novel Contribution

This study represents a novel contribution by developing a hybrid framework that concurrently brings together TAM, Privacy Calculus, and UTAUT, while also integrating trust, transparency, and institutional legitimacy. Most of the models and frameworks from prior studies have an individual application of TAM, Privacy Calculus, or UTAUT. The combined power of these theoretical perspectives signifies a unique way to examine the multi-dimensional attributes of AI adoption especially in a fast-growing market context. To illustrate this, we point out that, on its own, TAM could explain perceived usefulness, Privacy Calculus could explain the limitations of effectiveness alone of AI for adoption, and UTAUT could help contextualize demographic and cultural moderating influences. In combination, we provide a holistic socio-technical model of AI trust and adoption that furthers both scholarly and practitioner work.

### 5.3. Comparison with Industry Practices

This research article, published in the Journal of Cybersecurity and Privacy (2025, Volume 5, Issue 3), investigates how AI can strengthen fraud detection and address privacy concerns in mobile financial services (MFS) within emerging markets (Kenya, Nigeria, Bangladesh). The study employed a mixed-method approach with a quantitative survey (n=151) and qualitative analysis of open-ended responses.

Key findings include:
- 95.4% of respondents expressed privacy concerns, while 78.2% recognized the benefits of AI-driven fraud detection
- Regression analysis showed AI significantly improved perceived security (β=0.63, p<0.01), though transparency and explainability were critical determinants of trust
- 91.2% rated AI as superior to rule-based systems for fraud detection, but only 29.8% were satisfied with transparency
- 50.3% of respondents used MFS daily, and 54.9% felt very/extremely confident using AI-secured MFS
- 66.9% were uncomfortable sharing personal data with financial apps

The study integrates three theoretical frameworks: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Privacy Calculus, and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Qualitative themes revealed concerns about algorithmic opacity, privacy/data ownership, and socio-regulatory context. The authors propose promoting Explainable AI (XAI) systems, privacy-by-design user controls, and localized communication approaches to foster trust. The study serves as a guide for policymakers, fintech developers, and providers seeking to innovate with user protection in digital fintech.

## Abstract

The aim of this study is to evaluate the accuracy of machine learning techniques in addressing the problem of bias in criminal assessment prediction. Previous studies have shown that commercial software for criminal risk assessment produces biased predictions, no better than assessment by randomly selected people without criminal justice expertise (Dressel and Farid in Sci Adv 4(1):eaao5580, 2018. [https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580)). In this research, we reproduce the results of Dressel and Farid (Sci Adv 4(1):eaao5580, 2018. [https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580)), testing Logistic Regression (LR) and Support Vector Machines (SVM) on the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) dataset. In addition, we implement an eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) classifier and study the effect of hyper-parameter optimization and correlation-remover as debiasing techniques. We find that XGB performs better than Logistic Regression, and that debiasing techniques modestly improve accuracy of prediction. We conclude that bias mitigation techniques can be helpful up to a point but note that embedded bias in the data can persist in AI risk assessment tools, which can have profound social and ethical implications for individuals and for society.

## 1 Introduction

Few areas in modern society remain untouched by the promise and risk of AI systems. They are alternatively benign and threatening, depending on the point of view adopted [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR22 "Makridakis, S.: The forthcoming artificial intelligence (ai) revolution: Its impact on society and firms. Futures 90, 46–60 (2017). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.futures.2017.03.006
                  
                ")]. The European Union, for example, has introduced legislation that seeks to ‘...promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter...’ ([[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR10 "European Parliament CotEU Regulation (EU) no 2024/1689. (2024) 
                  https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689
                  
                ")], Art. 1.1, p.44). It has chosen to ban outright those systems it deems to present unacceptable risk, including AI practices for criminal predisposition profiling systems ’ ([[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR10 "European Parliament CotEU Regulation (EU) no 2024/1689. (2024) 
                  https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689
                  
                ")],Art. 5.1(d)). These developments are especially salient in criminal justice, where the consequences of predictive error can be severe for both individuals and society.

In the United States, law enforcement agencies and courts have long used actuarial risk assessment instruments (ARAIs) to inform decision-making in the criminal justice system, and in recent years these have included AI systems. Given the large disparity in race[Footnote 1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Fn1) in prison populations in the US, the use of such tools has given rise to accusations of racial bias [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR9 "Dressel, J., Farid, H.: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism. Sci. Adv. 4(1), eaao5580 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580
                  
                ")].

Bias in AI systems is often conflated with the concept of fairness and is complicated by the fact that absence of fairness may arise from various sources, for example, the sociotechnical environment in which a system is used or the data on which it is trained. Machine Learning algorithms trained on biased data may embed that bias and compound the problem. Researchers explain that bias can arise from the model [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR18 "Kim, J.Y., Cho, S.B.: An information theoretic approach to reducing algorithmic bias for machine learning. Neurocomputing 500, 26–38 (2022). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2021.09.081
                  
                ")] and the data used in the algorithm [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR38 "Waller, R.R., Waller, R.L.: Assembled bias: beyond transparent algorithmic bias. Mind. Mach. 32, 533–562 (2022). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-09605-x
                  
                ")].

Fairness is an elusive concept and hard to define, with potential for contradictory interpretation [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR29 "Pfeiffer, J., Gutschow, J., Haas, C., et al.: Algorithmic fairness in AI. Bus. Inf. Syst. Eng. 65, 1–14 (2023). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s12599-023-00787-x
                  
                ")]. In the law, for example, fairness is often equated with the principle of non-discrimination, while in finance the use of discriminatory pricing based on (say) age is considered perfectly acceptable. From an information systems perspective, fairness and bias in machine learning can be seen as a sociotechnical problem with possible negative impacts for groups of people when decision systems encode sensitive features, such as race, gender, age, or disabilities [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR39 "Weerts, H., DudÃ­k, M., Edgar, R., et al.: Fairlearn: assessing and improving fairness of AI systems. J. Mach. Learn. Res. 24(257), 1–8 (2023)")].

In 2016, the topic of machine bias was raised by a group of investigative journalists at ProPublica in their study on COMPAS, a proprietary AI machine learning recidivism prediction algorithm, designed to help officials make assessments on probation and parole clients [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR3 "Angwin, J., Larson, J., Kirchner, L., et al.: Machine bias: There’s software used across the country to predict future criminals. and it’s biased against blacks. (2016) 
                  https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing
                  
                "), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR21 "Larson, J., Angwin, J., Kirchner, L., et al.: How we analyzed the compas recidivism algorithm.(2016) 
                  https://www.propublica.org/article/how-we-analyzed-the-compasrecidivism-algorithm
                  
                ")].[Footnote 2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Fn2) Based on their analysis of data obtained on a subset of people scored by COMPAS, they concluded that the tool was biased against black defendants.

The ProPublica study generated significant debate and prompted a swift rebuttal from Northpointe, the company that developed COMPAS, which highlighted ‘statistical and technical errors such as misspecified regression models, wrongly defined classification terms and measures of discrimination, and the incorrect interpretation and use of model errors.’ ([[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR8 "Dieterich, W., Mendoza, C., Brennan, T.: Compas risk scales: demonstrating accuracy equity and predictive parity: performance of the compas risk scales in broward county. (2016) 
                  https://go.volarisgroup.com/rs/430-MBX-989/images/ProPublica_Commentary_Final_070616.pdf
                  
                ")],p.1). [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR12 "Flores, A.W., Bechtel, K., Lowenkamp, C.T.: False positives, false negatives, and false analyses: a rejoinder to machine bias: there’s software used across the country to predict future criminals and it’s biased against blacks. Fed. Probat. 80, 38–46 (2016)")] also strongly rejected the report’s conclusions, accusing ProPublica of conducting a study that lacked academic rigour. They warned that the ProPublica claims posed a risk of undermining the value of all ARAIs, noting that ‘The issue that is no longer up for debate is that ARAls predict outcomes more strongly and accurately than professional judgment alone.’ ([[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR12 "Flores, A.W., Bechtel, K., Lowenkamp, C.T.: False positives, false negatives, and false analyses: a rejoinder to machine bias: there’s software used across the country to predict future criminals and it’s biased against blacks. Fed. Probat. 80, 38–46 (2016)")],p.39).

Among the researchers supporting the ProPublica analysis were [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR9 "Dressel, J., Farid, H.: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism. Sci. Adv. 4(1), eaao5580 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580
                  
                ")], who used the same data to confirm ProPublica’s conclusions. They also compared the fairness of the COMPAS algorithmic prediction with the fairness of human agents and showed that random human prediction of recidivism is about as ‘accurate and fair’ as COMPAS, concluding that this casts doubt on the accuracy of algorithmic predictive tools. Finally, they questioned the value of using relatively large numbers of features as input to the predictive models (COMPAS uses up to 137 features) and showed that broadly the same outcome accuracy can be achieved with two features (‘age’ and ‘total number of previous convictions’).

Notwithstanding the ethical importance of this debate, the focus of this paper is on the performance of the COMPAS tool, rather than on a broader normative assessment of ARAI in the criminal justice system. It examines whether the reported disparity patterns produced by ProPublica can be replicated; whether adding race as an explicit feature changes predictive performance; and, whether common optimization and debiasing techniques reduce those disparities. In this respect, while it contributes peripherally to the debate, our study comprises a more technical assessment of the performance of the COMPAS tool. Our description of the controversy that has emerged following usage of COMPAS is included to provide further context and to ground our study in a broader research domain.

We sought first to validate the results of the Dressel and Farid study, and by extension the ProPublica study, and second to extend this earlier research by applying different analytic techniques to the data, including alternative classifiers, optimization, and the use of debiasing tools. We approached the problem in the following way. First, we adopted the same COMPAS dataset and used the same classifiers as Dressel and Farid (Logistic Regression (LR) and Support Vector Machines (SVM)) to validate their initial findings. Then we developed new experiments to see how we might improve the model’s predictive ability. Specifically, we implemented an eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) classifier and studied the effect of hyper-parameter optimization and correlation-remover as debiasing techniques. On all our experiments we performed a statistical analysis to confirm the validity of our conclusions and to eliminate random effects.

Our results show that Dressel and Farid’s analysis does confirm a racial bias. We found also that the use of a different classifier (XGB) improves accuracy. Regarding the number of features needed to produce the most accurate predictions, we confirmed findings that the use of as few as two of the most important features can deliver a similar outcome to seven (as in Dressel and Farid) or 137 (as for COMPAS).

We have structured our paper in the following way. Following the introduction (this section), we set out in section [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Sec2) the context of our research, and its relation to previous studies. We then describe in section [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Sec14) the methodology and techniques we used in our research, and the way in which we approached the two distinct parts of our practical experiments. Section [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Sec21) presents our results in tabular form with explanatory narrative, and in section [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Sec25) we discuss the implications of our results. Finally in section [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Sec26) we present a short conclusion and set out our ambitions for further research in this area.

## 2 Context and antecedents

Although the sectoral domain of our work lies in the broad field of criminal justice, our research is technical in nature. We seek instead to answer the following questions:

*   Can the results achieved by Dressel & Farid in their 2018 research be accurately reproduced, thereby validating their conclusions on AI-induced bias in the COMPAS system?

*   Can other debiasing techniques be used to improve classification accuracy using the same data set?

These are technical questions, and while they have significant normative implications, our concern is to validate technical outcomes using advanced AI techniques. For this reason, although we do not investigate legal or ethical aspects of the use of AI tools generally, we present a contextual overview of the concept of fairness and bias in machine learning. We also site our research in the context of the considerable body of work done on the COMPAS system, a proprietary software tool used in the criminal justice system in the US.

### 2.1 Bias, and how it is created in machine learning

A bias or distortion is present when an AI model produces outputs that are consistently wrong in a specific direction [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR2 "Andrae, S.: ökonometrie und maschinelles Lernen. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2023) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-41362-0
                  
                ")]. One of the challenges when using machine learning algorithms is the potential of a bias negatively affecting the results and the model’s fairness. Biases can originate from the data used (data-induced bias) or from the system (model-induced biases). Data-induced bias can be reduced by using a subset of the overall dataset to verify the model’s performance and behavior, but this is not foolproof, and it is possible that bias can be learned in the training [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR17 "Jörgens, D., Rieder, Y., Sinzinger, F.: Bias in machine learning und konsequenzen für die anwendung in der marktforschung. In: Keller, B., Klein, H.W., Wachenfeld-Schell, A. et al (eds) Marktforschung für die Smart Data World: Chancen, Herausforderungen und Grenzen. pp. 137–156. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2020) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-28664-4_11
                  
                ")]. The technical implementation of the model can also cause bias [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR17 "Jörgens, D., Rieder, Y., Sinzinger, F.: Bias in machine learning und konsequenzen für die anwendung in der marktforschung. In: Keller, B., Klein, H.W., Wachenfeld-Schell, A. et al (eds) Marktforschung für die Smart Data World: Chancen, Herausforderungen und Grenzen. pp. 137–156. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2020) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-28664-4_11
                  
                "), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR26 "Pagano, T.P., Loureiro, R.B., Lisboa, F.V.N, et al.: Bias and unfairness in machine learning models: a systematic review on datasets, tools, fairness metrics, and identification and mitigation methods. Big Data Cognit. Comput. 7(1), (2023) 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/bdcc7010015
                  
                , 
                  https://www.mdpi.com/2504-2289/7/1/15
                  
                ")]. After training, the model adjusts the parameters to suit the data and the problem and does not necessarily consider ethical values but represents the best combination of input and output values.

Other categories of bias exist. For example, [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR25 "Olteanu, A., Castillo, C., Diaz, F., et al.: Social data: biases, methodological pitfalls, and ethical boundaries. Front. Big Data 2(13), (2016) 
                  https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2886526
                  
                ")] explore the different biases regarding their presentation in social data, while [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR36 "Suresh, H., Guttag, J.: A framework for understanding sources of harm throughout the machine learning life cycle. In: Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization. pp. 1–9. ACM (2021) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3465416.3483305
                  
                ,")] use the machine learning life cycle as a reference to categorize bias. Although COMPAS programming and functioning is not publicly available, it uses data from public sources such as court and prison records as well as from questionnaires done with the defendants. If data was collected under biased decisions, the system may inherit bias.

#### 2.1.1 Data-induced bias

There are different reasons why the composition of data can cause distortions. Human prejudices may be accidentally included when defining the target variable’s definition, and what should be considered positive and negative [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR30 "Pohlink, C., Fischer, S.: Aus versehen verzerrt. In: Lichtenthaler U (ed) Künstliche Intelligenz erfolgreich umsetzen: Praxisbeispiele für integrierte Intelligenz. pp. 55–69. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2021) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-34670-6_4
                  
                ")]. This definition can be subjective and discriminatory, and this bias can be transferred to the data during collection and selection [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR26 "Pagano, T.P., Loureiro, R.B., Lisboa, F.V.N, et al.: Bias and unfairness in machine learning models: a systematic review on datasets, tools, fairness metrics, and identification and mitigation methods. Big Data Cognit. Comput. 7(1), (2023) 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/bdcc7010015
                  
                , 
                  https://www.mdpi.com/2504-2289/7/1/15
                  
                ")]. Other human bias can be described as historical or social because it reflects prejudices that were and are present in societal norms or stem from biases of past generations [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR26 "Pagano, T.P., Loureiro, R.B., Lisboa, F.V.N, et al.: Bias and unfairness in machine learning models: a systematic review on datasets, tools, fairness metrics, and identification and mitigation methods. Big Data Cognit. Comput. 7(1), (2023) 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/bdcc7010015
                  
                , 
                  https://www.mdpi.com/2504-2289/7/1/15
                  
                ")]. If AI tools are trained using historical data that embeds these biases, they will likely produce biased outcomes. Other historical data may reflect outdated processes or regulations, for example old bail system strategies and rules, and these can also result in suboptimal or harmful predictions [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR19 "Koepke, J.L., Robinson, D.G.: Danger ahead: risk assessment and the future of bail reform. Washington Law Rev. 93, 1725–1806 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3041622
                  
                ")].

Data quality plays an essential role in avoiding the most common cause of bias, the underrepresentation of certain groups [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR30 "Pohlink, C., Fischer, S.: Aus versehen verzerrt. In: Lichtenthaler U (ed) Künstliche Intelligenz erfolgreich umsetzen: Praxisbeispiele für integrierte Intelligenz. pp. 55–69. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2021) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-34670-6_4
                  
                ")]. It is possible that a group with certain features, for example racial minorities, is underrepresented in a dataset which can make this group less likely to be associated with a positive outcome. Bias can also be deliberate in not including certain groups, for example, in marketing. This programmed omission is also known as ‘masking’ [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR30 "Pohlink, C., Fischer, S.: Aus versehen verzerrt. In: Lichtenthaler U (ed) Künstliche Intelligenz erfolgreich umsetzen: Praxisbeispiele für integrierte Intelligenz. pp. 55–69. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2021) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-34670-6_4
                  
                ")].

#### 2.1.2 Bias mitigation

Mitigation techniques can usually be assigned into three categories: pre-, in-, and post- processing [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR5 "Barocas, S., Hardt, M., Narayanan, A.: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities. MIT Press (2023) 
                  https://fairmlbook.org/pdf/fairmlbook.pdf
                  
                ")]. This distinction relates to where the mitigation happens in the machine learning lifecycle.

Pre-processing techniques involve adjusting sample distributions of protected variables or transforming the data to mitigate bias, discrimination, and imbalances in the data before the data is used for training or analysis [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR7 "Caton, S., Haas, C.: Fairness in machine learning: a survey. ACM Comput. Surv. 56(7), 1–38 (2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3616865
                  
                ")]. Better data yields better outcomes, and pre-processing offers more flexibility because it is not tied to the later applied modeling techniques.

In-processing refers to a mitigation technique that applies to the model itself [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR7 "Caton, S., Haas, C.: Fairness in machine learning: a survey. ACM Comput. Surv. 56(7), 1–38 (2024). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3616865
                  
                ")]. Bias may accumulate in a model because of distributional effects or because the model tries to fulfill multiple objectives, such as balancing accuracy and fairness. In-processing techniques use optimization functions that include multiple fairness metrics, achieved through parameterization, and are less effective when the inner workings of the model are unknown.

Post-processing techniques seek to improve the fairness of a model already in use by applying various transformations to the model’s output [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR28 "Petersen, F., Mukherjee, D., Sun, Y., et al.: Post-processing for individual fairness. (2021). 
                  arXiv:2110.13796
                  
                ")]. This is less costly than retraining the model and is independent of the inner structure of the model and the training process [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR5 "Barocas, S., Hardt, M., Narayanan, A.: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities. MIT Press (2023) 
                  https://fairmlbook.org/pdf/fairmlbook.pdf
                  
                ")].

Pre- and post-processing techniques offer the most flexibility when working with existing models. The in-processing method offers more control while training the model.[Footnote 3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Fn3)

### 2.2 Fairness

[[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR6 "Calvi, A., Kotzinos, D.:Enhancing AI fairness through impact assessment in the european union: a legal and computer science perspective. In: Proceedings of the 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. FAccT ’23, pp. 1229–1245. Association for Computing Machinery, New York (2023) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3593013.3594076
                  
                ")] speak of ‘...the plurality of definitions of fairness in the legal, social and computer science domains...’ and note that a clear definition remains elusive ([[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR6 "Calvi, A., Kotzinos, D.:Enhancing AI fairness through impact assessment in the european union: a legal and computer science perspective. In: Proceedings of the 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. FAccT ’23, pp. 1229–1245. Association for Computing Machinery, New York (2023) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3593013.3594076
                  
                ")],p.1229). Even when the principle is mandated in law, for example in Article 5(1)(a) of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), it remains ambiguous [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR23 "Malgieri, G.: The concept of fairness in the GDPR. In: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. ACM, New York, NY, USA (2020) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3351095.3372868
                  
                ")]. Frequently, fairness is correlated with non-discrimination, but this is a narrow interpretation that fails to take account of the various ways in which unfairness can be manifested. Unsurprisingly, there is a large body of research investigating fairness from scholars and practitioners across the social sciences.

Algorithmic fairness is similarly contestable, with different and incompatible definitions, sometimes based on equally elusive concepts such as bias, equality, transparency and justice. For example, fairness in AI systems overlaps with the concept of bias, which can occur at any stage of processing. Yet framing fairness in AI systems in these terms can raise the same problematic questions, since they also are subjective and normative. For example, who defines what is ‘equitable’, and in what social or legal context? What are the criteria for determining whether an outcome is ‘just’? A further complication arises from the fact that societies and legal systems define fairness differently. This cultural and political variability makes it difficult to design AI systems that are deemed to be universally fair and raises questions about the ethics of allowing such systems to make important decisions such as whether an individual should be imprisoned.

Moreover, algorithmic fairness can vary from case to case, and designers may emphasize specific attributes. For example, a designer might consider that it is necessary to take historical and social disparities into account to achieve a fair outcome. Other designers might take a utilitarian approach, and design solutions that prioritize outcomes Aimed at achieving a greater social benefit at the expense of individual rights. These decisions can have significant social and political impact.

A related distinction in criminal justice is that between the fairness of the procedure used to assess individuals and the fairness of the outcomes that follow from that assessment. An algorithmic system may output consistent predictions but may reproduce harmful consequences across groups. Thus, technical fairness must be evaluated considering institutional contexts, human decisions, and consequences of systemic results [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR5 "Barocas, S., Hardt, M., Narayanan, A.: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities. MIT Press (2023) 
                  https://fairmlbook.org/pdf/fairmlbook.pdf
                  
                "), [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR40 "Wong, P.H.: Democratizing algorithmic fairness. Philos. Technol. 33, 225–244 (2020). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s13347-019-00355-w
                  
                "), [41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR41 "Zimmermann, A., Rosa, E.D., Kim, H.: Technology can’t fix algorithmic injustice. (2020) 
                  https://www.bostonreview.net/articles/annette-zimmermann-algorithmic-political/
                  
                ")]. In the case of COMPAS, fairness involves trade-offs between false positives and false negatives, and these trade-offs cannot be evaluated solely at the level of model performance.

A particular perspective on fairness relates to transparency, which requires that AI decisions be explainable and justifiable. However, many AI systems operate as ‘black boxes’, making it difficult to understand how and why a system outputs its decision [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR30 "Pohlink, C., Fischer, S.: Aus versehen verzerrt. In: Lichtenthaler U (ed) Künstliche Intelligenz erfolgreich umsetzen: Praxisbeispiele für integrierte Intelligenz. pp. 55–69. Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden (2021) 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-34670-6_4
                  
                ")].

### 2.3 COMPAS and subsequent research

#### 2.3.1 COMPAS

COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) is a software tool that belongs to the group of so-called risk assessment instruments (RAI) [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR4 "Bao, M., Zhou, A., Zottola, S., et al.: It’s compaslicated: the messy relationship between rai datasets and algorithmic fairness benchmarks. (2022) 
                  arXiv:2106.05498
                  
                ")]. RAIs seek to improve decision-making processes and to provide a more accurate classification than human judgment [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR14 "Gottfredson, S.D., Moriarty, L.J.: Statistical risk assessment: Old problems and new applications. Crime Delinq. 52(1), 178–200 (2006). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0011128705281748
                  
                ")]. In the modern era, automated RAIs use sophisticated modeling techniques (and increasingly, AI techniques) to assess risk in many different and complex domains such as finance, healthcare, engineering and the environment [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR35 "Skeem, J.L., Monahan, J.: Current directions in violence risk assessment. Curr. Dir. Psychol. Sci. 20(1), 38–42 (2011). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721410397271
                  
                ")]. They do this by considering various factors to predict and provide a score that portrays a likely outcome. Different assessment methodologies are deployed in different sectors and scenarios, with the objective of mitigating accidents, improving safety, and generally reducing individual and societal harm.

Risk assessment in the criminal justice system offers a singular example of the sensitivity of this activity and of its potential impact on the individual. Traditionally, this activity has been performed by specialist practitioners such as judges and law enforcement officials based on a variety of data including oral representation from affected parties. The potential for harm to the individual, to society or to both can be considerable if the risk assessment, which occurs at multiple stages in the criminal justice process, proves fallible [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR4 "Bao, M., Zhou, A., Zottola, S., et al.: It’s compaslicated: the messy relationship between rai datasets and algorithmic fairness benchmarks. (2022) 
                  arXiv:2106.05498
                  
                ")]. For example, experts are required to assess the risk that an incarcerated offender will re-offend if released, or the risk that an arrested suspect might commit a crime if released on bail. It is inevitable that such judgements are prone to human bias, which may include (among other factors) racial bias. This particular bias has acquired a heightened sensitivity because of the greater number of black and coloured offenders incarcerated in the US prison system.

COMPAS is a commercial tool used to help identify possible re-offending people with a criminal conviction, known as recidivists. It was developed by the US company Northpointe in 1998 and has since been transformed into Equivant [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR9 "Dressel, J., Farid, H.: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism. Sci. Adv. 4(1), eaao5580 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580
                  
                ")]. Since 2000, COMPAS has been used in various US jurisdictions to predict the likelihood of a suspect or prisoner’s risk of committing a misdemeanor or felony within a two-year period after an initial assessment.[Footnote 4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Fn4) COMPAS uses 137 features – data about an individual and their past criminal record – to generate their recidivism score - that is, the likelihood that they will reoffend [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR9 "Dressel, J., Farid, H.: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism. Sci. Adv. 4(1), eaao5580 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580
                  
                ")]. In the context of risk assessment, this score is known as the ‘target variable’. To prevent the software from being racially biased, an individual’s race is not one of the features included.

The biases inherent in COMPAS are noticeable in the choice of the target variable [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR11 "Fabris, A., Messina, S., Silvello, G., et al.: Algorithmic fairness datasets: the story so far. Data Min. Knowl. Disc. 36, 2074–2152 (2022). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10618-022-00854-z
                  
                ")]. The software is a tool to predict the likelihood of reoffence, yet the prediction label (the recidivism score) describes the possibility of a re-arrest. These are not the same: for example, the likelihood of re-arrest may depend on different policing practices and may occur more often for a specific group of people and in certain areas.

#### 2.3.2 ProPublica’s research and northpointe’s rebuttal

The use of COMPAS software has had a wide range of impacts on people’s lives, described vividly in an online article published in 2016 by a group of investigative journalists at ProPublica, a non-profit organization [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR3 "Angwin, J., Larson, J., Kirchner, L., et al.: Machine bias: There’s software used across the country to predict future criminals. and it’s biased against blacks. (2016) 
                  https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing
                  
                ")]. They showed how a false classification by COMPAS can have negative consequences for society or for an individual defendant and illustrated this by showcasing real stories of people affected by COMPAS scores. The ProPublica research underlined the twofold unfairness of false outcomes: first, innocent persons being treated harshly, and second, genuine lawbreakers being set free to potentially reoffend [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR3 "Angwin, J., Larson, J., Kirchner, L., et al.: Machine bias: There’s software used across the country to predict future criminals. and it’s biased against blacks. (2016) 
                  https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing
                  
                ")].

More worryingly, ProPublica concluded that for a particular data set, the score calculated by COMPAS was only ‘somewhat more accurate than a coin flip’. The results also showed that the software is more likely to falsely classify black defendants as possible future offenders two times more often than white defendants. In contrast, white defendants were often wrongly estimated to be at a lower risk of reoffending than black defendants. That means black individuals are more likely to be assessed by COMPAS as risky than white individuals [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR3 "Angwin, J., Larson, J., Kirchner, L., et al.: Machine bias: There’s software used across the country to predict future criminals. and it’s biased against blacks. (2016) 
                  https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing
                  
                ")].

In addition to laying bare the human impact of mistakes being made in the criminal justice system, ProPublica’s article also fueled concerns over use of AI tools in such sensitive areas and has led to ongoing debates about the continued use of COMPAS ([33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR33 "Räz T (2022) COMPAS: zu einer wegweisenden debatte ¨uber algorithmische risikobeurteilung. Forensische Psychiatrie, Psychologie, Kriminologie 16:300–306 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11757-022-00741-9
                  
                ")).

The researchers at ProPublica made their data and analytic techniques public, thus encouraging validation and further research on whether the recidivism algorithm in COMPAS includes a racial bias [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR40 "Wong, P.H.: Democratizing algorithmic fairness. Philos. Technol. 33, 225–244 (2020). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s13347-019-00355-w
                  
                ")]. A swift rebuttal of the study came from Northpointe, who did not publish the algorithms used by COMPAS but noted that not all the risk factors used in the calculations in COMPAS are available in the dataset. They accused ProPublica’s analysis of containing ‘several statistical and technical errors” ([[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR8 "Dieterich, W., Mendoza, C., Brennan, T.: Compas risk scales: demonstrating accuracy equity and predictive parity: performance of the compas risk scales in broward county. (2016) 
                  https://go.volarisgroup.com/rs/430-MBX-989/images/ProPublica_Commentary_Final_070616.pdf
                  
                ")],p.1). ProPublica and Northpointe also disagreed on the definition of fairness.

#### 2.3.3 Dressel and Farid’s analysis

[[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR9 "Dressel, J., Farid, H.: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism. Sci. Adv. 4(1), eaao5580 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580
                  
                ")] studied ProPublica’s claims and found that the accuracy of the COMPAS algorithm (about 65% in criminal assessment prediction) is comparable to that resulting from the assessment by random laypersons. They also found that using a linear classifier and fewer features (seven, and subsequently two, rather than the 137 used by COMPAS) can yield comparable results. The key seven features used in their first analysis were ‘sex’, ‘age’, ‘crime charge’, ‘criminal degree’, ‘non-juvenile prior count’, ‘juvenile felony count’, and ‘juvenile misdemeanor count’, and in the subsequent analysis the two features were ‘age’ and ‘total number of previous convictions’. They also used another AI classifier (a non-linear Support Vector Machine with a radial basis kernel) that can recognize more complex patterns to account for the linear classifiers’ potential lack of performance, but these showed nearly the same results [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR9 "Dressel, J., Farid, H.: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism. Sci. Adv. 4(1), eaao5580 (2018). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aao5580
                  
                ")].

### 2.4 COMPAS approach and critique

#### 2.4.1 Proxy features

Since the ProPublica article challenged the use of COMPAS for profiling potential recidivists, subsequent researchers have identified other flaws in the COMPAS approach, system and data. A particular weakness is that the over-policing of people affected by racism is reflected in the features used [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR38 "Waller, R.R., Waller, R.L.: Assembled bias: beyond transparent algorithmic bias. Mind. Mach. 32, 533–562 (2022). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-09605-x
                  
                ")]. None of the 137 features used by COMPAS is explicitly about ’race’, and the data was subject to ‘blinding’, a technique that involves the removal of sensitive attributes from the model.[Footnote 5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#Fn5)

However, the data (compiled from an individual’s personal data and from responses provided by individuals) contains other attributes that can be correlated indirectly with race [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR38 "Waller, R.R., Waller, R.L.: Assembled bias: beyond transparent algorithmic bias. Mind. Mach. 32, 533–562 (2022). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-09605-x
                  
                ")]. These so-called ‘proxy features’ might include an individual’s address, a proxy for race due to the geographic distribution of marginalized groups. Blinding is thus less effective because bias is introduced by inclusion of proxy features.

Moreover, it can happen that removal of sensitive features can be overcome by the adaptive nature of machine learning models, which also diminishes the effect of blinding. Machine learning programs make adjustments to compensate for mistakes made by their classification using the training dataset. This means they adapt to minimize the error and improve in subsequent iterations. Thus, removing a sensitive feature can negatively impact the model because it cannot review its own bias regarding that feature [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR38 "Waller, R.R., Waller, R.L.: Assembled bias: beyond transparent algorithmic bias. Mind. Mach. 32, 533–562 (2022). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-09605-x
                  
                ")].

Removing the sensitive attribute also has no impact on the proxies [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-026-01116-0#ref-CR16 "Johnson, G.M.: Algorithmic bias: on the implicit biases of social technology. Synthese 198(10), 9941–9961 (2021)")]. This is because the classifier uses the relationships and correlation patterns of the attribute to predict the target feature. These attributes that predict the outcome include sensitive and proxy features. Once the sensitive features are removed, the proxy feature will be the subsequent available correlation, leading to the same biases as before
</webpage_content>

This is a Springer Nature-hosted open-access research article published on April 23, 2026, in the journal AI and Ethics (Volume 6, article number 264), titled "AI and prediction of criminal justice risk: revisiting the COMPAS dataset, experiments, and the problem of algorithmic bias and fairness" by Sarah Kienzle, Gissel Velarde, and Brian Gannon.

The study evaluates the accuracy of machine learning techniques in addressing bias in criminal assessment prediction, reproducing and extending prior work by Dressel and Farid (2018). The authors test Logistic Regression (LR) and Support Vector Machines (SVM) on the COMPAS dataset, and additionally implement an eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) classifier with hyper-parameter optimization and correlation-remover as debiasing techniques.

**Key findings:**
- The authors confirm Dressel and Farid's finding of racial bias in COMPAS, validating ProPublica's 2016 conclusions that the tool was biased against black defendants.
- XGB performs better than Logistic Regression in predictive accuracy.
- Debiasing techniques modestly improve accuracy of prediction.
- Using as few as two features ('age' and 'total number of previous convictions') can produce similar outcomes to using 137 features.
- The authors conclude that bias mitigation techniques can be helpful up to a point, but embedded bias in the data can persist in AI risk assessment tools.

**Background context:** The paper provides extensive background on the COMPAS controversy, including ProPublica's 2016 investigation finding racial bias, Northpointe's rebuttal, and Dressel and Farid's 2018 study confirming the bias. The paper discusses types of bias (data-induced, model-induced), mitigation techniques (pre-, in-, and post-processing), and the contested concept of fairness in AI. The authors note that proxy features (correlated with race) can reintroduce bias even when race is explicitly removed from the model.

## 🎥 Explained: The COMPAS Algorithm Scandal: When AI Decides Who Goes to Jail ⚖️

---

### 🧭 A Deep Dive into the COMPAS Fairness Dilemma

#### ⚖️ The Algorithm’s Forked Tongue

> 🤖 *When algorithms speak with two voices, justice becomes a matter of mathematics.*

**📊 At a Glance**

* ⚖️ **System used:** the **COMPAS** risk assessment tool for predicting recidivism in criminal justice decisions
* 👥 **Most affected group:** defendants, especially Black defendants more likely to be mislabeled high risk in the ProPublica analysis
* ⚠️ **Core failure:** competing fairness metrics exposed that a model can be statistically "fair" by one definition and harmful by another
* 📉 **Outcome:** risk scores could influence bail, sentencing, and parole despite opaque logic and unequal error patterns

> ### ⚠️ Key Takeaway
>
> COMPAS showed that fairness is not a single metric. In high-stakes systems, choosing which error to minimize is also a political and moral choice.

---

## 🧩 1. What Happened: A Tale of Two Truths

For decades, the U.S. criminal justice system has moved toward **📊 evidence-based sentencing**.

The goal: reduce inconsistent judicial discretion.  
 The tool: actuarial risk models.  
 The promise: ⚙️ objectivity and scientific rigor.

That promise fractured in **2016** with controversy surrounding **COMPAS** — the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions system.

### 🥊 The Core Conflict

Two institutions. Two truths.

* 📰 **ProPublica** → investigative nonprofit
* 🏢 **Northpointe (now equivant)** → COMPAS developer

ProPublica analyzed ~10,000 defendants in Broward County, Florida.  
 Later benchmarks using **AIF360** standardized the dataset to **6,167 rows** (5,723 for Black and White defendants).

---

### 📌 Controversy Cheat Sheet

#### 🚨 The Accusation (ProPublica)

The algorithm is racially biased.

* Black defendants who did **not** reoffend were nearly **2× more likely** to be labeled **High Risk**.
* White defendants who **did** reoffend were more likely to be labeled **Low Risk**.

#### 🛡️ The Defense (Northpointe)

The algorithm is fair.

* It maintains **predictive parity**.
* A risk score has the same statistical meaning across races.

---

### 🧮 The Mathematical Deadlock

At the heart lies the **Fairness Impossibility Theorem**:

> ❗ No model can satisfy both equal error rates and predictive parity unless base rates are equal or accuracy is perfect.

Because arrest and recidivism rates differ across groups—driven by systemic factors like over-policing—both sides are technically correct.

⚠️ The result: a **mathematical conflict with human consequences**.

---

## 🔗 2. Impact: When Statistics Become Sentences

Choosing a fairness metric is not academic.  
 It defines **who loses freedom**.

When COMPAS labels someone **High Risk**, it influences:

* 💰 Higher bond
* 🚫 Denied parole
* ⛓️ Longer incarceration

### 📉 The Human Cost of Misclassification

| Metric | Black Defendants | White Defendants |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ❌ False Positive (High Risk, no reoffense) | **45%** | **23%** |
| ⚠️ False Negative (Low Risk, reoffended) | **28%** | **47%** |

### 🧠 Why This Matters

* 45% false positives → nearly half of law-abiding Black defendants lost liberty.
* 47% false negatives → the system extended more **benefit of the doubt** to White defendants.

👉 To understand why, we must examine the data feeding the machine.

---

## ☠️ 3. Lifecycle Failure: The Poisoned Well

COMPAS did not fail at prediction.  
 It failed at **data design**.

If training data reflects historical oppression, the algorithm becomes a ⚡ high-speed engine for reinforcing it.

### 🧬 The Proxy Variable Problem

COMPAS avoids race directly but uses proxies:

* 📍 **Zip Codes** → segregated, heavily policed neighborhoods
* 👥 **Family/Friend Victim History** → systemic inequality exposure
* 🚨 **Gang Affiliation** → subjective urban profiling
* 🏚️ **Socialization History** → housing instability, family disruption

These encode structural inequality while appearing neutral.

---

### ⚖️ Due Process vs Trade Secrets

In **State v. Loomis**, the Wisconsin Supreme Court allowed COMPAS use with disclaimers.

🧾 The problem:  
 Defendants cannot challenge a proprietary algorithm used to sentence them.

Trade secrets > due process.

---

### 🔧 Attempts at Reform

equivant’s COMPAS-R Core introduced:

* 🧼 Neutral language revisions
* ❌ Removal of ambiguous responses
* 🧪 Experimental bias-testing questions

These improve optics, not structural fairness.

---

## ⚔️ 4. Bias Types: A Clash of Definitions

Fairness is not one thing.

### 🎯 Three Competing Definitions

1️⃣ **Equalized Odds**  
 Equal error rates across groups.

2️⃣ **Predictive Parity**  
 Risk scores mean the same across groups.

3️⃣ **Historical Bias**  
 Ground truth reflects systemic inequality.

### ⚖️ The Trade-off

* 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Group fairness → correct systemic disadvantage
* 👤 Individual fairness → treat similar individuals consistently

Improving one often worsens the other.

👉 Justice becomes a **statistical choice**.

---

## 🌍 5. Global South Lens: Exporting Inequality

COMPAS is not just a U.S. story.

Western models are exported as “modernization tools” to the Global South.

But variables like:

* 🏠 Residential stability
* 💼 Vocational history

are not neutral where:

* Informal economies dominate
* Conflict causes displacement
* Colonial policies shaped land access

⚠️ Exporting such models risks **technological solutionism** — fixing justice with code while ignoring poisoned data.

---

## 🧠 6. Bigger Picture: Can We Code Our Way to Justice?

Technical fixes exist. None solve the root problem.

### 🛠️ Mitigation Strategies

| Strategy | Effectiveness | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ⚖️ Reweighing | Improves fairness metrics | Cannot fix biased data |
| 🧮 Prejudice Remover | Enforces independence from race | ~38% accuracy |
| 🔄 Calibrated Equalized Odds | Balances errors | Misses real recidivism |

---

### 🧭 Radical Proposal: Affirmative Algorithms

Use race as a corrective factor to counter systemic bias.

This acknowledges reality — and raises democratic questions.

---

## ❓ Curiosity Provocations

* 🎲 If the model is barely better than a coin flip, why use it for prison time?
* 🔒 Should trade secrets override a defendant’s right to examine evidence?
* 🗳️ If fairness definitions conflict, who decides which one governs justice?

---

## 🧵 Final Reflection: The Human System Behind the Machine

Algorithms reflect the systems that produce their data:

* 🚔 Over-policing
* 📉 Structural inequality
* 🏛️ Historical discrimination

Technical fixes treat symptoms.

👤 Human accountability must remain the final check.

> ⚠️ A black box cannot be the final word on human freedom.

# The COMPAS Algorithm Scandal: When AI Decides Who Goes to Jail

This case study (Part 4 of 13 in the "AI Fairness 101 — Real-World Incidents" series from GlobalSouth.AI) examines the 2016 COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) controversy in the U.S. criminal justice system.

## What Happened
ProPublica investigated ~10,000 defendants in Broward County, Florida, finding that COMPAS—a risk assessment tool used for bail, sentencing, and parole decisions—was racially biased. Black defendants who did **not** reoffend were nearly **2× more likely** to be labeled High Risk (45% false positive rate vs. 23% for white defendants). White defendants who **did** reoffend were more likely to be labeled Low Risk (47% false negative rate vs. 28% for Black defendants). The developer, Northpointe (now equivant), defended the algorithm as fair based on predictive parity.

## Core Conflict
The controversy revealed the **Fairness Impossibility Theorem**: no model can satisfy both equal error rates and predictive parity unless base rates are equal or accuracy is perfect. COMPAS uses proxy variables (zip codes, family/friend victim history, gang affiliation, socialization history) that encode structural inequality while appearing neutral.

## Legal & Global Implications
In **State v. Loomis** (2016), the Wisconsin Supreme Court allowed COMPAS use with disclaimers, despite defendants being unable to challenge a proprietary algorithm used to sentence them. The case study warns that Western models are exported to the Global South as "modernization tools," where variables like residential stability and vocational history are not neutral in contexts with informal economies, displacement, and colonial legacies.

## Key Takeaways
- Fairness is not a single metric; choosing which error to minimize is a political and moral choice
- Technical fixes (reweighing, prejudice remover, calibrated equalized odds) cannot fix biased data
- A radical proposal is suggested: using race as a corrective factor (affirmative algorithms) to counter systemic bias
- Final reflection: "A black box cannot be the final word on human freedom"

## [Understanding Algorithmic Accountability in Criminal Justice](https://study.com/academy/lesson/case-study-compas-algorithm-accountability-for-ai-harm.html)

**AI accountability** refers to the ethical, legal, and institutional responsibility borne by individuals and organizations when artificial intelligence systems produce harmful, discriminatory, or biased outcomes. Within criminal justice systems, algorithmic accountability becomes particularly significant because automated tools increasingly influence decisions affecting liberty, sentencing, parole, bail, and surveillance. The use of predictive technologies therefore raises fundamental questions regarding fairness, transparency, oversight, and responsibility when automated systems contribute to unequal or harmful outcomes.

AI-driven recidivism algorithms raise important ethical questions regarding transparency, fairness, bias, and accountability within criminal justice systems

![Image 5: Artificial intelligence and data systems associated with algorithmic accountability and decision-making](https://study.com/cimages/multimages/16/journalism_and_artificial_intelligence_53910988565667a78b4-fc06-4d9a-831b-fd218a30c5bb.jpg)

One of the most widely debated examples of algorithmic decision-making in criminal justice involves the **COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) recidivism algorithm**. Developed by Northpointe (now Equivant), COMPAS was designed to estimate the likelihood that defendants would reoffend if released. Courts and correctional agencies across the United States incorporated COMPAS risk scores into judicial decisions involving sentencing, parole, and pretrial release. However, public investigations and academic analyses later revealed substantial concerns regarding racial disparities and false-positive predictions affecting Black defendants at disproportionately higher rates.

The controversy surrounding COMPAS illustrates the complexity of assigning accountability when AI systems produce biased outcomes. Multiple stakeholders contribute to the design, implementation, interpretation, and oversight of algorithmic systems. Software developers construct and train predictive models using historical criminal justice data; judges and courts rely upon algorithmic recommendations during decision-making; and state agencies procure, authorize, and oversee system implementation. Because these actors operate within interconnected institutional structures, responsibility for harmful outcomes cannot easily be assigned to a single party.

Understanding algorithmic accountability therefore requires careful analysis of how technological systems interact with historical inequalities, institutional decision-making, and constitutional principles within criminal justice systems. The COMPAS case demonstrates that predictive technologies may reinforce existing disparities when algorithms rely upon biased historical data, insufficient oversight, or opaque decision-making structures. Consequently, the ethical evaluation of AI systems in criminal justice extends beyond technical performance to include broader concerns involving fairness, transparency, due process, and institutional responsibility.

## [The COMPAS Algorithm Case: A Professional Analysis](https://study.com/academy/lesson/case-study-compas-algorithm-accountability-for-ai-harm.html)

To understand how algorithmic accountability operates in practice, consider the work of a policy analyst employed by a state department of corrections who has been tasked with evaluating the use of risk assessment tools following public controversy over biased outcomes. This analyst must systematically examine each stakeholder's role and responsibility in the COMPAS system's deployment and impact.

The analyst begins by investigating the algorithm developers' responsibilities. Northpointe created COMPAS using historical criminal justice data to train machine learning models that predict recidivism risk. The analyst discovers that the company's accountability extends beyond simply building a functional algorithm. The developers had a responsibility to test for bias across different demographic groups, to validate their model's accuracy on diverse populations, and to provide clear documentation about the algorithm's limitations and appropriate use cases. When the ProPublica investigation revealed that COMPAS falsely flagged Black defendants as future criminals at nearly twice the rate of white defendants, questions arose about whether Northpointe had adequately fulfilled these responsibilities during the development phase.

The analyst then examines the role of judges and court officials who use COMPAS scores in their decision-making processes. These judicial actors bear accountability for understanding the tools they employ and for maintaining their independent judgment rather than deferring entirely to algorithmic recommendations. The analyst finds that many judges received minimal training on how to interpret COMPAS scores or understand their limitations. Some judges treated the numerical scores as objective facts rather than probabilistic estimates with significant margins of error. This raises questions about whether individual judges can be held accountable for biased outcomes when they were not adequately informed about the tool's potential for bias or given proper training on its appropriate use.

The analyst's investigation reveals that state agencies and court systems also bear significant accountability for their procurement and implementation decisions. These institutions had the responsibility to conduct due diligence before adopting COMPAS, including independent validation studies and bias testing. They also had ongoing obligations to monitor the algorithm's performance and impact on different populations. The analyst documents how many jurisdictions failed to establish adequate oversight mechanisms or to regularly audit the algorithm's outcomes for evidence of disparate impact. This institutional-level accountability encompasses not just the initial decision to adopt the technology but also the ongoing responsibility to ensure its fair and appropriate use.

## [Distributing Responsibility Among Multiple Stakeholders](https://study.com/academy/lesson/case-study-compas-algorithm-accountability-for-ai-harm.html)

The COMPAS case demonstrates that AI accountability within criminal justice systems requires distributed responsibility among developers, judges, courts, and state agencies rather than attribution of blame to a single actor. Each stakeholder exercises distinct authority over different stages of the algorithmic decision-making process and therefore bears unique ethical and institutional obligations regarding fairness, transparency, and oversight.

Developers of the recidivism algorithm bear primary responsibility for system design, bias testing, validation procedures, and transparency regarding algorithmic limitations. Ethical concerns emerged because COMPAS relied upon historical criminal justice data that reflected longstanding racial disparities in policing, arrest practices, and sentencing outcomes. Critics argued that developers had an obligation to conduct rigorous bias assessments, evaluate disparate impacts across demographic groups, and provide meaningful transparency concerning the system's predictive limitations and error rates. The proprietary structure of COMPAS additionally restricted independent external auditing, raising further accountability concerns regarding transparency and public oversight.

Judges and court officials also bear significant accountability because algorithmic recommendations do not replace independent judicial reasoning. Courts using COMPAS scores retained responsibility for ensuring that sentencing, bail, and parole decisions remained fair, individualized, and constitutionally sound. Ethical concerns arose when judges relied heavily upon numerical risk scores without fully understanding the limitations, potential biases, or statistical uncertainties associated with the algorithm. This raised broader questions concerning whether judicial actors received adequate training and whether overreliance upon automated recommendations undermined procedural fairness and individualized justice.

State agencies and correctional institutions additionally bear institutional accountability for procurement decisions, implementation practices, and ongoing oversight of algorithmic systems. Agencies adopting predictive technologies possess responsibility for conducting due diligence, establishing monitoring systems, auditing outcomes for disparate impact, and implementing corrective measures when harmful patterns emerge. The COMPAS controversy therefore illustrates how failures of accountability may occur simultaneously at technical, judicial, and institutional levels when adequate safeguards and oversight mechanisms remain absent.

## [Establishing Frameworks for Ongoing Accountability](https://study.com/academy/lesson/case-study-compas-algorithm-accountability-for-ai-harm.html)

The COMPAS case demonstrates the need for systematic approaches to algorithmic accountability that can address the complex, multi-stakeholder nature of AI system deployment. Effective accountability frameworks must establish clear expectations and obligations for each type of stakeholder while also creating mechanisms for coordination and oversight across the entire system lifecycle.

For algorithm developers, accountability frameworks should require comprehensive bias testing and validation studies before deployment, ongoing monitoring and reporting of system performance, and transparency measures that enable external auditing and validation. The proprietary nature of many commercial algorithms, including COMPAS, presents significant challenges for accountability because it prevents independent researchers and oversight bodies from examining how these systems work and whether they produce biased outcomes. Future frameworks must balance legitimate intellectual property concerns with the public's right to understand and evaluate the algorithms that affect their lives.

Judicial and administrative accountability requires both individual and institutional components. Individual practitioners need training and education to understand the tools they use, while institutions must establish policies and procedures that preserve human judgment and discretion. This might include requirements for judges to document how they use algorithmic recommendations in their reasoning, regular auditing of decision patterns for evidence of bias, and appeals processes that can address cases where algorithmic recommendations may have contributed to unfair outcomes.

Systemic accountability mechanisms must address the broader institutional and policy context in which algorithmic decision-making occurs. This includes procurement policies that require bias testing and validation, oversight bodies with the authority to audit and investigate algorithmic systems, and legal frameworks that can assign liability and provide remedies when algorithmic systems cause harm. The COMPAS case illustrates how the absence of such systematic accountability mechanisms can allow biased systems to operate for years without adequate scrutiny or correction.
