Various perspectives on the interrelation of these three digital divide levels exist within the digital divide literature. Ragnedda ([Citation 2017](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) posits that the third level involves the advantages derived from the first two levels, suggesting a linear progression from access to usage to outcomes. van Deursen and Helsper ([Citation 2015](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) highlight the necessity of shifting focus from merely considering usage skills differentiating groups that effectively can use technologies or cannot to the differences in the benefits and outcomes of using digital technologies. Blank and Lutz ([Citation 2018](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), for instance, found that elderly users benefit more from the Web than younger users due to a higher potential for overcoming inequalities. This suggests that the outcome divide of elderly users might be reduced to a greater extent than for younger users, as the Web may help overcome previous limitations elderly users faced with respect to participating in social and daily life (e.g. due to immobility). Elderly users can utilise the Web for telehealth services, social networking, and accessing government services, significantly enhancing their quality of life. Greater participation in various aspects of life narrows the overall outcome divide for seniors.

Merely reducing the digital divide in terms of usage (usage divide), however, does not necessarily lead to positive outcomes of human-AI interaction. For instance, increased AI usage can sometimes lead to stress and reduced well-being, thereby diminishing the overall benefits of human-AI interaction (Blank and Lutz [Citation 2018](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). This illustrates that positive usage (and, thus, a smaller usage divide) can sometimes lead to contradictory outcomes (such as a greater outcome divide). These contradictory outcomes are particularly important when it comes to AI technologies, given that AI’s greater autonomy and complexity can lead to several intended or unintended consequences for societies, individuals, and organisations (Baidoo-Anu and Owusu Ansah [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#); Dwivedi et al. [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). This necessitates differentiating between inequalities that hinder the creation of various outcomes as a result of AI utilisation, such as between inequalities that hinder the creation of successful outcomes through AI utilisation (in terms of increased performance and efficiency) and those that hinder sustainable outcomes (in terms of understanding AI’s implications and creating inclusive AI outcomes). This highlights the need to contextualise digital divide concepts (e.g. Keskin and Vermeulen [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#); Kitsara [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)).

The need for a specific conceptualisation of the AI divide can be illustrated through the four phases of digital transformation to AI transformation, following Davenport ([Citation 2018](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), which leads to changes in inequalities as described in the digital divide literature, as seen in Appendix 1. For instance, Klumpp ([Citation 2017](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) calls for more research that examines the so-called algorithmic divide as a narrow concept of the AI divide, focusing on disparities caused by algorithms. Luttrell et al. ([Citation 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) emphasise the importance of researching the AI divide in light of AI’s transformative impact on various domains. Carter, Liu, and Cantrell ([Citation 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) highlight the need to investigate AI’s implications for the digital divide by establishing comprehensive AI divide research frameworks that synthesise potential dividing factors and visible and invisible implications of AI. Carter, Liu, and Cantrell ([Citation 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) and Lutz ([Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) applied the concept of the digital divide as illustrated in Figure 1 with the linear three-level structure proposed by Wei et al. ([Citation 2011](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) to establish a sociotechnical framework for the AI divide. Following their work, the AI divides include the access divide (inequalities in access to AI in both private and non-private settings), usage divide (differences in skills, use, and participation in AI technology), and outcome divide (inequalities in effectively utilising AI outcomes).

Recent research on the AI divide, much like studies on the digital divide, has been approached from various perspectives and refer to a global divide, social divide, and democratic divide, for instance (Norris [Citation 2001](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). These include a societal or geographical perspective that examines how different nations or regions benefit from or are excluded from AI advances (e.g. through different digital connectivity standards); an organisational perspective focused on how institutions can leverage AI technologies; and an individual perspective that explores how individuals interact with and benefit from AI. For instance, Kitsara ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) investigated how AI innovations can exacerbate socioeconomic gaps, highlighting the divide between industrialised and developing countries as well as between privileged and less-privileged organisations and individuals (e.g. those with limited financial resources or governmental support). In a similar vein, the World Economic Forum adopted a societal perspective, distinguishing between leading AI countries and emerging ones (Bughin and van Zeebroeck [Citation 2018](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). Wu ([Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) deployed a societal perspective by investigating the AI divide of China’s society.

While much research has focused on one of these perspectives in isolation, it is essential to recognise their interdependencies. For instance, organisational decisions regarding AI implementation and training can significantly affect individuals’ use of AI technologies, including for personal activities such as leisure (Chowdhury et al. [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). This illustrates an interdependency between the individual and organisational perspectives. Factors such as education and cultural norms also impact how individuals perceive AI technologies and develop realistic narratives (Diederich et al. [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). Hence, to investigate the AI divide of individuals, organisations, and societies, it is crucial to consider all possible interdependencies between those perspectives. A comprehensive analysis requires attention to how these different levels – societal, organisational, and individual – interact and influence one another.

### 2.2. The need for SST to contextualise AI inequalities

Building on Vassilakopoulou and Hustad ([Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), who illustrate the digital divide as a sociotechnical phenomenon and highlight the necessity of understanding how technologies intersect with social phenomenon to link digital divide research with sustainability, we propose that SST offers a robust framework for examining the inequalities that hinder sustainable outcomes in human-AI interactions. A sociotechnical system consists of an arrangement of interdependent social and technical entities (e.g. humans, technologies) that collectively shape outcomes within a given context, such as an organisation or society (Leonardi [Citation 2012](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). By emphasising the interplay between these entities, SST provides a nuanced perspective on the complex interactions that influence AI-driven inequalities and their broader implications for sustainability.

SST is grounded in the broader theoretical lens of sociomateriality, which underscores the inseparability of technologies as material entities from the social practices of human actors as social entities (Orlikowski [Citation 2007](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). Together, both entities form the sociomaterial entanglement (Orlikowski [Citation 2007](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), which either can foster or hinder inequalities within human-AI interactions. Traditionally, technologies were viewed as passive tools used by humans; recent literature highlights how the increasing autonomy of AI technologies and their ability to actively shape interactions transform how technologies and humans shape each other and how they are shaped by human decision-making, organisational structures, and broader societal conditions (Endacott and Leonardi [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). Unlike conventional digital tools, AI systems do not merely mediate interactions but participate in them, influencing decision-making processes, organisational structures, and broader societal conditions (Endacott and Leonardi [Citation 2022](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). This evolving relationship between humans and AI (referred to as sociomaterial practices) calls for a deeper exploration of how sociotechnical dynamics reinforce or mitigate inequalities.

In the context of AI, sustainable outcomes can be linked to ethical principles for human-AI interactions that generate long-term, ethically grounded benefits (Heyder, Passlack, and Posegga [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). The sustainability of AI-driven interactions is not dependent solely on technological advancements, but is also shaped by the broader social subsystem in which AI is embedded. According to Leonardi ([Citation 2012](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), the social subsystem encompasses norms, guidelines, institutional structures, cultural frameworks, and values – all of which play a critical role in shaping human-AI interactions. Within this subsystem, both non-human elements (e.g. organisational policies, and regulatory frameworks) and human-related elements (e.g. values, and cultural norms) create a nested structure that enforces sociotechnical dynamics (Leonardi [Citation 2012](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#); Winter et al. [Citation 2014](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). These dynamics influence AI technologies as material entities and humans as social entities, operating at multiple levels, including societal, industrial, and organisational perspectives (Heyder, Passlack, and Posegga [Citation 2023](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). As a result, these interdependencies determine whether AI systems contribute to bridging or exacerbating digital inequalities, ultimately shaping what is commonly referred to as the AI divide (Carter, Liu, and Cantrell [Citation 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)).

AI-supported hiring processes offer an example of such sociotechnical dynamics in AI usage. Kelan ([Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#), 2) observed that human bias may be reproduced in AI-supported hiring, potentially leading to exclusion. Although AI hiring algorithms may enhance recruiters’ performance – reducing the AI outcome divide for recruiters – they might simultaneously hinder inclusiveness for applicants as other social entities interact with the same AI technology, leading to a greater AI outcome divide among applicants. Recognising different sociomaterial practices within AI usage cases can help us better understand the disparities in outcomes from human-AI interaction.

To summarise, SST serves as an appropriate theoretical framework for contextualising the digital divide in human-AI interactions, enabling a deeper understanding of how sustainable outcomes emerge – or fail to emerge – within the interdependent arrangement of AI technologies and human users. By structuring the findings of our systematic literature review within the SST framework, we aim to derive a comprehensive conceptualisation of the AI divide. This approach aligns with Avgerou ([Citation 2019](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), who advocates for a sociomaterial perspective in research on human-AI interactions, emphasising the need to consider both technological and social influences when analysing AI-related inequalities.

Figure 2 is an overview of how we apply Leonardi’s ([Citation 2012](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) SST conceptualisation to structure the systematic literature review findings within a conceptualisation of the AI divide. Whereas Figure 1 assumes a linear progression of the AI divide across three levels – the first-level divide (access divide), second-level divide (usage divide), and third-level divide (outcome divide) – Figure 2 takes a different approach by examining the interplay between these divide levels, allowing for a more nuanced analysis of their interdependencies as revealed through the systematic literature review.

Figure 2.  Adapted sociotechnical system of Leonardi ([Citation 2012](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)).

[![Image 5: Figure 2. Adapted sociotechnical system of Leonardi (Citation2012).](https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/76920fc6-32fb-4af0-844a-5383b67681e3/tbit_a_2500451_f0002_ob.jpg)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)

Display full size

## 3. Research method

To derive a conceptualisation of the AI divide and answer our RQ, we conduct a theoretical literature review to identify, describe, and transform relevant objects into a novel structure (Paré et al. [Citation 2015](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)). We followed the steps of Templier and Paré ([Citation 2018](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)) for a systematic and transparent search process.

_Literature search_: We searched for relevant literature by querying the title, abstracts, and keywords – if available – for the keywords in the two search strings. The first string is: (‘Artificial Intelligence Divide’ OR ‘Artificial Divide’ OR ‘AI Divide’ OR ‘Algorithmic Divide’); the second string is: (‘Artificial Intelligence’ OR ‘generative AI’ OR ‘AI-based digital assistant’ OR ‘AI-based assistant’ OR ‘AI assistant’ OR ‘AI-based conversational agent’ OR ‘AI agent’ OR ‘AI technology’) AND (‘inequalities’ OR ‘inequality’ OR ‘divide’ OR ‘gap’ OR ‘barrier’). We searched in the following databases: ACM Digital Library (ACM), AIS Electronic Library (AIS), Business Source Complete (BSC), IEEE Computer Society Digital Library (CSDL), Google Scholar (Scholar), Science Direct (SciDir), and Web of Science (WoS). The literature search, conducted in July 2023 and updated in July 2024, yielded 8709 overall hits. After eliminating duplicates (_n_ = 156), we yielded 8553 unique hits.

_Literature screening_: Due to ongoing debate and the great evolution of the academic literature on AI technologies, we did not restrict our search to specific quality criteria (such as outlet rankings) or to certain time limits. We applied format criteria through format screening, eliminating non-scientific (e.g. non-peer-reviewed), non-English, and incomplete articles. If available, we used database filter options to eliminate articles that did not fulfil format criteria. We excluded standalone literature reviews. To summarise, 2764 articles were eliminated due to format criteria, and 5789 articles remained for relevance screening.

We applied further relevance criteria by eliminating articles that do not focus on an assistive purpose of AI technologies that do not make dedicated contributions to the conceptualisation of the AI divide because they do not consider factors that differentiate between individuals, organisations, and societies that are or are not AI-capable, and that focus solely on the barriers to the adoption of AI for specific tasks without considering human-AI interaction within a sociotechnical system. In total, 5743 articles were excluded, and 46 articles remained. Appendix 2 provides further details on format and relevance screening.

_Backward and forward searches_: We also conducted four rounds of backward and forward searches. For backward search, we checked the sources cited in each of the remaining articles of our final sample. For forward search, we looked for articles that refer to each of the remaining articles, using Google Scholar’s ‘cited by’ function. This identified 86 articles, which we further checked against the aforementioned format and relevance criteria. In all, 73 articles were eliminated for having been already screened (52 in the first round of backward and forward search, 18 in the second round, 3 in the third round, and 1 in the fourth round). The process was repeated until no additional relevant articles were identified. This added another 13 articles, resulting in a total of 59 articles as our final sample. Appendix 3 provides overviews of the final sample and its database distribution.

Figure 3 is an overview of the search process, following the steps of Templier and Paré ([Citation 2018](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)).

Figure 3.  Search Process.

[![Image 6: Figure 3. Search Process.](https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/61297bae-13c1-414a-8f71-6f9a139c2814/tbit_a_2500451_f0003_ob.jpg)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)

_Literature analysis_: Overall, the literature review yielded a final sample of 59 articles, which were downloaded as PDFs and analysed through manual coding using Microsoft Excel. First, we structured the samples’ meta information (e.g. regarding the research domain, method, ranking of the publication outlet) to provide a descriptive overview of the different article types within the final sample. We then opted for qualitative analysis to structure the content of relevant articles. We used the theoretical background to structure the findings deductively (Mayring and Fenzl [Citation 2014](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2500451#)), applying inductive coding when novel concepts were identified. We conducted parallel coding to guarantee consistency during the coding process and used discussion rounds among the coders. Appendix 4 is a snapshot of coding.

This is a research article published in Behaviour & Information Technology (May 2025) titled "Bridging the gap: inequalities that divide those who can and cannot create sustainable outcomes with AI," authored by Teresa Hammerschmidt, Katharina Stolz, and Oliver Posegga.

The study investigates the "AI divide" — the gap between individuals, organizations, and societies that can generate successful and sustainable outcomes with AI and those who cannot. The authors argue that traditional digital divide concepts (access, usage, and outcome) are insufficient to capture AI's unique implications, particularly regarding sustainability and the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

**Methodology:** The authors conducted a systematic theoretical literature review (July 2023, updated July 2024) across seven databases (ACM, AIS, BSC, CSDL, Google Scholar, Science Direct, Web of Science), yielding 8,709 initial hits. After screening and backward/forward searches, 59 articles formed the final sample. They used sociotechnical systems theory (SST) to structure and analyze findings.

**Key Concepts:**
- The AI divide is conceptualized as a multi-level, circular construct, not a linear progression from access to usage to outcomes (as in prior digital divide models).
- The authors distinguish between inequalities that hinder performance-related outcomes (e.g., efficiency) and those that hinder sustainable outcomes (e.g., social, ethical, environmental impacts).
- SST is used to examine the interplay between social subsystems (norms, policies, culture) and technical subsystems (AI technologies) across individual, organizational, and societal levels.
- The study links AI divide research to the UN SDGs, particularly SDG#4 (education), SDG#5 (gender equality), SDG#10 (reduced inequalities), and SDG#16 (inclusiveness).

**Key Findings from the Literature:** The review identifies that AI's greater autonomy and complexity can lead to contradictory outcomes — for example, accessible generative AI tools like ChatGPT can reduce barriers to use (narrowing the AI divide) but also lead to non-mindful usage, decreased well-being, and overreliance on AI outputs (widening other aspects of the divide). The authors emphasize that positive usage does not necessarily lead to positive outcomes, and outcomes can differ across stakeholders (e.g., AI hiring tools may help recruiters but harm applicants).

**Conclusion:** The paper offers a conceptualization of the AI divide from a sustainability perspective, provides recommendations for practitioners on using AI for social good to support the SDGs, and outlines avenues for future research on AI inequalities.

# The Digital Divide: A Barrier to Social, Economic and Political Equity

Digital technologies are advancing fast, but 2.6 billion people remain offline, highlighting a growing global digital divide.

* [Analysis](https://www.ispionline.it/en/category/analysis) [Digitalisation, Cybersecurity and AI](https://www.ispionline.it/en/research/digitalisation-cybersecurity-and-ai) · [Geoeconomics](https://www.ispionline.it/en/research/geoeconomics)

![](https://www.ispionline.it/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/pexels-kevin-ku-92347-577585-scaled.jpg)

*“The digital economy is the economy of the future, yet 2.6 billion people remain offline. The digital divide is a major barrier to economic growth and sustainable development, with only 27% of the population in low-income countries that has access to the internet, compared to 93% in high-income ones. In a world where digital access drives opportunity, one third of the population is excluded from education, jobs, and financial services. Bridging the digital divide goes beyond technology—it is a fundamental driver of economic equality, social inclusion, and political participation. With an estimated $418 billion needed to connect individuals worldwide through digital infrastructure, prioritizing strategic investments, digital literacy, and cybersecurity is essential to unlocking global economic potential, fostering social inclusion, and building a more equitable and connected future for all.”*

Andrea Poggi | Head of DCM Public Policy & Stakeholder Relations Centre, DCM Innovation Leader

## Executive summary

Digital technologies are evolving at an extremely rapid pace, and they now permeate almost all aspects of societies, economies, and ordinary lives. Despite recent progress, 2.6 billion people remained offline as of 2024, with access to and use of technologies such as the internet and artificial intelligence being highly uneven – a disparity known as the “digital divide”.

Globally, developing countries continue to lag behind in internet access and technological adoption: in low and lower-middle income countries, only 27% and 53% of the population have, respectively, internet access, compared to 80% and 93% in upper-middle and high-income countries. Moreover, within countries, significant disparities emerge in levels of digitalization between urban and rural areas, often due to infrastructural limitations. Social inequalities also compound these challenges, as disadvantaged groups like women and young people are more prone to experiencing digital skills gaps. In low-income countries, for instance, 90% of adolescent girls and young women (15-24) remain offline, compared to 78% of their male counterparts.

The impacts of this divide are profound. From a social perspective, low levels of digital training can lead to fewer employment and career opportunities. In healthcare, without digital services patients in rural areas and developing countries risk being excluded from essential care. A limited digital adoption can also hinder economic growth: a 10% rise in mobile broadband penetration can increase per capita GDP by 1.5-1.6%. Lower use of modern digital technologies can harm financial inclusion and limit credit access for entrepreneurs, while also reducing foreign investment inflows by as much as 8%. Finally, digital inequalities can have major political implications, ranging from lower civic engagement to disruptions in democratic processes.

Closing the digital divide is not just a technological challenge. It is essential for fostering economic equality, social inclusion, and political participation and building a more prosperous future for all.

## Introduction

Digital technologies are evolving rapidly, permeating every aspect of economies, societies, and people’s lives. Global **internet penetration** kept growing from 65% in 2023 to 68% in 2024[[1]](#_ftn1). Despite this progress, **2.6 billion people** – one-third of the global population, mostly in low and lower-middle income countries[[2]](#_ftn2) – remained **offline** as of 2024[[3]](#_ftn3). This persistent “digital divide”[[4]](#_ftn4) underscores unequal access to the use of Internet, artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital technologies, deepening **disparities** among and within countries, **urban and rural areas**, as well as different social groups, with significant **socio-economic** and **political implications**.

## The different dimensions of the digital divide

The adoption and use of digital technologies varies widely across countries.In **low and lower-middle income countries**, only **27%** and **53%** of the population have, respectively, access to internet, compared to **80%** and **93%** in **upper-middle and high-income** countries[[5]](#_ftn5). **Affordability** remains a key barrier: users in lower-middle income economies spend **six times** more of their income on mobile broadband than those in high-income countries, while users in low-income nations pay **19 times** as much[[6]](#_ftn6) *(Fig. 1)*.

**Figure 1**: Price of Data-only mobile broadband (2GB) as % of gross national income per capita, 2023-2024

*Source:* *Facts and Figures 2024, The International Telecommunication Union (*[*ITU*](https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/ituint/viz/ITUFactsandFigures2024/Affordability01)*)*

**Geographical disparities** within countries are equally pronounced. In 2024, **global internet usage in urban areas** reached **83%,** compared to just **48% in rural regions**[[7]](#_ftn7), where infrastructural limitations hinder connectivity *(Fig. 2)*. This gap is narrower in high-income countries but significantly **wider in low and lower-middle income** ones.

**Figure 2**: Percentage of individuals using the Internet in urban and rural areas, 2024

*Source:* *Facts and Figures 2024, The International Telecommunication Union (*[*ITU*](https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/ituint/viz/ITUFactsandFigures2024/InternetUse07)*)*

Beyond internet access, disparities extend to **AI adoption**, development, and investment levels. China and India are the only countries facing significant gaps in internet penetration ranking among the 15 countries with the highest private **AI investment.** The IMF’s AI Preparedness Index[[8]](#_ftn8) – measuring digital infrastructure, human capital investment, STEM expertise, technological innovation, and regulatory adaptability (among other variables) – further highlights this divide. **Advanced economies** score an average of **0.68**, while **low-income countries** lag with an average score of **0.32**, thus highlighting significant disparities also in AI readiness and capacity[[9]](#_ftn9).

**Social inequalities** compound these challenges. **Women and** **young girls** face the largest disparities in digital access. In low-income countries, **90%** **of adolescent girls** and **young women** (15-24) remain **offline,** compared to **78%** of their **male counterparts** in the same age group[[10]](#_ftn10). This digital skill gap limits access to well-paying jobs, exacerbating workforce gender disparities and hindering economic independence.

Unequal digital adoption is closely linked to **investments in infrastructure** (i.e., cables, data centers, digital hubs). In 2023, the **investment needs** inglobal digital infrastructure to connect all the unconnected citizens globally were estimated at **$418 billion**[[11]](#_ftn11), with 73% ($305 billion) required in emerging markets and 24% ($102 billion) in low-income countries. **Advanced economies** accounted for **just 3%** of the total investment needs[[12]](#_ftn12).

The **investment gap** between nations spans multiple sectors, including **digital education,** with funding needs varying based on connectivity targets. In a ***basic offline scenario***[[13]](#_ftn13), the required capital expenditure totals **$67 billion**, with **78%** ($52 billion) needed for low and lower-middle-income nations[[14]](#_ftn14). A ***fully connected schools scenario*** raises expected costs to **$225** billion, with **81%** ($183 billion) allocated to these countries[[15]](#_ftn15). Extending connectivity to ***both schools and domestic environment*** escalates costs to **$1.4 trillion**, with over **70%** (over $1 trillion) required for low and lower-middle-income nations[[16]](#_ftn16), underscoring the vast financial commitment needed to bridge the digital education divide *(Fig. 3)*.

**Figure 3**: Capital and operational expenditure needed to achieve the digital transformation of education systems, 2024-2030.

*Source:* *2023 Global Education Monitoring Report,* [*UNESCO*](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/in/documentViewer.xhtml?v=2.1.196&id=p::usmarcdef_0000385723&file=/in/rest/annotationSVC/DownloadWatermarkedAttachment/attach_import_6afff820-3951-4702-bb7f-3293cdd981cd%3F_%3D385723eng.pdf&locale=en&multi=true&ark=/ark:/48223/pf0000385723/PDF/385723eng.pdf#p150)

## Social impacts of the digital divide

The digital divide and the limited access to education and training have significant **impacts on employment as well**, withmillions **being at risk of exclusion from emerging job opportunities.** As the job market evolves, **digital skills** are becoming essential across nearly all sectors: the **World Economic Forum** warns that nearly **40% of today’s skills will become obsolete**, with **60% of workers** estimated to be in need of reskilling **by 2030**[[17]](#_ftn17).

Vulnerable groups, such as young and women, are particularly exposed. **Young girls** are **35% less** likely than their male peers to have **digital skills**[[18]](#_ftn18). Gender disparities place adolescent girls and young women in a position of disadvantage regarding internet use, job opportunities, and access to essential services, worsening inequality, and perpetuating gaps in the labor market. As a result, **women remain underrepresented in technology** ­and **AI-related roles**, limiting innovation and diversity of thought. In the absence of a significant contribution from female perspectives, AI can perpetuate or even amplify discrimination and reflect unconscious biases, as well as reinforce gender stereotypes[[19]](#_ftn19). Women, in particular, play a pivotal role in **global agriculture**, especially in developing countries, where the sector represents a **large part of the economy** and where they produce up to **80% of food**. At the same time, the **lack of access to technological resources** can prevent them from fully benefiting from **agritech advancements**, hindering the **development of the agricultural sector** of these countries in general[[20]](#_ftn20).

The digital divide also affects the **healthcare sector**, where **digital health** is revolutionizing patient care in clinics, hospitals, and at home. Access to digital health is scarce, as some countries lack structured systems, restricting their ability to provide **remote medical consultations**, electronic health records, and AI-powered diagnostics. Even in countries with advanced digital health services, literacy barriers prevent many from fully benefiting from these advancements[[21]](#_ftn21). Although over **70% of countries have digital health strategies in place**, many lack financial commitments, standardized frameworks, and cohesive governance, limiting their effectiveness[[22]](#_ftn22).

## Economic impacts of the digital divide

Limited digital adoption can hinder progress and **slow down economic growth**. Broadband access plays a crucial role in economic development, with several studies **linking higher broadband penetration to increased GDP**. A review of such studies conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic found that a **10%** rise in mobile broadband penetration **increased per capita GDP by 1.5-1.6%**[[23]](#_ftn23).

**On the other side, lack of digital financial services** may lead to **financial exclusion**, restricting **credit access**, **entrepreneurship**, and **income growth**. **Low and middle-income countries** without a proper digital public infrastructure in financial services may miss the opportunity of **20 to 33% faster GDP growth** in the upcoming years[[24]](#_ftn24). Such infrastructure also benefits **enterprises**, especially MSMEs: digital financial services could help bridge capital gaps, expanding access to funding for up to **19 million MSMEs by 2030**[[25]](#_ftn25).

Data show that governments leveraging digital solutions also attract more investments. **Developing countries** that offer online services, either as an information portal or within a single window (a transactional portal where business registration or licensing can be conducted online) see, on average, **8% higher Foreign Direct Investments inflows**. These online services also boost business registration rates, with beneficial effects especially on **women**, **young entrepreneurs**, and **people living outside urban areas** – groups disproportionately affected by the digital divide[[26]](#_ftn26).

## Political impacts of the digital divide

Digital technologies also have profound impacts on political issues. Parliaments worldwide are embracing digital transformation to enhance **efficiency**, **transparency**, and **participation**: currently, **68% of them** have adopted **multi-year digital strategies**, while **73%** are implementing structured **modernization programs**[[27]](#_ftn27). However, in **low-income nations**, **75%** of parliaments consider the **lack of internet access** as a barrier to **public participation**, compared to just **6%** in **high-income countries**[[28]](#_ftn28).

Weak digital and cybersecurity capabilities expose institutions to **growing threats**, potentially exacerbating economic and political instabilities. AI-related incidents surged **1278%** between 2022 and 2023[[29]](#_ftn29), compounding political risks as well: deepfake technologies and AI-generated misinformation may erode trust in governance, enabling malicious actors to **manipulate public perception** and **disrupt democratic processes**. Those countries where traditional media is weak and digital literacy is limited are particularly **vulnerable** to misinformation that spreads at a much faster rate due to a **lack of fact-checking mechanisms** and **digital awareness**.

**Research, data and case studies demonstrate that bridging the** **digital divide** is not just about the technological sphere. It is a key **driver for promoting economic equality**, **social** **inclusion**, and **political participation**. Without strategic investments in infrastructures, digital literacy, and cybersecurity, disparities will continue to widen, **limiting global economic potential** and **deepening social inequalities.**

args.summary:
This ISPI analysis, dated April 4, 2025, examines the global digital divide and its wide-ranging consequences. As of 2024, 2.6 billion people (one-third of the global population) remain offline, with stark disparities between high-income countries (93% internet access) and low-income countries (27%). The divide encompasses access, affordability, AI adoption, and digital skills, and it has three major dimensions:

**Social impacts:** Limited digital training reduces employment opportunities; 90% of adolescent girls in low-income countries are offline vs. 78% of boys; women are underrepresented in tech/AI roles; and digital health access remains scarce, with over 70% of countries having digital health strategies but lacking financial commitments.

**Economic impacts:** A 10% rise in mobile broadband penetration increases per capita GDP by 1.5-1.6%; lack of digital financial services limits credit access for entrepreneurs; developing countries with online government services attract 8% higher FDI inflows. An estimated $418 billion is needed to connect all unconnected citizens globally.

**Political impacts:** In low-income nations, 75% of parliaments cite lack of internet access as a barrier to public participation (vs. 6% in high-income countries). AI-related incidents surged 1,278% between 2022-2023, and deepfakes/AI-generated misinformation threaten democratic processes, especially where digital literacy is low.

The article argues that bridging the digital divide requires strategic investments in infrastructure, digital literacy, and cybersecurity to promote economic equality, social inclusion, and political participation.

# Digital divide

## Digital divide throughout the world and why it causes inequality

[R&D](https://www.iberdrola.com/label/rd)

ICT (Information and Communication Technologies) offer many advantages: greater access to information, cost reduction in the labour sector, greater connectivity between people, etc. However, digitalisation is not happening equally all over the world, because imbalance exists and this is known as the digital divide.

![brecha](/documents/20125/40063/brecha_746x419.jpg/3d792e08-53b8-e041-9a9b-367c0d0de5aa?t=1626848447143)

In 2020 our lives changed completely when COVID-19 locked us in our homes for months and forced us to study, work and see each other through a screen. **Years later, the online format and [working from home](https://www.iberdrola.com/talent/telecommuting-advantages-and-disadvantages) are here to stay**, with more and more companies opting for this option in combination with face-to-face to carry out their business. However, not everyone has the same opportunities to be connected. According to a study by the International Telecommunications Union (ITU), a specialised agency of the United Nations (UN), **33% of the world's population - 2.6 billion people - have no access to the internet or have never used it**. 

### What is the digital divide?

Inequality in access to the Internet and ICT is known as the digital divide. **In 2023, 70% of men used the internet, compared to 65% of women**. Some 17% more women worldwide are offline than men, according to the ITU report.  

This gap becomes even wider when we talk about regions: in January 2024, **in India only 47.6% of its inhabitants didn’t have Internet access, compared to 10 % of Europeans and Americans.**

The data shows the technological gap that separates some countries from others, despite the fact that 3G and 4G networks, while awaiting the massive expansion of [5G](/innovation/what-is-5g-advantages), are already reaching almost every corner of the planet. Here, it is important to distinguish between access to the Internet and digital literacy, that is, **the learning process that enables a person to acquire the skills to understand and benefit from the educational, economic and social potential of the new technologies.**

![mapa](/documents/20125/4747505/mapa-mundial-internet-746-EN.jpg/a142dc54-e708-b83d-4ebe-58cf15a65ad8?t=1732724313186)

![](/documents/20125/3997223/ico-simple-descargar-verde.png/ac4a2888-dad2-33ee-679b-44136f6c2049?t=1709288789404)  [SEE INFOGRAPHIC: The Internet world map [PDF]](/documents/20125/4747505/mapa-mundial-internet-746-EN.pdf/41f01722-4195-7459-efc7-62faaa5bf543?t=1732724314535)

![](/documents/20125/3997223/ico-simple-descargar-verde.png/ac4a2888-dad2-33ee-679b-44136f6c2049?t=1709288789404)

### Causes and types of digital divide

The digital divide was initially attributed to underdevelopment and was perceived as something temporary that would disappear with the popularisation of technology. Instead, **the divide persists today despite the mass marketing of electronic devices with Internet access.** The causes can range from the high price of the above-mentioned devices to the lack of knowledge about their use or the lack of infrastructure for their access. In this regard, we review the types of digital divide:

A few years ago, ITU established the Digital Access Index (DAI), which measures the overall ability of a country's citizens to access and use ICT. This index takes into account various variables grouped around five categories, which are as follows: **quality, infrastructure, knowledge, accessibility and use.**

### Consequences of the digital divide

**Technological discrimination is a form of poverty and social exclusion, depriving some citizens of essential resources for development and wealth generation.** We saw this a lot during the COVID-19 pandemic, as many students and workers found it difficult to work from home and follow classes online. We review the main effects of the digital divide below:

![](/documents/20125/3332222/ico-agricola-tricolor.png/7b572387-8c84-35cf-0dd9-9e3850e01103?t=1708360791786)

Lack of communication and isolation

People in remote areas who do not have access to the Internet are **disconnected**. Something similar happens to urban residents who are disconnected which causes social isolation.

![](/documents/20125/3332222/ico-libros-verde-naranja.png/296ccc07-8e37-e60e-dfab-24f3f3239c96?t=1708091013404)

Barrier to studies and knowledge

The coronavirus pandemic in 2020 exposed **the digital divide in the world of education** with  teachers and students out of the loop because they lack sufficient technology and digital skills. It also increases lack of knowledge by limiting access to knowledge. Since then, however, more and more people have gained access to technologies and have acquired the skills necessary to use them.

![](/documents/20125/3332222/ico-maletin-verde-azul.png/20db75d8-8558-c6ac-7bcd-48305e3fc21c?t=1708359490783)

Accentuates social differences

Digital illiteracy reduces the [chances of finding a job](https://www.iberdrola.com/talent/how-to-prepare-for-job-interview) and **accessing quality employment**, which has a negative impact on the workers' economy.

![](/documents/20125/3332222/ico-igualdad-genero-tricolor.png/389020a1-a68f-c985-da61-0626522feb7e?t=1730734752081)

Gender discrimination

As we saw at the beginning, the digital divide negatively **affects women more than men**, which violates the principles of [gender equality](https://www.iberdrola.com/sustainability/committed-sustainable-development-goals/sdg-5-gender-equality).

![](/documents/20125/1388596/Edadismo+130x190.jpg/df330ac6-ca00-3f40-958c-6eb56bb97e1a?t=1731670427599)

#### What is ageism?

The UN identifies it as a global problem.

![](/documents/20125/40810/blended-learning130x190.jpg/4a08d2e1-9ab2-600b-516d-020b8a469340?t=1731670761802)

#### How does blended learning work?

It combines remote and face-to-face teaching.

![](/documents/20125/41590/diversidad-inclusion-laboral-130x190.jpg/4082b7e8-d5a2-9a4b-3dc2-ed54fdc41a7e?t=1715858522377)

#### Generational diversity in the workplace

Different generations coexist in the labour market.

### Strategies on bridging the digital divide

The UN includes the reduction of the digital divide (SDG 9) in its Sustainable Development Goals. That is why, in many places initiatives have been launched **to facilitate access to technology**. Here we mention some of the most relevant ones:

**SheCodes Foundation.** This project in Ghana aims to **teach 2,000 women to write code and handle [Artificial intelligence (AI)](https://www.iberdrola.com/innovation/what-is-artificial-intelligence) tools** completely free of charge. There are currently 1,454 women enrolled in the initiative. Similar projects to bridge the digital divide have also emerged in other countries like Peru and Spain.

**The European Union's DigComp framework**. In the update to this document, the EU sets out **250 examples** of knowledge, skills and attitudes to help citizens interact confidently and securely with digital technologies, and new and emerging technologies such as IoT.

args.summary:
This article from Iberdrola discusses the digital divide—the inequality in access to the Internet and Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) worldwide. Key points include:

- **Scale of the problem**: According to the International Telecommunications Union (ITU), 33% of the world's population (2.6 billion people) have no access to the internet or have never used it.

- **Gender gap**: In 2023, 70% of men used the internet compared to 65% of women. Some 17% more women worldwide are offline than men.

- **Regional disparities**: As of January 2024, 47.6% of India's inhabitants lacked internet access, compared to only 10% of Europeans and Americans.

- **Causes and types**: The divide persists despite mass marketing of devices. Causes include high costs, lack of knowledge, and insufficient infrastructure. The ITU's Digital Access Index (DAI) measures access across five categories: quality, infrastructure, knowledge, accessibility, and use.

- **Consequences**: The digital divide leads to lack of communication and isolation, barriers to education and knowledge, accentuated social differences, and gender discrimination. It is described as a form of poverty and social exclusion.

- **Strategies to bridge the gap**: The UN's SDG 9 targets reducing the digital divide. Examples include the SheCodes Foundation in Ghana (teaching 2,000 women to code) and the EU's DigComp framework (250 examples of digital skills).

The article notes that the COVID-19 pandemic exposed the digital divide in education, with teachers and students lacking sufficient technology and digital skills.

# How AI Is Transforming Creativity in 2026

![How AI Is Transforming Creativity in 2026](https://www.ekascloud.com/public/uploads/img/news/img7e3bae82b14c36b78415a3a0543b7e97.png "How AI Is Transforming Creativity in 2026")

The year 2026 represents a remarkable turning point in the relationship between artificial intelligence and human creativity. What once seemed like science fiction—machines composing music, generating artwork, writing stories, and producing videos—has become an everyday reality. Artificial Intelligence is no longer just a tool for automation and data analysis; it has evolved into a powerful partner in creative processes across industries.

From digital art and filmmaking to marketing campaigns and software development, AI is reshaping how creative work is produced, distributed, and experienced. Artists, designers, writers, and innovators are now collaborating with intelligent systems that can generate ideas, accelerate workflows, and unlock entirely new forms of expression.

However, the rise of AI-driven creativity also raises important questions: Is AI truly creative? Does it enhance human imagination or threaten traditional creative professions? And how will creativity evolve in a world where machines can generate art, music, and stories?

This blog explores how artificial intelligence is transforming creativity in 2026, the technologies behind this transformation, and what the future may hold for creators in the age of intelligent machines.

---

# The Evolution of Creative Technology

Creativity has always been influenced by technological advancements. Each new technology has changed the way artists and creators express their ideas.

For example:

* The invention of the camera revolutionized visual art and photography.
* Digital tools transformed graphic design and animation.
* The internet enabled creators to distribute their work globally.

Artificial intelligence represents the next major evolution in creative technology.

Unlike previous tools, AI can actively participate in the creative process. It can analyze vast amounts of creative data, learn artistic styles, and generate entirely new content based on patterns it discovers.

This shift marks the transition from **technology as a tool** to **technology as a creative collaborator**.

---

# What Is AI-Driven Creativity?

AI-driven creativity refers to the use of artificial intelligence systems to assist in generating or enhancing creative content.

These systems rely on advanced technologies such as:

* Machine learning
* Deep learning
* Generative AI models
* Natural language processing
* Computer vision

Generative AI models are particularly important in creative applications. These models can generate new images, music, text, and videos by learning from large datasets.

For example:

* AI can generate realistic digital artwork based on simple text prompts.
* Music generation tools can compose melodies in different styles.
* AI writing assistants can produce articles, scripts, and marketing content.

These capabilities allow creators to experiment with ideas faster and push the boundaries of imagination.

---

# AI in Digital Art and Design

One of the most visible impacts of AI on creativity is in digital art and design.

AI-powered design tools can now generate illustrations, logos, visual effects, and concept art within seconds. Artists can describe their ideas in text, and AI systems transform those descriptions into detailed visuals.

This technology has become especially popular in industries such as:

* Game development
* Film production
* Advertising
* Graphic design

AI tools allow designers to explore hundreds of visual variations quickly, helping them refine their ideas and discover new creative directions.

Rather than replacing artists, AI often acts as a **creative accelerator**, enabling professionals to focus on refining concepts and storytelling.

---

# AI and the Future of Music Creation

Artificial intelligence is also revolutionizing music production.

AI-powered music tools can analyze musical patterns from thousands of songs and generate new compositions that match specific styles or moods.

Musicians and producers use AI to:

* Create background music
* Generate melodies and harmonies
* Experiment with new sound combinations
* Produce music faster

AI can also help musicians remix existing tracks or create personalized music experiences for listeners.

Streaming platforms are increasingly exploring AI-generated music tailored to individual user preferences.

While AI-generated music is still evolving, it is opening new possibilities for creative expression in the music industry.

---

# AI-Powered Content Creation

Content creation has experienced one of the most dramatic transformations due to AI.

Writers, marketers, and journalists are now using AI tools to generate articles, blog posts, product descriptions, and social media content.

AI-powered writing assistants can:

* Suggest headlines and topics
* Generate drafts of articles
* Improve grammar and readability
* Optimize content for search engines

This technology significantly speeds up the content creation process.

In 2026, many media organizations use AI to assist with research, data analysis, and content production.

However, human writers still play a critical role in ensuring accuracy, creativity, and emotional depth.

---

# AI in Film and Video Production

The film and entertainment industries are also embracing AI-powered creative tools.

AI technologies can assist filmmakers with:

* Scriptwriting
* Video editing
* Visual effects generation
* Animation
* Scene generation

AI-powered video editing tools can automatically analyze footage and suggest edits, transitions, and visual enhancements.

In animation and visual effects, AI helps artists generate complex scenes and realistic environments more efficiently.

Some studios are even experimenting with AI-generated characters and digital actors.

While AI cannot replace the storytelling expertise of filmmakers, it can significantly reduce production time and costs.

---

# AI and the Democratization of Creativity

One of the most exciting aspects of AI-driven creativity is that it is making creative tools accessible to more people than ever before.

In the past, producing high-quality artwork, music, or videos required expensive equipment and professional training.

AI-powered tools now allow beginners to create impressive content with minimal technical skills.

For example:

* Entrepreneurs can design marketing graphics using AI tools.
* Students can produce professional presentations with AI assistance.
* Social media creators can generate videos and artwork quickly.

This democratization of creativity is empowering individuals worldwide to express their ideas and share their stories.

---

# Human Creativity vs Machine Creativity

Despite the impressive capabilities of AI, there is still an ongoing debate about whether machines can truly be creative.

Human creativity involves emotions, cultural experiences, and personal perspectives. Artists draw inspiration from their lives, memories, and social environments.

AI systems, on the other hand, generate content by analyzing patterns in existing data.

They do not possess emotions, intentions, or personal experiences.

As a result, many experts believe that AI does not replace human creativity but instead enhances it.

The most powerful creative outcomes often occur when **humans and AI collaborate**.

---

# Ethical Challenges in AI Creativity

As AI becomes more involved in creative industries, several ethical challenges have emerged.

## Copyright and Ownership

When AI generates artwork or music, questions arise about who owns the content.

Is it the creator who used the AI tool, the developer who built the AI model, or the dataset that trained the AI?

Legal systems around the world are still adapting to these questions.

---

## Impact on Creative Jobs

Some creators worry that AI could reduce demand for traditional creative professionals.

While AI may automate certain tasks, it is also creating new opportunities in areas such as:

* AI-assisted design
* Creative direction
* AI content editing
* Digital storytelling

The creative workforce is evolving rather than disappearing.

---

## Authenticity in Creative Content

Another concern is the authenticity of AI-generated content.

As AI-generated art, music, and videos become more realistic, it may become difficult to distinguish between human-created and machine-generated works.

This raises questions about transparency and artistic integrity.

---

# The Rise of AI-Assisted Creative Workflows

In 2026, many creative professionals are adopting **AI-assisted workflows**.

Instead of starting from scratch, creators use AI to generate initial ideas or drafts and then refine them manually.

For example:

* A writer may use AI to generate article outlines.
* A designer may create concept art using AI-generated images.
* A filmmaker may use AI to generate visual storyboards.

This approach combines the speed of AI with the creative judgment of humans.

As AI tools continue to improve, creative workflows will likely become even more collaborative.

---

# AI and Personalized Creative Experiences

Artificial intelligence is also enabling personalized creative experiences.

Streaming platforms, gaming companies, and digital media providers use AI to tailor content based on user preferences.

For example:

* AI can generate personalized music playlists.
* Video platforms can recommend content tailored to viewer interests.
* Interactive storytelling platforms can create unique narratives for each user.

In the future, AI may allow audiences to actively participate in shaping the creative content they consume.

---

# The Future of Creativity in the AI Era

The relationship between AI and creativity will continue evolving in the coming years.

Several trends are likely to shape the future of creative industries.

## AI-Human Collaboration

The most successful creative projects will likely involve collaboration between human creators and AI tools.

Humans will provide imagination, emotion, and storytelling, while AI will assist with data analysis, content generation, and production efficiency.

---

## AI-Generated Virtual Worlds

AI technologies may enable the creation of fully immersive virtual environments for gaming, entertainment, and education.

Creators will be able to generate entire worlds using AI-powered design tools.

---

## New Creative Professions

As AI becomes more integrated into creative industries, new job roles will emerge.

Examples include:

* AI creative directors
* Prompt engineers for generative AI
* AI-assisted storytellers
* Digital experience designers

These roles will require a combination of artistic skills and technical knowledge.

---

# Why Creators Should Learn AI Skills

For artists, designers, writers, and content creators, learning how to use AI tools is becoming increasingly important.

Understanding AI technologies allows creators to:

* Work more efficiently
* Experiment with new creative techniques
* Expand their professional opportunities

Creative professionals who embrace AI will likely gain a competitive advantage in the digital economy.

Educational programs and online courses are now helping creators learn how to integrate AI into their workflows.

---

# Conclusion

Artificial intelligence is transforming creativity in 2026 in ways that were unimaginable just a few years ago.

From digital art and music production to filmmaking and content creation, AI-powered tools are enabling creators to explore new ideas, accelerate their workflows, and reach global audiences.

While AI cannot replicate the emotional depth and lived experiences that shape human creativity, it serves as a powerful collaborator that enhances the creative process.

The future of creativity will not be defined by machines replacing humans but by **humans and AI working together to unlock new possibilities**.

As technology continues to evolve, the creators who embrace AI as a partner will be the ones who shape the next generation of art, storytelling, and digital innovation.

# Why 2026 Will Be The Year That Creativity And AI Find Their Balance

![Forbes Technology Council](https://blogs-images.forbes.com/assets/images/avatars/blog-3949_400_6d18078e84d93600baaf18165a1394f8.jpg)

By[George Toh](https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/people/georgetoh/ "https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/people/georgetoh/"),

Forbes Councils Member.

for [Forbes Technology Council](https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/)

COUNCIL POST

Expertise from Forbes Councils members, operated under license. Opinions expressed are those of the author.

 | Membership (fee-based)

*George Toh, Vice President & GM - Visual Business,* [*Lenovo*](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/) *Intelligent Devices Group.*



As AI matures from novelty to necessity, I believe 2026 will mark a turning point: the year creative professionals truly balance productivity with purpose.

Nearly two-thirds of creative professionals using AI state that it’s reducing the time they spend on tasks [by about 20%](https://blog.adobe.com/en/publish/2024/02/02/creative-pros-generative-ai-usage). However, I don’t believe the next frontier is about gaining more hours. It’s about how organizations can reduce burnout, protect their top creative talent and sustain high performance over time.

Working at the intersection of technology and creative workflows, I’ve seen that adding more capability doesn’t always translate to better outcomes. In many cases, the real opportunity lies in simplifying how creatives interact with their tools so they can stay focused on the work itself.

In this article, I’ll explore how AI is evolving from task automation into a personalized, human-centered creative partner. From adaptive displays that respond to eye strain and cognitive load to personalized, on-device intelligence that protects creative control, AI is beginning to optimize not just productivity, but human energy.

## AI moves from task automation to human enablement.

In 2026, I believe AI will evolve into an adaptive partner that understands cognitive load focus patterns and moments of strain. AI is increasingly shifting from simply responding to commands to becoming more context-aware of users behind the work.

In conversations with creative professionals, a recurring theme is that even small interruptions (searching for files, adjusting settings or reorienting between tasks) can break momentum. Those insights have reinforced the importance of designing systems that anticipate needs rather than react to them. A critical success factor for AI at scale is effective human-AI collaboration for optimized workflows.

For creative teams across design, marketing and content, this means moving past frictionless workflows into frictionless thinking. In practice, this looks like automatically organizing reference materials, surfacing campaign files or adapting display settings to shift from detailed design work to collaborative review.

For example, this might look like adjusting color temperature and brightness automatically to reduce eye fatigue, or providing natural‑language interaction, auto‑connect features and multi‑device windowing. In this way, AI can respond to human needs in real time to let creators stay focused instead of working against their tools.

Further, AI that evolves alongside the individual—learning their habits, preferences and goals—is likely to represent the next wave for personalization. Instead of replacing human originality, AI can help creators stay in flow longer with fewer interruptions, fewer tedious steps and fewer compromises. For business leaders, this shift represents a path to higher-quality output, faster time-to-market and reduced creative fatigue, which all support long-term team performance and influence retention.

Non-IT functions in marketing are set for [faster growth](https://s7d1.scene7.com/is/content/Lenovoassetsprod/CIO%20Playbook%202026%20-%20WW_V2pdf?refId=32c4fb94-6127-41c9-b523-c148a0cfeec2) in AI implementation. I’ve also seen that when teams are equipped with tools that reduce repetitive work, the impact goes beyond efficiency. It changes how people engage with their work, leading to higher satisfaction.

## Reclaimed time becomes a catalyst for creativity and well-being.

The global strain of constant digital engagement is reaching a tipping point, with [68% of employees](https://moorinsightsstrategy.com/microsoft-work-trend-index-2025-shows-workplace-capacity-strain/) reporting they struggle with work pace and volume, as well as burnout. This will be the year technology stops optimizing solely for output and starts optimizing for human energy.

AI-driven PCs are one example of how this new design philosophy is taking shape, and their demand is only [growing](https://www.researchandmarkets.com/reports/6173308/ai-pc-market-industry-trends-global-forecasts) as AI monitors continue embedding features to adjust brightness, color temperature and contrast automatically to support natural circadian rhythms.

Technology that supports well-being can ultimately fuel better ideas, stronger leadership and longer-lasting careers. More broadly, organizations see measurable value with reduced burnout correlating with lower turnover costs, stronger creative continuity and higher campaign effectiveness.

In an increasingly competitive creative economy, one of the best ways to differentiate will be to use technology to reclaim time and enhance focus.

## Personalization preserves creative control.

As AI becomes more autonomous, trust becomes foundational. Creatives need confidence that their tools enhance their voice, not override it. In this context, personalization is no longer about automation for its own sake, but about preserving control while reducing friction.

Across the display category, this shift is already taking shape in how tools are being designed to align more closely with real creative workflows. Capabilities such as color accuracy, cross-device consistency and flexible connectivity are becoming baseline expectations rather than differentiators in professional environments. As a result, display technologies are increasingly evolving to support high-fidelity work without introducing additional friction, reflecting a broader movement toward tools that integrate more seamlessly into the creative process rather than interrupt it.

In 2026, the most sought‑after creative tools will be those that are powerful, intuitive and deeply respectful of personal creative identity.

## Conclusion

This year signals a shift from AI as an accelerant to AI as an enabler of human potential. From reducing digital fatigue to enhancing creative flow and building trust through personalization, the moment when productivity and purpose finally align is now.

As AI matures, it will only get better at helping creative professionals reclaim time, replenish energy and reimagine what’s possible when technology works in harmony with the human mind. For businesses, the implications are also significant: Tools that support sustained creative flow and boost productivity protect their talent pipeline and deliver better work over time.

# Democratizing AI: Benefits, Challenges and Governance

Democratization of AI is a hot topic as AI implementation broadly takes effect. But what does its adoption compel regarding governance – best practices around scope of access to AI applications, data security, accuracy, source traceability and intellectual property protection – which will be critical to achieving economic benefits and responsible use?

Tecnovy, a training and IT consulting company, frames up the situation: “Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies becoming accessible to everyone are at the forefront of technological transformation in today’s world. This process offers wider audiences opportunities for innovation and creativity, enhances efficiency in business processes and makes advanced technologies more accessible. However, alongside these positive developments, it also brings significant barriers such as data security, ethical issues and regulatory challenges.”1

---

## **AI Exploration and Implementation Are Mushrooming**

* 40% of companies globally have reported they are using AI within their company
* Another 42%are exploring the use of AI technologies in their business
* Over 50% of U.S. companies with more than 5,000 employees currently use AI. This number grows to 60% for companies with more than 10,000 employees.

[*Exploding Topics*](https://explodingtopics.com/blog/companies-using-ai)

---

## **AI Democratization Defined**

AI democratization is commonly defined as providing AI technology access to non-technical users. The definition can also include the provision of “user-friendly resources such as pre-built algorithms, intuitive interfaces and high-performance cloud computing platforms.”2 The goal is to enable in-house developers who lack AI development expertise to create machine learning (ML) applications and other AI-driven software, and to embed AI functionality into business-processes applications.

There is a caveat, however.

There must be guardrails or rules of the road, if you will, set and enforced by the enterprise. Most IT experts would agree that not every employee automatically gets or is granted on-demand access to AI. Enterprise AI implementation requires policies and protocols that stipulate who can access data and other assets based on their role. This process needs to detail the “reading in” and “reading out” of employees as they join or leave the organization.

## **AI Governance**

![A diagram showing the risks associated with AI democratization.](https://www.coresite.com/hubfs/blog%20images/body/Democratization%20of%20AI/risk%20framework%20from%20NIST%20copy%202.webp)

At the center of the framework is governance: The overarching aims are risk reduction, AI training, impact assessment and human/AI teaming. Follow the link below to find details on Map, Measure and Manage elements of NIST’s framework.   
Source: [NIST AI Risk Management Framework Playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/)

 

ChatGPT was launched in late 2022. By January 2023, ChatGPT had become what was then the fastest-growing consumer software application in history, gaining over 100 million users in two months.3 The rapid adoption of ChatGPT spurred the release of numerous competing products such as Copilot, Gemini, Grok and others.

The breakneck rate at which these products have been officially and unofficially implemented has outpaced many organizations’ abilities to develop governance policies. An ISACA (Information Systems Audit and Control Association) [Generative AI 2023 Pulse Poll](https://www.isaca.org/about-us/newsroom/press-releases/2023/ai-policies-are-low-use-is-high-and-adversaries-are-taking-advantage-says-new-ai-study) found that “many employees at respondents’ organizations are using generative AI, even without policies in place for its use. Only 28% of organizations say their companies expressly permit the use of generative AI, only 10% say a formal comprehensive policy is in place, and more than one in four say no policy exists and there is no plan for one. Despite this, over 40% say employees are using it regardless – and the percentage is likely much higher given that an additional 35% aren’t sure.”4

IBM defines AI governance as “the processes, standards and guardrails that help ensure AI systems and tools are safe and ethical. AI governance frameworks direct AI research, development and application to help ensure safety, fairness and respect for human rights. Governance also aims to establish the necessary oversight to align AI behaviors with ethical standards and societal expectations so as to safeguard against potential adverse impacts.”5

 As AI implementation continues to expand, it’s imperative that organizations develop, communicate and enforce rules of the road to ensure the appropriate use of AI. This will enable:

* Gaining the efficiencies, innovation and other benefits of the evolving technology
* Mitigating negative consequences such as intellectual property infringement, inaccuracies due to the use of flawed data or models and/or illegal or unethical use of AI

One way your organization might begin this process is by reviewing policies that were defined for the [democratization of data](https://hbr.org/2023/11/5-pillars-for-democratizing-data-at-your-organization), using them as guides for AI governance policies.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has developed an [Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf) as well as other [AI-related documents](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) to help guide your process. ISO/IEC 42001 has also developed an AI management system standard, providing organizations with a framework to establish, implement, maintain, and improve AI management systems, focusing on responsible and ethical AI development and use.

IT consulting and services provider Infosys offers advice on establishing control for data, AI models and usage and consumption. In a blog by Sunil Senan, SVP of Infosys, their [three steps to building data and AI governance](https://www.apmdigest.com/first-3-steps-building-data-and-ai-governance) are:

* Outline an organization-wide strategy
* Establish an operating model
* Operationalize the data and AI governance framework

We encourage you to follow the link provided to get a full understanding of the approach, which is based on principles of responsible AI use: trust, ethics, privacy, compliance and security.

## **AI Democratization Potential Benefits and Challenges**

Like all technologies, AI presents organizations and end users with a mix of benefits and challenges. When discussing AI democratization, key benefits and challenges include:

Benefits

* Increased employee productivity
* Enhanced idea generation, content creation and innovation
* Better and faster data analysis
* More informed business forecasting
* Improved risk management

Challenges

* Evaluating the pros and cons of implementing AI based on specific use cases
* Preventing access to AI models, data and tools by bad actors
* Preventing development of biased models and/or malicious model modification
* Minimizing the potential for intellectual property infringement or inaccuracies
* Minimizing the potential for leveraging AI as a cyberattack surface to access, hijack or damage internal networks, information or infrastructure
* Preventing shadow IT – i.e., the use of any software, hardware or IT resource used on an enterprise network without the IT department’s approval knowledge or oversight
* Ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements such as HIPAA, the U.S. Privacy Act of 1974, GDPR, California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and other state consumer and data privacy acts as well as additional industry-specific regulations regarding the protection of sensitive data

## **Critical Factors for Enterprise AI Implementation Success**

As high-density computing goes, most current applications don’t get much more demanding than AI. For instance, on average, a ChatGPT query uses nearly 10 times as much electricity to process as a Google search.6 According to Lucas Beran, Research Director at Dell’Oro Group, “The average rack power density today is around 15 kW/rack, but AI workloads will dictate 6 - 120 kW/rack to support accelerated servers in close proximity."7 And Goldman Sachs Research forecasts AI will drive a 165% increase in data center power demand by 2030.8

This will require substantially more power and cooling capacity in data centers. Beyond an environment supporting very high-density computing, successful implementation of AI applications will depend on:

* Training and upskilling for business users and developers not yet familiar with AI basics
* Rapid, secure interconnection between users and cloud-, premises- and partner-based applications and data stores
* Physically secure and cyber-secure facilities and IT equipment
* AI usage monitoring to ensure compliance with organizations’ AI governance policies

Increasingly, organizations are finding it impractical, inefficient and very costly to meet these requirements – particularly the escalating infrastructure demands – in on-premises deployments. Furthermore, the costs for implementing AI in the cloud can be higher than desired, especially after models have been trained and during [inferencing](https://research.ibm.com/blog/AI-inference-explained), the process of running live data through a trained AI model to make a prediction or solve a task. All of this contributes to a growing trend to move AI workloads to colocation data centers.

## **Colocation Becoming a Preferred Choice for AI Hosting**

Among organizations’ reasons for hosting their IT hardware, software and critical overall operations in colocation facilities are the need for:

* Robust, secure, redundant infrastructure expressly designed to support high-density computing
* Resilient, low-latency connectivity environments (from cloud to edge) including inter-site connectivity that enables virtually unlimited dynamic scalability and the ability to deploy distributed workloads
* Ability to rapidly access and transport massive volumes of data
* 24/7 onsite availability of expert staff to help with planning, implementation, monitoring and remote hands services
* Reduced total cost of operations

The rapid evolution of AI and its application to nearly every aspect of business and life means that AI governance policies will need to keep pace to ensure the integrity of new applications and capabilities. It also means the infrastructure requirements to support this evolution will need to keep pace, which is an additional reason to host your AI, IT assets and applications in a high-performance colocation environment.
