## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272)Abstract

### Background

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming health education by enabling personalized, adaptive, and scalable approaches that may enhance aspects of health literacy. Despite rapid adoption, comprehensive synthesis of AI tools’ impact on health literacy as social innovation is limited. Understanding these effects guides educators, developers, and policymakers in designing potentially effective, inclusive, and ethical AI interventions. This review examines generative AI models, chatbots, and adaptive learning systems in supporting health literacy globally.

### Methods

A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Literature was identified primarily through PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. Connectedpapers.com was used exclusively as a citation chasing tool, performing both backward and forward reference searches to identify thematically linked studies not captured by database searches. All records retrieved via Connected Papers were subjected to the same eligibility criteria as database-sourced studies, covering publications from 2000–2025. A total of 75 peer-reviewed empirical and theoretical studies focusing on AI tools for health literacy and social innovation were included. Titles, abstracts, keywords, and full texts were screened using predefined criteria. Data were managed and de-duplicated using Zotero. Screening and eligibility decisions were recorded in Excel spreadsheets. Thematic synthesis was conducted manually. PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S checklists were used to ensure transparent reporting.

### Results

AI research in health education was minimal until 2020 but rose sharply from 2021, peaking in 2023–2024 with generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT). Of the 75 included studies, 68 (90.7%) were co-authored by two or more researchers, 54 (72.0%) were published as Open Access, and review articles dominated with 41 studies (54.7%), while empirical research was limited, highlighting moderate to weak evidence. Research focused on personalized AI tools and learning effectiveness, with limited exploration of ethics, technical barriers, or social innovation. Findings suggest that AI interventions may improve readability, metacognitive engagement, cultural accessibility, and learner autonomy in the short term, particularly when multifaceted. However, evidence for long-term behavior change and real-world impact is sparse, indicating caution in generalizing results. Challenges include algorithmic bias, digital inequity, and lack of transparency, emphasizing the need for inclusive, equity-driven AI strategies.

### Conclusion

AI-powered tools have potential to support health literacy and learner-centered innovation, while contributing to social impact. Multifaceted, adaptive interventions may offer greater benefits than single-tool approaches. Findings provide preliminary guidance for standardized training, AI literacy integration, and policy frameworks, while acknowledging the current limitations in evidence, generalizability, and long-term outcomes.

**Keywords:**Artificial intelligence (AI), Health education, Health literacy promotion, Personalized learning tools, Digital health education, Systematic literature review

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272)Background

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful catalyst for innovation, particularly within healthcare and education [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR1)]. As a defining pillar of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, AI enhances operational efficiency and enables personalized, data-driven interventions [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR2), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR3)]. While considerable attention has been devoted to AI’s role in clinical diagnostics and administrative automation [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR5)], its pedagogical applications in health education remain comparatively underexplored [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR6)]. Increasingly, AI is being recognized not merely as a technological tool but as a driver of social innovation, capable of expanding access to reliable health information, supporting individualized learning pathways, and advancing health literacy across diverse populations [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR7), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR8)].

Recent advances in personalized AI technologies, such as intelligent tutoring systems [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR9)], conversational health agents [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR10), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR11)], wearable health monitors [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR8)], and AI-driven diagnostic tools, including PathAI and Zebra Medical Vision [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR12)], have generated new opportunities for promoting health literacy through interactive and multilingual content delivery. These innovations have proven particularly effective in enhancing knowledge retention, facilitating early intervention, and empowering individuals to engage in preventive self-care [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR13)].

Social Innovation (SI) is conceptualised as new or improved strategies, practices, and models that address unmet social needs and generate positive, equitable, and sustainable societal change. In health education, SI emphasises inclusivity, accessibility, and the empowerment of individuals and communities through tools that reduce health disparities and enhance health literacy. Positioning AI as a form of SI allows examine not only the functional capabilities of AI-based learning tools but also their broader societal impact. This includes their potential to democratize access to health information, support culturally responsive learning, and address systemic inequities in digital health education [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR10)].

Global partnerships between major technology firms and healthcare organizations, such as Microsoft Azure’s collaborations with Isomorphic Labs, exemplify the growing commitment to deploying AI-powered education platforms on a broader scale [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR14), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR15)]. Collectively, these initiatives reflect a paradigm shift towards accessible, context-sensitive, and user-centered health education models, further reinforcing AI’s transformative role in fostering socially impactful learning environments [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR16)].

Building on the foundational role of AI in health education, emerging technologies now offer unprecedented opportunities to enhance health literacy through personalized, multilingual, and culturally responsive learning experiences [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR9), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR10)]. AI-powered tools, including intelligent tutoring systems, health-focused chatbots, wearable health devices, and diagnostic platforms, have demonstrated strong potential in enhancing knowledge retention, facilitating early diagnosis, and promoting self-care, particularly among digitally underserved populations [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR8), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR13)]. These tools leverage real-time data to deliver interactive and adaptive content tailored to diverse user needs.

AI plays a growing role in addressing systemic health inequities by adapting educational content to different languages, literacy levels, and cultural backgrounds [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR17)]. Through features such as voice-assisted interfaces and context-aware feedback mechanisms, these technologies facilitate comprehension and engagement among users with varying levels of digital proficiency [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR8)].

Beyond information delivery, AI actively shapes health behavior through data-driven messaging and intelligent recommendation systems that support informed decision-making and preventative care [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR16)]. Interactive chatbots and virtual assistants also provide ongoing motivation through timely, personalized guidance [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR18)].

Building on these advancements, recent research highlights the emergence of AI-intelligentized assistants, systems that extend beyond content delivery to provide empathetic, contextual, and adaptive interactions. These assistants include AI mental health companions and virtual health coaches guiding users in lifestyle, nutrition, and preventive care [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR19)]; conversational AI chatbots for interactive guidance [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR20)]; emotionally intelligent systems that respond to user emotions and sustain engagement [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR21)]; adaptive learning platforms tailored to individual knowledge levels; and AI-powered wearable devices providing real-time feedback [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR22)]. Their use in health education and behavioral promotion is further supported by systematic reviews of AI-driven virtual assistants in physical activity and preventive health contexts. Collectively, they enhance health literacy, support engagement, and promote equitable access to health education, particularly for vulnerable or digitally underserved populations. However, realizing the full potential of these innovations requires sustained attention to ethical safeguards, algorithmic transparency, and user-centered design to foster trust, inclusivity, and responsible adoption [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR23), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR24)].

Despite notable progress in AI-driven health education, several structural and ethical barriers persist, constraining its effective and equitable deployment. Chief among these is the persistent digital divide, which limits access to AI-based educational tools among marginalised populations [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR7), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR25)]. Disparities in digital literacy and baseline health knowledge further shape users’ engagement with, and trust in, AI-generated content [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR26), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR27)]. Ethical challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and misinformation, complicate the integration of AI within educational contexts [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR28), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR29)]. Exacerbating these challenges is the lack of standardised evaluation frameworks and the limited empirical evidence on the educational outcomes of AI interventions [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR12), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR23)]. While AI technologies have shown considerable promise in areas such as diagnostics and predictive modelling [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR30)], their educational utility, particularly in influencing health behaviours and promoting literacy, remains under-examined. Few studies have systematically assessed the effectiveness, ethical viability, and contextual relevance of AI-powered educational interventions. Given the growing reliance on digital platforms for the dissemination of health information, there is a pressing need for rigorous research that investigates the role of AI in public health education. In response, this study undertakes a systematic examination of AI applications in health education, with particular emphasis on their capacity to enhance health literacy.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272)Research aims

Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews) guidelines [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR31)], this study seeks to generate actionable insights and policy-relevant recommendations that facilitate the effective integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into health education tools. The ultimate goal is to offer scalable, personalized, and context-sensitive solutions for promoting health literacy across diverse populations.

This review adopts the perspective of Social Innovation (SI), understood as a transformative approach that extends beyond technological advancement to create positive societal outcomes. The study not only evaluates the educational effectiveness of AI-driven health tools but also highlights their potential societal benefits, including improving access, addressing disparities, and empowering diverse learner populations. The review is structured around the following four core objectives:_RO1._ To identify the most widely adopted AI-driven personalized learning tools in health education, with an emphasis on their functionalities, implementation contexts, and pedagogical characteristics._RO2._ To evaluate the effectiveness of these tools in enhancing health literacy by synthesizing findings from experimental, applied, and empirical studies._RO3._ To investigate the ethical and technical challenges associated with AI applications in health education, and to propose evidence-based recommendations to address these concerns._RO4._ To explore current research gaps in the deployment and evaluation of AI-powered interventions for health education.

The structure of this paper is as follows: next section outlines the research methodology; then descriptive results and a thematic synthesis of the selected studies are presented; the following section offers a critical discussion of key findings, identifies research gaps, and outlines directions for future inquiry; and finally the last section concludes with the main takeaways and implications for AI-enhanced health education.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272)Method

To ensure methodological rigor and academic transparency, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted, guided by the structured methodology proposed by Behera et al. [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR32)]. This approach was selected for its comprehensive, replicable, and transparent framework for identifying, analyzing, and synthesizing relevant literature on AI applications in health education. Concurrently, the PRISMA 2020 statement was adhered to document the review process and enhance clarity and transparency in reporting. The combined application of these frameworks ensured a structured and rigorous methodology for identifying, screening, and synthesizing research focused on AI-driven tools in health education and literacy. The SLR was implemented in four principal stages: (1) planning and protocol design; (2) identification and screening; (3) eligibility assessment using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria; and (4) data extraction, analysis, and synthesis.

### Step 1: planning and conducting the review protocol design

In the initial phase of the study, a comprehensive and structured search strategy was developed following the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) framework proposed by Behera et al. [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR32)]. The review protocol guided the identification, selection, and organization of studies on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in health education and literacy, with a particular emphasis on social innovation. The search was conducted across three leading academic databases, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and PubMed, which are widely recognized for their coverage of peer-reviewed literature in the fields of health, education, and computer science [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR33)].

The search strategy employed a well-defined set of keywords aligned with the study’s core objectives. These included terms such as “Artificial Intelligence”, “Personalized AI-Driven Learning Tools”, “Health Education”, “AI in Education”, “Health Promotion”, “Health Literacy”, “Digital Health”, “Personalized Health Education”, “Social Innovation”, “AI for Social Innovation”, “Ethical Issues”, “Personalized Learning Tools”, and “Chatbots”. Boolean operators (AND, OR) were applied to combine keywords effectively, and the search was restricted to the title, abstract, and keyword fields to maximize relevance and precision.

Subject filters were applied within each database as follows:

Scopus: Computer Science, Medical Sciences, Health Professions, and Social Sciences.ScienceDirect: Health Sciences and Education.PubMed: Medical Education and Digital Health Technologies.

The search was limited to studies published between January 2000 and June 2025, ensuring the inclusion of both foundational and contemporary research. This timeframe allowed for a holistic understanding of the evolving integration of AI in health education and its alignment with digital transformation trends. Although AI technologies in health and informal education date back several decades, practical adoption of AI tools within formal health education settings accelerated in the early 2000s, driven by advancements in intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, and natural language processing capabilities. Documented uptake in medical curricula began emerging after 2000, as highlighted by Li and Wu [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR34)], rendering this period an appropriate baseline for the review. This rigorous search protocol ensured that the included studies were aligned with the review’s conceptual scope and methodological rigour, enabling a focused and replicable analysis.

To enhance transparency, documentation and reproducibility, complete search strings for each database were documented according to PRISMA-S guidelines. The final searches were conducted between May 10 and June 15, 2025. A detailed record of all search strings, field restrictions, and limits is included in Appendix A (PRISMA-S Table).

### Step 2: screening and selection process

Following the initial search, data were managed and de-duplicated using Zotero, a widely recognized open-source reference management tool that facilitates transparent data handling, supports de-duplication of bibliographic entries, and enables structured organization, tagging, and collaborative screening. Using Zotero’s duplicate detection feature, 153 duplicate records were automatically identified and removed. Screening and eligibility decisions were recorded in Excel spreadsheets, and thematic synthesis was conducted manually. Additionally, 98 records were automatically excluded based on pre-applied database filters, including non-English publications, conference abstracts, editorials, book chapters, and duplicate records detected through automated de-duplication tools, resulting in 820 records subjected to title and abstract screening. The screening process was conducted in two structured phases:

#### Initial screening

Titles and abstracts were assessed to exclude irrelevant studies, particularly those unrelated to AI in health education, health literacy, or personalized AI-driven learning tools.

#### Full-text review

Remaining articles were evaluated in full against the inclusion and exclusion criteria outlined in Step 3.

### Qualitative analytical framework

To ensure transparency, validity, credibility, replicability, and interpretive rigor, the included studies underwent a structured thematic analysis. Two reviewers independently coded qualitative data extracted from the studies, identifying recurring patterns, themes, and subthemes relevant to AI-driven health literacy interventions. Discrepancies in coding were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached, with a third senior reviewer consulted when needed to arbitrate. This process ensured systematic, transparent, and credible analysis, guiding the descriptive synthesis while enhancing the validity of the qualitative appraisal.

The screening and data extraction were conducted systematically: titles and abstracts were assessed against predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria, full texts were evaluated for eligibility, and data were extracted using a structured matrix.

All reviewers underwent training in systematic review methodology, including calibration on a pilot sample to ensure consistency. Discrepancies at any stage were resolved through discussion, and a third senior reviewer acted as an arbiter when consensus could not be reached. This dual-review process ensured methodological rigor and transparency, with minor subjective judgments representing a potential limitation.

Following these procedures, the included studies underwent qualitative appraisal for methodological quality. To ensure transparency and interpretive rigor, the methodological quality of the included studies was appraised qualitatively rather than through standardized scoring systems. Given the heterogeneity of designs (descriptive, survey-based, and quasi-experimental), formal risk-of-bias instruments (e.g., JBI, RoB 2, AMSTAR 2) were not applied. Instead, two reviewers independently examined each study for methodological clarity, transparency of data collection and analysis, and alignment with the review objectives. Discrepancies were discussed until consensus was achieved. This qualitative appraisal guided the descriptive analysis and thematic synthesis phases by assigning greater interpretive weight to studies demonstrating robust design and transparent reporting.

To ensure comprehensive coverage and mitigate potential keyword or disciplinary bias, the Connected Papers platform was used on 15 June 2025 as a citation chasing tool, performing both backward and forward reference searches to identify thematically linked studies not captured by database searches. Five seed papers were selected based on high citation impact and relevance to AI-driven health education and literacy [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR1), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR8), [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR39), [95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR95), [105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR105)]. For each seed paper, both forward and backward citation tracing were conducted using the co-citation graph, yielding eight additional records. All records were manually screened against the predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria. After full-text evaluation, four studies met al.l criteria and were included in the final synthesis [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR35)–[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR38)], while four were excluded due to insufficient methodological detail or lack of educational focus. All titles, screening notes, and inclusion/exclusion decisions are documented in the screening log (Appendix B, CSV format) to ensure transparency and replicability (see Figs. [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Fig1), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Fig2), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Fig3) and [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Fig4)).

In each Connected Papers network diagram, the studies positioned on the right-hand side represent those included in the final synthesis, while the studies displayed on the left-hand side are related works that did not meet the inclusion criteria but were identified as thematically relevant during citation chasing. This visual distinction clarifies the relationship between included and excluded studies and improves the interpretability of the search and selection process.

### Step 3: inclusion and exclusion criteria

To ensure methodological consistency and relevance, a clear set of inclusion and exclusion criteria was applied during the full-text screening phase.

#### Inclusion criteria

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they were published in peer-reviewed academic journals ranked Q1 or Q2 according to Scimago Journal Rankings (scimagojr.com). This restriction was applied to ensure the inclusion of studies with high methodological rigor, validated research designs, and robust peer-review processes. Focusing on Q1 and Q2 journals prioritizes reliable and high-impact evidence, enhancing the credibility and consistency of the review findings. Only articles written in English and published between January 2000 and June 2025 were considered, capturing both foundational and contemporary developments in AI. Eligible studies focused on the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in health education or the promotion of health literacy through personalized AI-driven learning tools. Research addressing ethical, technological, or accessibility challenges within AI-enabled health education was also included. Accepted study types comprised empirical studies, conceptual frameworks, mixed-methods research, and systematic or scoping reviews that contributed meaningfully to understanding how AI technologies, such as chatbots, machine learning algorithms, large language models (LLMs), or adaptive learning systems, are designed and implemented to enhance personalized digital health education.

#### Exclusion criteria

Studies not written in English, not peer-reviewed, or failing to meet standards of academic quality and transparency were excluded. In line with Tranfield et al. [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#CR39)], conference proceedings, book chapters, editorials, theses, dissertations, and all forms of grey literature were also excluded. The exclusion of grey literature was deliberate to ensure methodological rigor, reliability, and transparency, as such sources often lack formal peer review and standardized reporting, which may introduce bias, limit replicability, and reduce overall evidence quality. Additionally, studies focusing exclusively on clinical applications of AI (e.g., diagnostics, decision support systems, or treatment planning) without an explicit educational component were excluded. Articles lacking sufficient methodological detail, those unavailable in full text, or those published outside the defined timeframe (2000–2025) or in journals not ranked Q1 or Q2 were also excluded. Ultimately, only studies that fully aligned with the review’s central focus on AI-enabled health education and literacy were retained for final analysis.

A total of 1,071 records were initially retrieved from Scopus, ScienceDirect, and PubMed. Following the removal of 153 duplicates and the exclusion of 98 entries based on language and document type, 820 records remained for title and abstract screening. After a rigorous full-text eligibility assessment in accordance with the defined criteria, 75 studies were ultimately included in the final synthesis, 71 identified through database searches and four through Connectedpapers.com. ### Step 4: data extraction, analysis, and synthesis

Following the final selection of eligible studies, essential information was systematically extracted and organized into a structured data matrix. Extracted data encompassed authorship, publication year, country of origin, study objectives, research methodology (qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, or review), target population, educational setting, type of AI application, and reported outcomes related to health education and health literacy. Special attention was given to ethical, technical, and social issues addressed in the studies.

This dataset formed the foundation for a thematic analysis, through which the research team identified recurrent patterns, emerging insights, and notable gaps in the current literature. The thematic synthesis was structured around four core dimensions: (1) types and features of personalized AI-driven learning tools; (2) their effectiveness in improving health literacy; (3) ethical, technical, and accessibility challenges; and (4) research gaps and methodological limitations. The entire synthesis process was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, ensuring transparency, methodological rigor, and replicability. The results of this synthesis are presented in the subsequent Results section.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272)Results

### Descriptive analysis

The descriptive analysis of publishing trends on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in health education and healthcare systems between 2000 and 2025 reveals a clear temporal evolution in research focus. Between 2000 and 2019, fewer than five relevant papers were published per year, indicating that AI had not yet been conceptualized as an instructional or pedagogical tool in health education. A substantial increase emerged from 2021 onward, with publication activity peaking in 2024 (see Fig.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Fig6)). This surge aligns with the global adoption of generative AI technologies, particularly AI chatbots and intelligent tutoring systems, across academic and clinical education contexts.

Fig. 6Growth trend of publications on artificial intelligence in health education (2000–2025).Source: Author’s analysis based on data retrieved from the Scopus database

#### Temporal distribution of publications

The analysis of 75 eligible studies (Fig.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Fig7)) shows that no studies met the review criteria before 2020, with the first qualified papers appearing that year. A sharp increase was observed during 2023–2025, accounting for 85% (_n_ = 64) of the total studies. The yearly distribution indicates a clear growth in research activity over time. Only 2.67% of the studies were published in 2020 and 4% in 2021, reflecting limited early attention to the topic. The proportion increased to 8% in 2022 and 16% in 2023, showing gradual academic engagement. The peak occurred in 2024, with 40% of all studies published that year, demonstrating strong research momentum. Although the share slightly declined to 29.33% in 2025, it still reflects a high level of productivity compared to earlier years. This trend corresponds to the emergence of tools such as ChatGPT, signaling the early phase of AI integration in health curricula, primarily through pilot initiatives and adaptive learning platforms. These findings suggest that AI supports learner engagement, personalized feedback, and skill acquisition in clinical reasoning and decision-making. From a psychological perspective, technological readiness and perceived usefulness appear to enhance both institutional adoption and student motivation, reflecting a shift toward learner-centered pedagogy that fosters autonomy and adaptive skill development.

#### Authorship patterns and collaborative dynamics

The analysis of authorship patterns among the 75 included studies reflects a clear tendency toward collaborative research (see Table[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Tab2)). Specifically, 90.7% (_n_ = 68 of 75) of publications were co-authored by two or more researchers, whereas only 9.3% (_n_ = 7 of 75) were single-author studies. This predominance of multi-author works suggests that AI research in health education is inherently interdisciplinary, often requiring expertise across health sciences, educational theory, artificial intelligence, computer science, and data analysis.

Such collaboration may positively influence the design and implementation of AI-driven educational interventions, as studies involving diverse expertise tend to produce more comprehensive and pedagogically sound health literacy tools. Multi-author studies frequently report improved learner engagement, enhanced comprehension of complex health topics, and more effective integration of AI tools into curricula, compared to single-author studies. Additionally, team-based scholarship enables robust validation of AI models, addressing both technical reliability and ethical considerations. The limited number of individual-authored studies highlights potential challenges in visibility and independent innovation, particularly in multi-institutional contexts. General, these patterns underscore the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration for advancing evidence-based AI interventions in health education and their psychological outcomes.

#### Journal quality and source distribution

Analysis of the publication sources indicates that the majority of the 75 included studies were published in high-impact journals, with 72% (_n_ = 54 of 75) appearing in Q1 journals and 28% (_n_ = 21 of 75) in Q2 journals, based on Scimago Journal Rankings (see Table[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825272#Tab3)). The research primarily addressed medical education, digital health, and interdisciplinary care, with BMC Medical Education (_n_ = 12) and JMIR Medical Education (_n_ = 6) being the most frequent outlets.

This distribution demonstrates that AI in health education is largely investigated in journals with rigorous peer-review standards and high methodological quality. High-impact publications provide robust evidence that AI-driven interventions can enhance health literacy, improve learner engagement, and support adaptive learning processes. For example, studies in BMC Medical Education (_n_ = 12) reported measurable gains in students’ comprehension of complex health topics using AI-powered chatbots or personalized learning platforms. Similarly, JMIR Medical Education studies (_n_ = 6) documented improvements in metacognitive skills, self-directed learning, and autonomous problem-solving among health profession students exposed to AI-based tools. args.summary:
This is a systematic review published in BMC Medical Education (2025) examining the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for social innovation in health education, specifically focusing on promoting health literacy through personalized AI-driven learning tools. The review was conducted by Dina Mansour Tbaishat and Maha Waleed Elfadel, following PRISMA guidelines.

**Methodology:** A systematic literature review was conducted across Scopus, ScienceDirect, and PubMed (2000-2025). Connectedpapers.com was used as a citation chasing tool. After screening 1,071 initial records, 75 peer-reviewed studies (Q1/Q2 journals) were included in the final synthesis.

**Key Findings:**
- AI research in health education was minimal until 2020 but rose sharply from 2021, peaking in 2023-2024 with generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT).
- Of the 75 included studies, 68 (90.7%) were co-authored by two or more researchers, 54 (72.0%) were Open Access, and review articles dominated (54.7%), while empirical research was limited.
- Research focused on personalized AI tools and learning effectiveness, with limited exploration of ethics, technical barriers, or social innovation.
- AI interventions may improve readability, metacognitive engagement, cultural accessibility, and learner autonomy in the short term.
- Evidence for long-term behavior change and real-world impact is sparse.
- Challenges include algorithmic bias, digital inequity, and lack of transparency.

**Study Objectives (RO1-RO4):**
1. Identify most widely adopted AI-driven personalized learning tools in health education.
2. Evaluate effectiveness of these tools in enhancing health literacy.
3. Investigate ethical and technical challenges.
4. Explore current research gaps.

**Conclusions:** AI-powered tools have potential to support health literacy and learner-centered innovation with social impact. Multifaceted, adaptive interventions may offer greater benefits than single-tool approaches. The review provides preliminary guidance for standardized training, AI literacy integration, and policy frameworks, while acknowledging current limitations in evidence, generalizability, and long-term outcomes.

# Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Social Good: Building the Future with AI

![Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Social Good: Building the Future with AI](https://ebbamkciiebhjmsfroii.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/project-images/Blogs/1770213129554-Artificial_Intelligence_AI_for_Social_Good_Building_the_Future_with_AI.jpg)

In an era where technology evolves at breakneck speed, artificial intelligence (AI) emerges as a transformative force with the potential to drive positive societal change. While discussions often highlight risks like job displacement and ethical dilemmas, this series shifts the focus to AI's role in fostering equity, justice, and sustainability. As we enter 2026, AI adoption in the nonprofit sector is accelerating, with 47% of professionals already saving 1-3 hours weekly through AI tools, and 56% planning further adoption. This momentum underscores AI's shift from experimental pilots to core infrastructure in social good organizations.

"AI for Social Good: Building the Future with AI" explores how AI can tackle global challenges such as climate change, healthcare inequities, education access, and poverty alleviation. With the global AI market projected to contribute $15.7 trillion to the economy by 2030, nonprofits and impact-driven entities are leveraging AI for enhanced efficiency and measurable outcomes. This optimistic lens positions AI not as a threat, but as a collaborative partner for humanity, especially in sustainable development goals (SDGs).

Beyond the tech, this series centers on the people shaping and benefiting from AI. It inspires corporate leaders, investors, policymakers, philanthropists, and changemakers to harness AI ethically for societal benefit. Through case studies, expert analyses, and actionable insights, we provide a blueprint for integrating AI into corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives, impact investing strategies, and nonprofit partnerships.

As you explore this content, remember: AI for social good is a collective call to action. In 2026, with agentic AI systems expected to handle 15% of routine decisions autonomously by 2028, it's time to redefine technology's role in serving humanity. Join us in creating a world where AI amplifies equity and sustainability.

## Key Trends in AI for Social Good in 2026

Drawing from recent reports and projections, here are updated trends shaping AI's impact:

| Trend | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| **AI as Organizational Infrastructure** | Nonprofits are institutionalizing AI, reshaping job descriptions and workflows. Larger organizations (revenues over $1M) adopt AI at twice the rate of smaller ones, saving 15-20 hours weekly on administrative tasks. This addresses the "AI gap," urging shared resources for equitable access. |
| **Agentic and Green AI** | Agentic AI evolves from tools to autonomous agents, reducing burdens in mission delivery like workforce development and climate resilience. Sustainability is key, with AI projected to cut global emissions by 3.2-5.4 gigatonnes of CO₂ equivalent annually by 2035, offsetting data center energy demands doubling by 2030. |
| **Ethical Governance and Sovereignty** | Updates to standards, like Social Current's COA Accreditation revisions in spring 2026, emphasize human oversight and transparency. Sovereign AI initiatives reduce foreign tech dependence, with investments like India's $1.25B in multilingual models. |
| **Impact on SDGs** | AI boosts healthcare (market to $504B by 2032 with 90-95% diagnostic accuracy), education (personalized learning for 250M out-of-school children), and agriculture (precision farming reducing 40% crop losses from pests). |
| **Funding and Collaboration** | 63% of funders prioritize collective outcomes, with 86% advising stringent data hygiene for AI tools. "Outcome-as-a-Service" appeals to 48% of nonprofits, shifting from SaaS to AI-driven results. |

To optimize for search and provide value, here are answers to frequently searched queries:

| --- | --- |
| **What is AI for social good?** | AI for social good refers to using artificial intelligence to address societal challenges, promoting equity and sustainability. In 2026, it's integral to nonprofit operations, with 77% of companies exploring AI. |
| **How can corporations partner with nonprofits on AI initiatives?** | Corporates can fund AI tools, provide expertise, or co-develop projects. Impact investing in AI yields returns through CSR alignment, with 84% of professionals emphasizing human-centered personalization. |
| **What are the ethical considerations in AI for nonprofits?** | Key issues include bias mitigation, data privacy, and human oversight. New regulations like the EU AI Act and South Korea's AI Basic Act (effective 2026) guide responsible use. |
| **How does AI impact job creation in social sectors?** | While AI may displace 85 million jobs by 2025, it creates 97 million new ones, netting 12 million gains, focusing on AI literacy and ethical roles. |
| **What trends should investors watch in AI for social impact?** | Look for green AI, agentic systems, and sovereign AI. Projections show AI reducing disaster costs by $70-110B annually by 2050. |

## Highlights

*   •The healthcare sector is a significant driver of climate change. 
*   •More sustainable AI practices can mitigate the environmental impact while harnessing AI's potential. 
*   •Robust policy and governance are crucial for responsible and sustainable AI in healthcare. 
*   •Collaboration among stakeholders can foster innovation and drive sustainable AI adoption. 

## Abstract

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare has revolutionized the industry, offering significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and patient outcomes. However, the increasing adoption of AI systems also raises concerns about their environmental impact, particularly in the context of climate change. This review explores the intersection of climate change and AI in healthcare, examining the challenges posed by the energy consumption and carbon footprint of AI systems, as well as the potential solutions to mitigate their environmental impact. The review highlights the energy-intensive nature of AI model training and deployment, the contribution of data centers to greenhouse gas emissions, and the generation of electronic waste. To address these challenges, the development of energy-efficient AI models, the adoption of green computing practices, and the integration of renewable energy sources are discussed as potential solutions. The review also emphasizes the role of AI in optimizing healthcare workflows, reducing resource waste, and facilitating sustainable practices such as telemedicine. Furthermore, the importance of policy and governance frameworks, global initiatives, and collaborative efforts in promoting sustainable AI practices in healthcare is explored. The review concludes by outlining best practices for sustainable AI deployment, including eco-design, lifecycle assessment, responsible data management, and continuous monitoring and improvement. As the healthcare industry continues to embrace AI technologies, prioritizing sustainability and environmental responsibility is crucial to ensure that the benefits of AI are realized while actively contributing to the preservation of our planet.

*   ### [A design framework for operationalizing trustworthy artificial intelligence in healthcare: Requirements, tradeoffs and challenges for its clinical adoption](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1566253525008747)

2026, Information Fusion  Show abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds great promise for transforming healthcare, particularly in disease diagnosis, prognosis, and patient care. The increasing availability of digital medical data, such as images, omics data, biosignals, and electronic health records, combined with advances in computing, has enabled AI models to approach expert-level performance. However, widespread clinical adoption remains limited, primarily due to challenges beyond technical performance, including ethical concerns, regulatory barriers, and lack of trust. To address these issues, medical AI systems must align with the principles of Trustworthy AI (TAI), which emphasize human agency and oversight, algorithmic robustness, privacy and data governance, transparency, bias and discrimination avoidance, and accountability. Yet, the complexity of healthcare processes (e.g., screening, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment) and the diversity of stakeholders (clinicians, patients, providers, regulators) complicate the integration of TAI principles. To bridge the gap between TAI theory and practical implementation, this paper proposes a design framework to support developers in embedding TAI principles into medical AI systems. Thus, for each stakeholder identified across various healthcare processes, we propose a disease-agnostic collection of requirements that medical AI systems should incorporate to adhere to the principles of TAI. Additionally, we examine the challenges and tradeoffs that may arise when applying these principles in practice. To illustrate the discussion, we focus on cardiovascular diseases, which is a field marked by both high prevalence and active AI innovation, and demonstrate how TAI principles have been applied and where key obstacles persist.    
*   ### [Adversarial artificial intelligence in radiology: Attacks, defenses, and future considerations](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211568425001044)

2025, Diagnostic and Interventional Imaging  Show abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming radiology, with applications spanning disease detection, lesion segmentation, workflow optimization, and report generation. As these tools become more integrated into clinical practice, new concerns have emerged regarding their vulnerability to adversarial attacks. This review provides an in-depth overview of adversarial AI in radiology, a topic of growing relevance in both research and clinical domains. It begins by outlining the foundational concepts and model characteristics that make machine learning systems particularly susceptible to adversarial manipulation. A structured taxonomy of attack types is presented, including distinctions based on attacker knowledge, goals, timing, and computational frequency. The clinical implications of these attacks are then examined across key radiology tasks, with literature highlighting risks to disease classification, image segmentation and reconstruction, and report generation. Potential downstream consequences such as patient harm, operational disruption, and loss of trust are discussed. Current mitigation strategies are reviewed, spanning input-level defenses, model training modifications, and certified robustness approaches. In parallel, the role of broader lifecycle and safeguard strategies are considered. By consolidating current knowledge across technical and clinical domains, this review helps identify gaps, inform future research priorities, and guide the development of robust, trustworthy AI systems in radiology.

![AI](https://www.refontelearning.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,width=1200,quality=75,fit=scale-down/https://assets.refontelearning.com/images/hero/ai-for-good-how-machine-learning-is-driving-social-impact.webp)

# AI for Good: How Machine Learning is Driving Social Impact

Thu, Sep 25, 2025

An algorithm that can predict floods days in advance, giving communities time to evacuate. A computer vision model that identifies signs of diabetic eye disease before symptoms worsen. These are not science fiction – they are real examples of AI for Good in action. *Artificial intelligence for social impact* is about leveraging machine learning and data to address global challenges in healthcare, education, the environment, and beyond. Rather than focusing solely on profit, **AI for Good** initiatives use technology to improve lives and create positive change.

In fact, an estimated 87% of AI projects never make it out of the lab into widespread used. Bridging this gap between ideas and impact requires skilled people who can apply technical know-how to social causes. In this article, we’ll explore how machine learning is driving social impact across key sectors and how you can get involved in this rewarding field. Along the way, we’ll highlight how **Refonte Learning** and similar programs provide the training to turn your AI skills into tools for good.

## Understanding AI for Good and Its Importance

**AI for Good** refers to the intentional use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to solve social, environmental, and humanitarian problems. It aligns with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals by applying advanced algorithms to issues like poverty, health, and climate change. [Machine learning](https://www.refontelearning.com/blog/how-to-become-a-machine-learning-engineer) models can sift through huge datasets – medical records, satellite images, social media trends – to uncover patterns and insights that humans might miss. The power of *machine learning for social impact* lies in its ability to process data at scale and provide decision-makers with actionable information.

For example, predictive models can warn of natural disasters earlier or pinpoint communities most in need of resources, helping organizations be better prepared. Importantly, AI for Good emphasizes ethical AI development. That means ensuring fairness, transparency, and privacy in AI systems so that these technologies benefit society equitably. Organizations worldwide, from nonprofits to tech companies, are investing in AI for social good projects, and skilled professionals are needed to build and deploy these solutions. **Refonte Learning** recognizes this demand and offers programs that teach not only core data science skills but also their application to real-world problems, preparing learners to contribute confidently to high-impact AI projects.

## Transforming Healthcare and Saving Lives

One of the most profound impacts of AI for Good is in healthcare. Machine learning algorithms are augmenting how doctors diagnose and treat patients, often with life-saving results. For instance, Google’s DeepMind has developed models that can analyze retinal scans and detect over 50 eye diseases – potentially preventing blindness by enabling earlier treatment. Similarly, AI systems can examine X-rays or MRIs faster than human radiologists, flagging subtle anomalies like early-stage tumors that might be overlooked.

In public health, *machine learning in healthcare* helps predict disease outbreaks by analyzing patterns in epidemiological data. This was evident during the COVID-19 pandemic, where AI models aided in forecasting infection spikes and optimizing resource allocation. Another remarkable example is an AI-driven diagnostic tool for diabetic retinopathy now used in countries with limited specialist. By catching this diabetes-related eye disease early, the tool has protected the vision of thousands in underserved communities. Professional training programs now include hands-on projects with medical datasets and healthcare use cases to prepare future data scientists for these roles. Such practical training means graduates are ready to join hospitals, health tech startups, or global health organizations using [AI](https://www.refontelearning.com/study-and-internship/ai-developer-program) to save lives. In all these applications, human oversight remains key – AI assists clinicians, making healthcare more proactive and precise without replacing the compassionate care that professionals provide.

## Protecting the Environment and Tackling Climate Change

Another critical domain for AI for Good is environmental conservation and climate action. Around the world, **machine learning** models are helping protect our planet by monitoring ecosystems, optimizing resource use, and fighting climate change. For example, scientists and conservationists use AI to analyze satellite imagery and sensor data to track deforestation and illegal activities in real time. The Rainforest Connection project places solar-powered listening devices in forests, using *AI-driven sound analysis* to detect chainsaw noises and alert rangers to poaching or illegal logging as it happen. This technology empowers swift action to protect endangered rainforests and wildlife.

In climate science, AI improves predictions of extreme weather and natural disasters. Advanced models can forecast hurricanes, floods, and wildfires with greater lead time and accuracy, allowing communities to prepare and potentially saving lives. Machine learning also aids renewable energy management – for instance, optimizing wind farm output by predicting wind patterns, which has increased energy production forecasting accuracy by about 20% according to DeepMind’s research. Additionally, AI supports agriculture through precision farming: analyzing soil and weather data to advise farmers on planting and irrigation, thereby boosting yields and food security. These environmental applications show how *AI for Good* can contribute to sustainable development. Educational programs often integrate real-world projects into the curriculum. For example, learners might work on a capstone project to analyze climate data or use computer vision to recognize pollution in waterways. By engaging with these scenarios, participants gain experience in applying AI to environmental challenges. Through knowledgeable mentorship, they learn best practices for building models that are both effective and ethically responsible, ensuring technology is used to protect our planet for future generations.

## Advancing Education and Social Equity

Education is another area seeing benefits from *AI for social good*. Machine learning is personalizing learning experiences and extending educational opportunities to underserved communities. A great example is the use of intelligent tutoring systems that adapt to each student’s needs. One such system, Carnegie Learning’s MATHia platform, uses reinforcement learning algorithms to tutor students in math and adjust in real time to their problem area. This personalized approach has proven especially helpful for learners with dyslexia or dyscalculia, who might struggle in traditional classrooms.

Beyond individualized tutoring, AI is also enabling global access to education. Language processing algorithms power real-time translation tools, breaking down language barriers so students and professionals worldwide can learn from the same resources. In regions with teacher shortages, AI-driven apps provide basic tutoring in reading and math, ensuring children don’t fall behind. Importantly, AI in education can help identify at-risk students early. Predictive models analyze factors like attendance and grades to alert educators when a student may need extra support. By intervening sooner, schools can improve graduation rates and promote equity. Forward-thinking training programs encourage educators and technologists to collaborate on these kinds of applications. For instance, a course project might involve building a simple recommendation engine for educational content or analyzing school data to improve resource allocation. Through such interdisciplinary learning, professionals from different backgrounds – teachers, data scientists, software developers – can upskill and work together to design AI solutions that broaden opportunities. The result is a workforce adept at using AI not just for commercial gain, but to uplift communities and expand access to knowledge.

## Actionable Tips: How You Can Contribute to AI for Good

* **Build a Strong Foundation:** Start by developing solid data science and machine learning skills. Courses and internships from **Refonte Learning** provide hands-on experience with AI tools and techniques, giving you the confidence to tackle social impact projects.
* **Join AI for Good Communities:** Engage with organizations like global AI-for-good initiatives, hackathons, or local data-for-good meetups. Collaborating on volunteer projects is a practical way to apply your skills and learn how AI can help nonprofits and communities.
* **Work on Meaningful Projects:** Focus your portfolio on projects that have a humanitarian or social angle. For example, try creating a model that analyzes public health data or an app that improves accessibility for people with disabilities. Mentors in the industry often guide students through such capstone projects, which you can showcase to potential employers.
* **Stay Informed and Ethical:** Keep up with news and research on *AI ethics* and responsible AI guidelines. Understand bias in algorithms and the importance of transparency. By following ethical best practices, you ensure your AI solutions are fair and trusted by the communities they serve.
* **Collaborate Across Disciplines:** AI for Good often requires teaming up with experts in healthcare, environment, education, or social sciences. Be open to learning from domain experts and end-users. Effective communication and empathy will help you design AI solutions that truly address real-world needs.

## Conclusion

Machine learning for social impact is more than a buzzword – it’s a growing movement that is already transforming lives around the world. From saving patients in hospitals to protecting endangered environments, *AI for Good* shows the power of technology when paired with purpose. Demand for professionals with these skills is rising, creating exciting career opportunities. Platforms like [**Refonte Learning**](https://www.refontelearning.com/) make this journey accessible by blending AI training with real-world impact projects. Now is the time to gain those skills, join the movement, and help shape a future where AI benefits all of humanity. Take the leap into AI for Good and let your work be part of the solution.

## FAQs

**Q:** What does AI for Good mean?  
**A:** AI for Good refers to using artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies to solve social, environmental, or humanitarian challenges. It means applying AI beyond commercial purposes to benefit society, such as improving healthcare, education, and sustainability in ethical and inclusive ways.

**Q:** How can I start a career in AI for social impact?  
**A:** Begin by building your data science and machine learning skills through courses or programs like those at **Refonte Learning**. Practical experience is crucial, so work on projects that tackle real-world problems and consider internships or volunteering with organizations that use AI for social good. Networking with professionals in the field can also open doors and mentorship opportunities.

**Q:** What are some examples of AI being used for social good?  
**A:** There are many inspiring examples. In healthcare, AI helps doctors detect diseases early by analyzing medical images. For environmental protection, machine learning models monitor deforestation and track wildlife to combat poaching. In education, AI-powered tutoring systems personalize learning for students with diverse needs. These applications show how AI can positively impact various sectors.

**Q:** Why are ethics important in AI for Good?  
**A:** Ethics are crucial because AI systems can affect people’s lives in significant ways. AI for Good initiatives must ensure fairness, transparency, and privacy so that solutions do not unintentionally harm or discriminate against any group. Emphasizing ethics builds trust and makes sure the technology truly benefits communities. Ethical training helps professionals design responsible AI solutions.

**Q:** How does Refonte Learning help in pursuing AI for Good?  
**A:** **Refonte Learning** offers training and internship programs that cover the technical skills needed for AI careers and focus on real-world applications. Students learn by working on projects that often align with social impact, guided by experienced mentors. This practical, purpose-driven approach prepares graduates to contribute to AI for Good projects with confidence and competence.

# The United Nations’ leading platform on Artificial Intelligence

AI for Good is **unlocking AI’s potential to serve humanity**.

AI for Good is organized by ITU in partnership with over 50 UN Sister Agencies and co-convened with the Government of Switzerland.

[About us](https://aiforgood.itu.int/about-ai-for-good/)

### **Join the #AIforGood movement**

Bringing stakeholders together to harness AI’s potential to solve global challenges.

### Solutions & Knowledge​

Developing AI standards to create more opportunities for innovation and digital transformation worldwide.

### Skills & Capacity​ ​

Empowering people with the tools and knowledge to thrive in the AI era—nurturing the future wave of innovators.

### Standards & Policy​

Examines the current state of AI standardisation and explore the evolving role of emerging AI technologies and standards in supporting policy frameworks and innovation.

args.summary:
The webpage is the official homepage of the ITU's "AI for Good" initiative, described as the United Nations' leading platform on Artificial Intelligence. It is organized by ITU in partnership with over 50 UN sister agencies and co-convened with the Government of Switzerland. The initiative's mission is unlocking AI's potential to serve humanity.

The site highlights three main areas of action:
1. **Solutions & Knowledge**: Includes the flagship AI for Good Global Summit (next scheduled for the week of 21-25 June 2027 in Geneva, Switzerland), the UN AI Resource Hub, the AI for Good Global Commission, the Innovation Factory (startup pitching and accelerator platform), the Neural Network community (60K+ AI enthusiasts), the Canvas of the Future art contest, the Film Festival, the Impact Awards, and the Discovery Webinar Series.
2. **Skills & Capacity**: Includes the AI Skills Coalition (free AI courses), the Impact Initiative (aiming to raise CHF 20M+ annually for developing countries), the AI Readiness Framework, Innovate for Impact, the Robotics for Good Youth Challenge (40+ countries), Machine Learning Challenges, and the Young AI Leaders Community.
3. **Standards & Policy**: Includes the International AI Standards Exchange (ISO/IEC/ITU), ITU-T AI Focus Groups, AI Multimedia Authenticity Standards collaboration, the UN Inter-agency working group on AI (co-led by ITU/UNESCO), the Global Initiative on AI for Health (with WHO/WIPO), the Global Initiative on AI for Food Systems, the Global Initiative on Resilience to Natural Hazards, and Quantum for Good.

Upcoming events listed include: an ITU AI/ML Challenge launch (10 Sep 2026), an AI Readiness hackathon in Saudi Arabia (14 Sep 2026), a webinar on ML for ICT infrastructure detection (15 Sep 2026), a webinar on computational opportunities for climate modelling (23 Sep 2026), and multiple Innovation Factory pitching sessions through late 2026.

### **Who Are These Users? The 5 Stages of AI Maturity**

Not everyone is a power user. In 2026, we can clearly see five distinct “personas” emerging, ranging from those who actively avoid the tech to those building their entire business on top of it.

1. **The AI Skeptics**  
   *Who they are:* The “wait-and-see” group.  
   *The Vibe:* Caution over curiosity.  
   *The Insight:* These users aren’t necessarily anti-technology; they are anti-risk. They have seen the headlines about hallucinations and data privacy leaks, and they simply don’t trust the output yet. For them, the potential efficiency isn’t worth the headache of fact-checking every single sentence. They are waiting for the guardrails to get stronger before they jump in. Generative AI statistics prove this: [53% of consumers](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-09-03-gartner-survey-finds-53-percent-of-consumers-distrust-ai-powered-search-results0) still distrust AI-generated search summaries and results.
2. **The AI Novices**  
   *Who they are:* The “willing but blocked.”  
   *The Vibe:* FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out) without the know-how.  
   *The Insight:* These people aren’t Skeptics, as they actually want to use AI. The problem is they don’t know where to start. They are often paralyzed by the “blank prompt” problem or are waiting for permission from their company to use these tools officially. They are sitting on the sidelines, watching colleagues zoom past them, just waiting for someone to show them the ropes.
3. **The AI Experimenters**  
   *Who they are:* The “Life Hackers” and corporate dabblers.  
   *The Vibe:* “Let’s see what this button does.”  
   *The Insight:* For this group, AI isn’t a workflow; it’s a sporadic superpower. They use it for specific, isolated tasks, like planning a vacation itinerary, rewriting a tough email, or brainstorming party ideas. They haven’t fully integrated it into their daily grind, but they keep the tab open just in case they need a quick creative boost.
4. **The AI Practitioners**  
   *Who they are:* The daily drivers.  
   *The Vibe:* “I can’t imagine doing this manually anymore.”  
   *The Insight:* This is the workforce of the future. For Practitioners, AI has moved from a novelty to a necessity. It is their always-on copilot for coding, drafting reports, and analyzing messy spreadsheets. They have moved past the “wow” factor and are focused purely on utility, using the tech to clear the boring parts of their day so they can go home on time.
5. **The AI Experts**  
   *Who they are:* The “Data Pioneers.”  
   *The Vibe:* Automation over conversation.  
   *The Insight:* While everyone else is busy chatting with a bot, Experts are busy building systems that run themselves. They have moved beyond simple prompts to deploying “autonomous agents”—software that plans, executes, and finishes complex workflows without human hand-holding. They aren’t just using AI to do their job faster; they are redesigning what “the job” actually looks like.

Nearly half say it’s likely; more than a third say it’s certain. At the other end of the spectrum, only **2%** are sure they won’t invest more, and just **1%** are actively cutting Gen AI budgets.

Put simply: resistance is fading. Key artificial intelligence statistics show that by 2026, AI agents won’t be limited to innovation teams or IT pilots. They’ll be deployed across more departments, doing more real work, and quietly reshaping how organizations operate.

## How Does Adopting Generative AI Impact Businesses in Terms of Benefits and Risks?

* [74% of executives](https://www.capgemini.com/be-en/insights/research-library/generative-ai-built-for-business/) believe the benefits of Gen AI outweigh the risks. Such a positive outlook is fueled by numerous [Generative AI examples](https://masterofcode.com/blog/generative-ai-examples) across different sectors.
* [Institutions using artificial intelligence](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2023/11/02/new-study-validates-the-business-value-and-opportunity-of-ai/) report an **18% boost** in customer satisfaction, productivity, and market share, with an average return of **$3.50 for every $1 invested**.
* [63% of organizations](https://inthecloud.withgoogle.com/roi-of-generative-ai/dl-cd.html) have experienced business growth from GAI, with **77%** reporting elevated leads and client acquisition, and **71%** creating new products or services.
* **70%** of companies reveal grown revenue and **61%** higher conversion rates.
* **45%** of firms have seen doubled employee performance due to GAI, with **59%** citing surged accuracy and **54%** experiencing faster time to market.
* **85%** of enterprises indicate escalated user engagement and **80%** higher buyer satisfaction due to Generative AI insights.
* **56%** of establishments register improved security posture, with **82%** better able to identify threats and **71%** seeing faster resolution times.
* [Veteran organizations](https://www.ibm.com/thought-leadership/institute-business-value/en-us/report/generative-ai-customer-service) employing artificial intelligence for over three years document a **25% reduction** in cost per contact, with a **30% drop** for those applying [Generative AI](https://masterofcode.com/generative-ai-development-company) to one or two customer service use cases. These figures are further validated by real-world deployments. According to data verified through Master of Code Global’s [AI Pilot Program](https://masterofcode.com/ai-pilot) for an Energy Sector client, facing a massive backlog of 4,300 blocked invoices per month, automating their workflows yielded immediate results. The deployed pilot solution managed to close 98.68% of conversations without human or portal redirect, automatically saving 99.35% of valid meter readings directly to SAP, while maintaining a 93% positive customer satisfaction rate.
* [78% of businesses](https://www.accaglobal.com/gb/en/professional-insights/technology/digital-horizons.html) report increased flexibility and higher service quality, while **72%** see strengthened sustainability, transparency, and regulatory compliance. **52%** of them witness enhanced internal efficiency and streamlined processes.

### Generative AI Statistics: Return on Investment

* [50% of executives](https://go.thoughtspot.com/white-paper-economist-ai-future-of-financial-services.html) consider achieving ROI a primary success measure for intelligentization projects.

* Current GenAI scenarios showing **26–34%** ROI include customer service, productivity, sales and marketing, digital commerce, back-office processes, and manufacturing.
* **86%** of companies using this intelligent technology in production report revenue growth, with an increase of **6%** or more in annual income.
* **84%** of organizations move an AI-based use case from concept to launch within six months, with the rise in profits reported within a year of deployment.

### Risks and Challenges: Fair Gen AI Statistics

Transparency follows closely, highlighted by **47%** of respondents as a top-three ethical priority.
* [Novice users](https://www.ibm.com/thought-leadership/institute-business-value/en-us/report/generative-ai-customer-service) are concerned about information security (**44%**) and the difficulty of integrating LLMs into processes (**38%**). Veteran users worry about meeting social responsibility (**46%**) and environmental sustainability goals (**42%**), as well as ensuring compliance with customer data regulations (**40%**).
* **79%** of executives say artificial intelligence ethics is important, but fewer than **25%** have implemented formal ethical practices.

  + Microsoft’s travel article mistakenly listed a food bank as a destination
  + A Texas A&M professor gave his class “Incomplete” grades after ChatGPT incorrectly claimed their essays were AI-generated
  + Bard (now Gemini) falsely stated that the James Webb Space Telescope took the first exoplanet photo
  + Bard and Bing Chat inaccurately reported a ceasefire in the Israel–Hamas conflict

## What Is the Impact of Generative AI on Workplace Dynamics?

An interesting fact is that around [61.5% of companies](https://www.jasper.ai/the-prompt/ai-business-trend-report) with 11–1,000 employees are using artificial intelligence in their workflows. What’s even more compelling is that **75%** of users aim to automate tasks by implementing this technology.

Most workers believe Gen AI usage can boost productivity, especially those who interact with models frequently. [82% of professionals using it weekly](https://www.pymnts.com/study_posts/millennials-most-likely-to-see-workplace-perks-from-genai/) report increased efficiency. * AI-experienced workers say innovative systems manage overwhelming workloads (**92%**), boost creativity (**92%**), and help focus on crucial processes (**93%**). - **Pilot Purgatory is Real:** 88% of organizations use AI in at least one function, but 62% remain stuck in experimentation, with only 7% having fully scaled AI across the enterprise.

## Business Impact

- 79% of executives say AI ethics is important, but fewer than 25% have implemented formal ethical practices.

- 78% of employees bring their own AI tools to the workplace.
- Only 39% of personnel have received proper AI training.
